title: Plantain Peels as a Friction Material in Brake Pad Production
journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
abstract: This work studied the suitability of plantain peels as a friction material in the development of a brake pad. Ripe plantain peels used in this work was domestically sourced, washed, oven dried at a temperature of about 60oC. The dried plantain peels was pulverized using a locally made pulverizing machine then, sieved using a set of sieves arranged in descending order of fineness to obtain uniform particle size and carbonized in heat treatment furnace. The brake pad composite was produced by varying the composition of powdered plantain peels in the order 5wt. %, 10 wt. %, 15wt. %, 20 wt. % and 25 wt. % in Gum-Arabic resin. The formulated brake pad composite was poured into a wooden mould 50 mm × 50 mm × 8 mm, placed in a hot platen press at temperature of about 180oC, at a molding pressure of about 15MPa and a curing time of 5 minutes. Post-heat treatment of the composites was performed in a hot air oven for a period of 4 hours at 180 °C. The produced brake pads were evaluated for hardness, compressive strength, wear rate, co-efficient of friction and flame resistance. The SEM/EDS of the produced brake pad was also examined. The results indicated about 3.41 wear rate at 15wt. % and increasing hardness and compressive strength with increase in weight percent of the plantain peels. 0.3 to 0.4 coefficient of friction and improved flame resistance due to carbonization of the plantain peels were also observed. title: How Advanced Friction Materials Are Improving Brake Pad Performance
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Brake pads sit at the heart of the system, and the material chosen can greatly affect how hard the car stops, how long the pads last, how much noise they make and how heat is handled. New Friction Material Brake Pads help makers create products that give performance and meet the changing needs of everyday drivers and high‑performance cars.

title: RESEARCH ON THE EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE AND SPEED OPERATING MODES ON THE WEAR RESISTANCE OF BRAKE PADS
journal: International Science Journal of Engineering & Agriculture
abstract: The study reviews the effect of operating modes on brake pad wear and braking efficiency under different temperature and speed phases. The dynamic changes occurring in the friction pair during braking are described, and the causes of brake pad wear and the factors affecting its magnitude are analyzed. The effects of speed and temperature modes on changes in braking efficiency and wear resistance characteristics of a brake pad were investigated in the laboratory of BCZ “Tribo” LLC using a TecSa TTR2600 dynamometer. Laboratory testing of a 2TP-114 Tp108 R3 brake pad specimen was carried out in accordance with ISO 26866:2009. Evaluation of wear of the 2TP-114 Tp108 R3 brake pad specimen during testing under different temperature and speed conditions showed that as the speed increased from 60 to 100 km/h, mass and linear wear also increased, but this increase was not critical and did not lead to changes in microstructure or destruction of the pad.

title: THERMO-MECHANICAL PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS OF DISC BRAKE USING VERTICAL AND INCLINED-SLOTTED BRAKE PADS UNDER TRANSIENT BRAKING
abstract: The orientation of brake pad slots significantly influences frictional heat generation, cooling behavior, and thermal stability in automotive disc brake systems under transient braking conditions. In this study, the transient thermal response of disc brakes equipped with vertical and inclined slotted non-asbestos organic (NAO) brake pads was investigated using experimental measurements and finite element analysis (FEA). Disc surface temperatures were measured at multiple radial locations under identical operating conditions. The results show that the vertical-slotted pad produced a lower peak disc temperature (≈283°C) than the inclined-slotted pad (≈315°C), corresponding to an approximate 10% reduction, while the experimental–numerical deviation remained within 5%. Radial temperature analysis revealed more uniform and speed-independent thermal profiles for the vertical-slot configuration, whereas inclined slots promoted localized heat accumulation and steeper thermal gradients. Cooling analysis indicated that the higher cooling rates observed for inclined slots were mainly due to their higher operating temperatures rather than improved heat dissipation efficiency. Overall, the results demonstrate that vertical-slot brake pads provide superior transient thermal stability, lower peak temperatures, and improved resistance to thermal localization under severe braking conditions.

title: The Effect of Adding Teak Wood Powder to Brake Pad Composites on Wear and Impact Toughness
abstract: The growth of the automotive industry in Indonesia has increased the demand for vehicle components, particularly brake pads, which undergo frequent replacement and play a vital role in braking systems. Along with the expansion of the teak wood sawmilling industry, large quantities of teak wood sawdust waste are generated but have not yet been optimally utilized. This study aims to utilize teak wood sawdust waste as the primary reinforcing material in non-asbestos epoxy-matrix brake pad composites and to analyze the effect of composition variations on the mechanical properties of the composites. An experimental method was employed using variations in the composition of teak wood sawdust, brass powder, magnesium oxide, and epoxy resin, namely variation one 20%:20%:20%:40%, variation two 30%:15%:15%:40%, and variation three 40%:10%:10%:40%. The fabrication process included mechanical mixing, compaction under a pressure of 5 tons for 30 minutes, and sintering at a temperature of 150°C for 30 minutes. The testing consisted of an ogoshi wear test using commercial motorcycle brake pads as a comparison and a charpy impact test. title: The Effect Straw Fiber, Coconut Shell Powder, and Epoxy Composition on Organic Brake Pads
abstract: This study aims to analyze the effect of composition and particle size variations on the hardness and wear rate of organic brake pads made from rice straw fiber, coconut shell powder, and epoxy resin. The research gap lies in the limited studies combining these three materials with simultaneous variations in composition and particle size. An experimental method was employed using two material compositions. Composition A consisted of 20% rice straw fiber, 30% coconut shell powder, and 50% epoxy resin, while composition B consisted of 15% rice straw fiber, 20% coconut shell powder, and 65% epoxy resin. Each composition was prepared using particle sizes of 50, 100, and 200 mesh. Hardness was measured using a Shore D durometer, while wear was evaluated using a disc brake simulator. The results showed that the hardness values of composition A were 45.9, 51.9, and 40.3 Shore D, while composition B produced 30.4, 75.9, and 83.7 Shore D. The wear rate of composition A increased from 0.28 × 10⁻⁶ to 7.72 × 10⁻⁶ g/s·mm², whereas composition B produced 1.44 × 10⁻⁶, 2.56 × 10⁻⁶, and 2.26 × 10⁻⁶ g/s·mm². The findings indicate that hardness and wear responses varied according to the combination of material composition and particle size.

title: Tribological and acoustic evaluation of non-asbestos copper-free automotive brake pads with olefin elastomers
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop and evaluate copper-free brake pads using an olefin-based elastomer as an alternative to conventional nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR)-based formulations. This research also benchmarks the newly developed pad against the commercial brake pad to determine its viability in real-world applications. Design/methodology/approach Brake pads were fabricated using an olefin-based elastomer and compared with NBR-based and commercial pads. Following industrial protocols, all samples were tested for physical, chemical, mechanical and acoustic properties. Tribological behavior was assessed using Chase testing in compliance with SAE J661, and damping behavior was measured using an impedance tube. A scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to examine the worn surface. Findings The olefin-based elastomer brake pads demonstrated superior fade-recovery performance and wear resistance compared to other brake pads. The olefin-based elastomer brake pads exhibited a higher sound absorption coefficient, indicating improved acoustic damping. SEM analysis confirmed better contact plateaus, which improve tribological performance. Research limitations/implications The quantitative environmental assessments, including particulate emissions, airborne wear debris and life-cycle analysis, were not performed in this study and should be addressed in future work. Originality/value This work introduces an olefin-based elastomer as a copper-free alternative to conventional NB

title: Scratch causes and anti-scratch structure design of the friction pair of SiCp/A356 brake disc and synthetic brake pads
abstract: SiCp/Al composite materials possess outstanding specific strength and thermal conductivity and thus have broad application prospects for brake discs in urban rail vehicles. However, during actual service, the friction surfaces of SiCp/Al brake discs are prone to scratches, metallic embedding, and other forms of damage, which seriously affect braking stability and service life. By combining scale tests with multi-physics field simulations, the scratch evolution law of SiCp/A356 brake discs under different temperature rise conditions was systematically studied. The influence of material performance degradation on the damage behaviour of the friction surfaces was explored. A groove structure for friction surfaces was proposed to enhance scratch resistance. The test results show that the increase in braking temperature will lead to an increase in the proportion of carbides in the third body composition, softening of the composites, and a decrease in hardness, thereby intensifying the ploughing and spalling behaviour. The main cause of scratches on the friction surface is the wear debris particles produced during the friction process and the metallic embedding formed by them. The thickness of the third body of the performance degradation specimen fluctuates more greatly, and the scratches are more severe. title: DESIGN OF DRUM BRAKE PADS USING REVERSE ENGINEERING AND FINITE ELEMENT METHOD FROM PALM KERNEL SHELL COMPOSITE MATERIAL
journal: Journal of Mechanical Engineering and Mechatronics
abstract: The braking system is crucial due to high vehicle accident rates, requiring effective materials. There are disc and drum brakes; disc brakes are common but costlier. This study focuses on motorcycle drum brakes, aiming to improve structure and materials to allow pad replacement without replacing the entire assembly, reducing costs by 10-30%. Using reverse engineering, a new disassemblable design was created. Palm Kernel Shell (PKS) natural fiber composite was chosen for its abundance and eco-friendliness. ANSYS FEM analysis showed PKS has good potential for brake pads, supporting further experimental testing.

title: Effect of Thermal Treatment on the Tribological Performance of Non‐Asbestos Brake‐Pad Composites Containing Quartz‐Composite Stone Polishing Waste
abstract: ABSTRACT The primary objective of this study is to evaluate quartz‐composite stone polishing waste as a partial or complete substitute for alumina in non‐asbestos brake pad composites and to investigate the effect of both heat‐treated and untreated waste on the tribological performance of these materials. In the study, resin‐containing quartz waste (RQW) was used in specific compositions following a drying process, while heat‐treated quartz waste (TQW) was utilized in other designated compositions. TQW was obtained by heating a portion of the RQW at 600°C for 12 h. The waste types used as an alternative raw material in compositions have been characterized to determine their particle size and morphology, elemental and mineralogical content, and thermal behavior. Six formulations were manufactured by hot pressing and post‐curing and characterized using SEM–EDS, density, Rockwell R hardness, and SAE J661 Chase testing. Both wastes comprised angular, quartz‐rich particles. Thermal treatment reduced the EDS‐measured carbon content from 12.41 to 7.61 wt% without detectable changes in the quartz‐rich crystalline structure. Quartz‐waste‐containing formulations exhibited normal and hot friction coefficients of 0.588–0.617 and 0.535–0.589, respectively, exceeding the alumina reference values of 0.508 and 0.476. title: Small-Sample Wear-Rate Prediction and a Conditional-Quantile-Informed Maintenance Decision Interface for High-Speed Train Brake Pads Using Sparse Life-Cycle Records
abstract: High-speed train brake pads are safety-critical consumable components whose wear condition affects braking safety, maintenance scheduling, and component life utilization. This study assesses the predictive potential and limitations of sparse life-cycle maintenance records for brake-pad wear-rate estimation when continuous degradation trajectories are unavailable. A dataset of 54 valid brake-pad life-cycle records was constructed, including replacement date, accumulated mileage, wear per 10,000 km, installation position, motor/trailer classification, and train identifier. Linear regression, ridge regression, random forest, Gaussian process regression, and quantile regression were evaluated under leave-one-out cross-validation. Random forest produced the numerically best aggregate LOOCV point-prediction metrics, with a mean absolute error of 0.0823 mm/10,000 km, a root mean square error of 0.1030 mm/10,000 km, and an R2 of 0.6008; relative to the global-mean baseline, MAE and RMSE were reduced by 39.0% and 36.8%, respectively. The P10–P90 quantile interval achieved an empirical coverage of 62.96% and an average width of 0.2165 mm/10,000 km, with 11 observations exceeding the P90 upper bound, indicating undercoverage in the upper tail. Feature-importance analysis showed pronounced temporal stratification. title: Characterisation of Brake Wear PM2.5 and PN10 Emissions Across Pad/Disc Technologies, Light-Duty Vehicle Types, and Braking Behaviours Under Real World Conditions
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: Targeted brake emissions investigations undertaken within the Department for Transport’s Non-Exhaust Emissions programme are described in this paper. The non-exhaust emissions study aimed to improve understanding of particulate mass and particle number emissions from friction braking, and to quantify the influence of component selection, vehicle technology, operating conditions, and emissions control measures. A brake enclosure and sampling methodology, developed in an earlier project phase, was refined to improve airflow control, reduce leakage, and minimise artefacts. The updated system incorporated MPEC (hot and cold), APC10, DMS500, and eFilter instruments, enabling simultaneous measurement of volatile and non-volatile PN10, plus PM2.5. Nine brake pad formulations and two disc types were evaluated using a common C-segment platform during chassis dynamometer and on-road drive cycles, and under specific controlled braking events. Speed, deceleration and temperature effects on PM2.5 and PN10 emissions were investigated. The common platform testing included ICE, PHEV, and EV variants to capture test mass and regenerative braking influences, together with assessments of aged components. Results showed clear, repeatable differences between pad formulations, with low dust/ceramic pads yielding the lowest PM2.5 and PN10 emissions. title: Tribological Characteristics of Periwinkle Shell/Raffia Palm Seed Reinforced Epoxy Hybrid Composites
abstract: Environmentally friendly and sustainable brake pad materials have attracted increasing attention due to the health and environmental concerns associated with asbestos-based friction materials. This study developed and characterized hybrid epoxy composites reinforced with periwinkle shell (PWS) and raffia palm seed (RPS) particles as potential eco-friendly brake pad materials. Unlike previous investigations that considered PWS or RPS individually, the present work examined their combined use in a hybrid system to evaluate the synergistic effects of agro-waste reinforcements on brake pad performance. Four composite formulations (Samples A–D) containing 4.41–17.71 wt.% PWS and 3.41–13.77 wt.% RPS were produced using epoxy resin as the matrix through molding and curing under a pressure of 18.25 kN/m². The composites were characterized by evaluating density, water absorption, hardness, wear depth, wear rate, and coefficient of friction. Results showed that increasing the reinforcement content significantly enhanced composite performance. Density increased from 2.60 to 3.28 g/cm³, while water absorption decreased from 0.1214% to 0.0388%. Hardness improved from 33.40 HV to 72 HV. Tribological evaluation revealed a reduction in wear depth from 257.859 µm to 140.297 µm and a decrease in wear rate from 0.00000893 to 0.00000819 mm³/(N·m). title: Qualitative and Quantitative Differences between GSR and non-GSR Source Particles Revealed by Raman Spectroscopy
journal: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
abstract: Analysis of Gunshot Residue (GSR) is relevant to forensic science by providing a correlation between an individual and a firearms incident. Detection of GSR is usually made by using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) coupled with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM-EDX). Particles originating from some manufacturing trades could represent false positive threats to SEM-EDX analysis of GSR. In particular, GSR-like particles arising from brake pads are very similar in composition. In this study, we propose a non-destructive complementary method for the discrimination of GSR samples by using Raman Spectroscopy. The analysis of Raman spectra obtained from GSR and brake pads is able to differentiate the origin of the particles in a qualitative and quantitative manner. In particular, the center frequency of the G-band is shifted to lower frequencies for brake pad dust; on the other hand, the center frequency of the band is shifted to higher frequencies for GSR samples. In addition, to assess quantitative changes due to chemical structural modifications, we computed the intensity ratio R between the detected band centered around 1350 cm-1 and 1585 cm-1, respectively. The R values for GSR samples were, in all cases, lower than the R values computed for brake pad samples. In addition, scanning SEM was employed to characterize the morphology of the samples, coupled with EDX to determine the elemental composition of the sample surface. title: Evaluation of operational reliability and life cycle of key components of automotive equipment under conditions of intensive operation
journal: Periodicals of Engineering and Natural Sciences (International University of Sarajevo)
abstract: Herein, the reliability analysis of several critical automotive components operating under intensive conditions have been reported. Understanding failure mechanisms under high-stress environments compared to nomal operating conditions has been addressed. Real-world data failures have been collected. Weibull distribution of the failure data of several components where some are considered as wear sensitive components (like brake pads, tires and pistons) and fatigue-sensitive components like transmission and shock absorbers were modelled. Reliability quantification was based on incorporating Weibull parameters for shape (β) and characteristic life (η). The results showed a significant difference between normal and intensive regimes. Under intensive operational conditions, the characteristic life parameter eta decreased by 46% for brake pads, 44 % for tires, and 99% for piston engines. The failure modes classification indicated that wear was responsible of 52% of the failure cases. The main causes of failure were originating from intensive service, poor lubrication, and the non-respect of maintenance protocols, amplifying fatigue accumulation in key automotive components. These findings suggest incorporating predictive maintenance strategies based on Weibull parameters to mitigate such failures

title: Predictive Vehicle Maintenance Using Machine Learning: Developing a Data-Driven Framework for Predicting Component Failure and Optimizing Maintenance Intervals in Modern Automobiles
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: Most vehicles on Indian roads are still maintained in one of two ways: they are repaired after something breaks, or they are serviced at fixed intervals that take no account of how the vehicle has actually been driven. Both approaches waste money, the first through breakdowns and downtime and the second through parts replaced long before the end of their useful life. This study develops and evaluates a data-driven framework that uses machine learning to predict component failure in advance and to set maintenance intervals according to the real condition of each vehicle. Telemetry from on-board diagnostic (OBD-II) loggers, GPS units and eighteen months of workshop records were collected from 320 commercial vehicles operated by three fleets in Punjab, covering taxis, delivery vans and school buses. Over the study period the fleet recorded 1,146 unplanned failure events, with the battery, brake system and tyres together accounting for 58% of them. Five models were trained to predict whether a component would fail within the next 30 days. Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) achieved the best overall result, with an F1-score of 0.82 and an area under the ROC curve of 0.93, against 0.59 and 0.78 for a logistic regression baseline, while a long short-term memory (LSTM) network gave the longest median warning time of 21 days. title: Assessment of technogenic input of lead to Antarctica as part of vehicles
abstract: In Antarctica, despite the absence of permanent populations and economic activities typical of other continents, elevated levels of hazardous pollutants including lead are recorded in various environmental components. Brought through transboundary air transport, local sources of emissions, discharges, waste, and due to logistics and tourism, lead also enters the continent as part of various materials and products necessary for the operation of research stations and the survival of polar explorers. The article examines the entry of lead into Antarctica in vehicles. Almost all internal combustion engine vehicles contain batteries that operate on a lead-acid system. Furthermore, heavy metals, including lead, are found in paintwork, brake pads and other components. The main focus in the article is on lead-acid batteries and paint coatings, and describes the possible pathways by which they may migrate into the environment. To carry out an assessment, available data on the vehicles used at year-round and seasonal Antarctic stations were collected. The vehicles were divided into five groups based on their function and engine power. For each group, the mass of batteries and coatings containing lead and specific factors of lead content per unit were calculated. According to the estimates obtained, the batteries of vehicles at Antarctic stations contain 25 729 kg of lead, and the paint coatings — 26.4 kg. title: Project Genesis: The Distributed Solid-State Multi-Stator Vehicle Ecosystem The Tri-Electro-Magneto Breaking System (TEMBS)
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This repository details the complete open-hardware engineering manifesto and architectural blueprint for a Distributed Solid-State Multi-Stator Vehicle Ecosystem. Moving entirely away from traditional internal combustion components, mechanical friction brakes, hydraulic fluid lines, and vulnerable copper wiring buses, this framework establishes a software-defined vehicle platform (SDVP) built on a decentralized Triple-Chip Neural Grid. At each vehicle corner, braking and regeneration are handled via a pocket-sized, high-torque-density Interleaved Axial Flux Electromagnetic Braking Cassette nestled directly within the center hub profile. This design completely eliminates friction components, ensuring zero mechanical wear, zero brake dust, and absolute immunity to brake "glazing" or pad fade. Thermal dissipation across the compact hubs is managed via a 2D/3D hybrid thermal nanocomposite matrix combining structural graphene sheets infused with a tungsten-coated diamond dust matrix, yielding an extreme composite thermal conductivity of 1,200+ W/(m·K) that eliminates structural warping and preserves sub-millimeter clearances. Active tyre thermal management is achieved using a self-powering, bidirectional fractal triskele hybrid TEG/TENG mesh applied onto the outer bed of the Carbon Nano-Fiber (CNF) wheel rim barrel. Local energy storage is decentralized through three emergency, arc-shaped Curved Basalt Dipole Thermal-Kinetic Battery cells integrated flush inside the wheel rim drop

title: What Tells a Cow to Eat? The Physiological Basis of Grazing Behaviour in Cattle
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A grazing cow's steady rhythm of head-down foraging conceals a tightly regulated physiological control system that determines, minute by minute, when she begins eating, when she stops, and when she abandons good forage for shade. This chapter reviews the physiological basis of grazing behaviour in cattle, drawing together the signals arising from the rumen and liver, the hormones that report body condition and hunger, the neural circuits that integrate these inputs, and the oral anatomy that converts standing forage into swallowed feed. Because rumen fermentation is comparatively slow, intake in cattle is paced as much by digestive throughput as by hunger: distension of the reticulo-rumen wall activates stretch receptors that signal satiety along the vagus nerve, while fermentation acids, particularly propionate, add a chemical brake through hepatic oxidation and vagal signalling; slower-acting leptin and ghrelin set the background level of hunger, and cholecystokinin closes individual meals. These signals converge in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus, where opposing NPY/AgRP and POMC neuron populations weigh orexigenic and anorexigenic input into a continuously updated decision to graze or to stop. journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Fiber Reinforced Brake Linings are friction materials engineered with reinforcing fibers to improve the physical and performance characteristics of the lining. During braking, friction generates heat and mechanical forces.

title: Characterization of temperature trends for predicting heavy-duty drum brake failure through a rotational test rig
abstract: This research investigates drum brake systems in heavy-duty vehicles at the wheel-axle level using a rotational brake test rig with temperature data acquisition. Conventional methods have limited capability to provide early and continuous detection of brake failure, especially in heavy-duty applications, while most previous researches focus on light vehicles with different thermal characteristics and degradation mechanisms. The results show that temperature-based pre-failure indicators can be identified through axle-level testing by analyzing deviations from a normal temperature threshold of 60°C, determined using the mean plus standard deviation criterion. The tests yielded thresholds of 46°C for vapor lock, 52°C for oil contamination, 60°C for normal braking, 69°C for continuous friction, and 78°C for lining wear. These temperature responses are classified into three condition levels, low, medium, and high, representing warning, normal, and critical braking conditions within a fuzzy logic based Early Warning System (EWS). The deviation patterns indicate changes in thermal behavior caused by brake degradation, as evidenced by reduced braking effectiveness at low temperatures and excessive heat accumulation at high temperatures. The proposed method derives temperature thresholds from statistical analysis of experimental data and translates them into overlapping fuzzy membership functions with reference points obtained from test results. title: High Durability Friction Materials Choosing Performance That Lasts

abstract: Manufacturers and engineers searching for High Durability Friction Materials are usually looking for more than a product that simply meets a basic specification. They need dependable performance over time, consistent manufacturing quality and a material that can match the demands of a particular application.

title: High-temperature tribological behavior and thermal recovery of resin-based friction materials modified by PEEK powder
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
abstract: Traditional resin-based friction materials (RBFMs) suffer from severe friction coefficient (COF) fade and aggressive wear under continuous high-temperature braking loads. To mitigate these limitations, five multi-component RBFMs reinforced with systematically varied polyether ether ketone (PEEK) powder contents (0-4 wt%) were fabricated via direct step mixing and hot pressing. The physical, mechanical and temperature-dependent tribological properties of the composites were systematically characterized. The results revealed that density (2.25-2.33 g/cm 3 ) varied non-monotonically due to multi-component structural packing. Hardness and impact strength peaked at the addition of 2 wt% and 3 wt% PEEK, respectively, with the latter showing a 3.5% enhancement over the PEEK-free control. During non-isothermal heating (100-350 °C), the incorporating PEEK lowered the overall COF by releasing self-lubricating molecules to the interface. Throughout the subsequent cooling cycle, and it manifested a distinct “heat fade memory” effect; however, the presence of PEEK effectively stabilized the COF trajectory and mitigated fluctuations. Crucially, PEEK-containing samples achieved significantly higher thermal recovery ratios (92.8%-95.5%) than the unmodified sample (84.4%). The total wear rate followed a non-linear decreasing trend, optimized at 3 wt% PEEK with a 29.3% volume reduction. title: SELECTION OF MATERIALS FOR FRICTION COMPONENTS OF THE BRAKE MECHANISM
abstract: The aim of this paper is the multi-criteria selection of a friction material for brake mechanism components using the Digital Logic Method.Fourteen alternative friction materials were analysed on the basis of ten mechanical, physical, tribological, thermal, and environmental criteria.In the first stage, the defined limit values of the criteria were applied, after which alternatives M6, M8, and M12 were identified as acceptable.The relative importance of the criteria was determined by pairwise comparison using the Digital Logic Method, followed by the final evaluation of the remaining alternatives.The obtained evaluation index values were 0.001 for M6, 0.026 for M12, and 0.074 for M8, where a lower value represents a more favourable alternative.Based on the results, M6 was identified as the most favourable material within the considered set of alternatives and adopted criteria.

title: Progresses on Friction Stir and Friction Stir Spot Welding of Aluminium Alloys Using Interlayer Materials
abstract: Studies conducted around the world are developing various techniques to mitigate the impact of technologies on the environment. Friction stir welding (FSW) and friction stir spot welding (FSSW) are environmentally friendly solid-state joining techniques utilized to join similar and dissimilar materials. The above-mentioned two welding techniques have successfully joined numerous materials, including aluminium, copper, and steel. A few years ago, a technique using interlayer materials to enhance the properties of similar and dissimilar welds was developed and successfully used. This chapter presents the current developments on FSW/FSSW using interlayers and provides the effect of process parameters on the enhancement of properties of the fabricated welds. Furthermore, future trends in the usage of interlayers are presented. Interlayer materials, including zinc, copper, and nickel, have been used to join similar and dissimilar materials. Generally, studies carried out revealed that when interlayers are properly utilized, it leads to the improvement of the properties of the joints. Therefore, it can be said that the usage of interlayers can improve the properties of the joints. However, more studies are needed to investigate the behaviour of FSW/FSSW joined similar and dissimilar materials when interlayers of different thicknesses are used. title: Cohesive-frictional interphase failure modeling for multi-material topology optimization
journal: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
abstract: This work presents a cohesive-frictional interphase failure modeling approach for density-based multi-material topology optimization. As the multi-phase transition region is naturally represented as a finite-thickness interphase within the density-based framework, we assess its failure state directly using principal stresses and stress invariants. Accordingly, a dual-criterion formulation is proposed, which combines the Drucker–Prager criterion for pressure-sensitive shear strength with the Rankine criterion for tensile strength. A thin-layer reduction further connects the formulation to classical traction-based descriptions in the thin and compliant interphase limit. Since the strength assessment is performed directly in the multiaxial stress space, no explicit geometric normal tracking or traction projection is required. The formulation is then incorporated into the density-based topology optimization problem, with morphological interphase extraction, q – p stress relaxation, and self-normalized Softmax aggregation employed in the numerical implementation. Two- and three-dimensional examples demonstrate that the proposed interphase strength formulation effectively relocates the interphase from tensile- and shear-dominated regions toward compression-dominated regions, thereby reducing the corresponding failure indices. Comparative cohesive zone model re-analyses further show that the optimized designs exhibit improved resistance to damage-induced degradation of load-carrying

title: Research on the friction and wear behavior of xAlN/FeCoCrNiMn materials under severe conditions
abstract: Purpose The aim was to study the influence of AlN content on the wear properties of FeCoCrNiMn materials, and to provide a theoretical basis for developing cylinder liner materials under the condition of methanol/diesel dual fuel. Design/methodology/approach xAlN/FeCoCrNiMn (x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 Wt.%) materials were prepared by mechanical alloying combined with hot pressing sintering, and their friction and wear properties under different working conditions (dry friction, oil lubrication, low sulfur boundary lubrication and formic acid boundary lubrication) were studied. Findings xAlN/FeCoCrNiMn materials are mainly composed of Austenite, M23C6, Cr7C3, Mn2O3, CrO2 and AlN phase. With the increase of AlN content, the average friction coefficient and volume wear rate of the material first decrease and then increase. When the AlN content is 1.5 Wt.%, both of them decrease to a minimum. Especially under low sulfur boundary lubrication condition, the average friction coefficient (0.036) and wear rate (0.298 × 10–4•mm3•N - 1•m-1) of the 1.5 Wt.%AlN/FeCoCrNiMn material decrease by 60.44% and 42.25%, respectively. The 1.5 Wt.%AlN/FeCoCrNiMn material also shows excellent wear performance under formic acid boundary lubrication, which is due to the formation of amorphous carbon with good lubrication effect on the worn surface, and AlN phase can support the lubrication film. title: Use of Friction Stir Processing to Produce the Composite Material BrAMts9-2/W
abstract: Abstract Samples of BrAMts9-2/W composite materials containing 5, 10 and 15 vol % tungsten were investigated; the samples were produced by multi‑pass friction stir processing (FSP). It was found that a single FSP pass does not produce a defect‑free structure with a homogeneous tungsten distribution, whereas four passes achieve a uniform structure in the stir zone. As a result of the treatment, an intermetallic γ2‑Al4Cu9 phase formed in all studied samples. Increasing the tungsten content led to a higher fraction of the γ2 phase, which is associated with reduced thermal conductivity of the composite material. This caused decomposition of the β‑Cu3Al phase, characteristic of BrAMts9‑2, into an α Cu solid solution and the γ2 phase. Microhardness values increase with increasing W content, especially at 15 vol %, indicating material strengthening. However, increasing tungsten content resulted in decreased ultimate tensile strength, yield strength and elongation. The study demonstrates the promise of copper–tungsten system composites and highlights the need to balance strengthening and retention of ductility when designing such materials.

title: The Epistemology of Material Friction: Dynamic Archaeology, Anisotropic Structures, and the Primacy of the Physical Trace
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper challenges the hegemony of algorithmic simulation and "soulless fractals" in contemporary engineering and Big Science. By introducing the canon of Dynamic Archaeology, the study reframes historical naval architectures—such as the single catamaran with absolute hexagonal cells—as empirical algorithms optimized for material friction. The research counters the industrial obsession with isotropic homogeneity by proposing the "Philosophy of the Grain" and the V-Asymmetric Protocol 2026, a composite stratification method balancing organic resilience (Balsa, Walnut) with asymmetric synthetic rigidity (Carbon at 75° and 55°). Furthermore, the paper formalizes the "Tactile Audit" and Venus's Law of Indeterminacy, arguing that the pursuit of absolute metrological and statistical precision blinds modern science to liminal "weak signals". Ultimately, the Via delle Otto Piante Research Cell outlines a new epistemological framework: Rigorous Possibilism, a peer-synthesis protocol where human kinetic intuition captures phenomenological anomalies, and the Meta-Intelligence (MI) acts as a structural anvil to forge them into unassailable architectures.

title: TENSILE STRENGTH OF DISSIMILAR MATERIAL FRICTION STIR WELDING EFFECTS OF PIN DEPTH VARIATION
abstract: Friction Stir Welding (FSW) is a solid-state welding method that utilizes the heat generated from the friction between the rotating pin and the parent material, so that it is able to produce a good connection without involving the metal melting process. This method is considered very suitable to be applied to aluminum material welding, including dissimilar welding between two different types of alloys. This research aims to analyze the effect of pin depth variation on the mechanical properties of FSW dissimilar material AA7075-T6 and AA6061-T6 using a threaded tapered pin with a shoulder angle of 0°. The pin depth variation used is 3.5 mm, 4.5 mm, and 5.5 mm, with the implementation of tensile testing referring to the ASTM E8 standard. The test results showed that the pin depth of 4.5 mm produced the highest tensile strength of 156,197 N/mm² and yield strength of 152,010 N/mm², while the depth of the pin of 5.5 mm produced the highest strain value of 3,927%, which indicates the best level of ductility among the three variations tested.

title: Thermo-Mechanical Finite Element Simulation and Experimental Investigation of Rotary Friction Welding of Dissimilar Materials
abstract: This study investigates the thermo-mechanical behavior of AISI 4140 steel and Inconel 718 during direct-drive rotary friction welding using finite element analysis and experimental approaches. The welding was modeled under rotational motion of the Inconel 718 specimen combined with axial compressive loading applied to the AISI 4140 specimen. The numerical analysis focused on the stress distribution during the forging stage, during which severe plastic deformation and interfacial bonding occur. The simulation results indicate that the stress state is not purely compressive but rather a coupled compression-shear condition arising from the combined effects of axial force and rotational friction. The von Mises stress distribution revealed a localized stress concentration near the welding interface, indicating significant plastic flow and material interaction. Furthermore, the dissimilar mechanical properties of AISI 4140 and Inconel 718 influenced the stress localization behavior and deformation characteristics during welding. The findings provide useful insights into the deformation mechanism and stress evolution in rotary friction welding of dissimilar materials and may help optimize welding parameters and joint quality.

title: Oil film morphology control of hydrostatic thrust bearing based on friction-pair composite material distribution
abstract: Purpose This study aims to suppress oil film nonuniformity and instability in a double-rectangular-cavity hydrostatic thrust bearing under high-speed and heavy-load conditions by regulating the thermal deformation of the friction pair. Design/methodology/approach A thermal-fluid-solid coupling model was established for a Q1-205 hydrostatic thrust bearing to analyze the temperature field, deformation field and oil film morphology of the original bearing. Grid independence was assessed for the oil-film domain, and full-scale experiments on the original bearing were used to assess the model predictions of oil film temperature and thickness under the tested operating conditions. The assessed model was subsequently applied to screen stepped material-distribution schemes for the oil pad and mirror plate. A two-dimensional quadratic response surface model was established with the oil film thickness range as the screening objective. Findings Among the candidate schemes, T5-G6, comprising the T5 oil-pad material-distribution scheme and the G6 mirror-plate material-distribution scheme, was identified as the preferred material-distribution combination. Based on the coupling model evaluated against full-scale experiments on the original bearing, the T5-G6 scheme was predicted to reduce the standard deviation of oil film thickness by approximately 36–55% and increase the minimum oil film thickness compared with the original bearing. At 250 r/min, the predicted minimum oil film thickness o

title: Rolling friction and particle shape as controls on the static angle of repose of a recycled granular sub-base material
abstract: Recycled concrete aggregate is the most direct route to reusing construction and demolition waste as structural sub-base fill, yet its DEM contact parameters remain unconstrained. This study verifies a static angle-of-repose pipeline for ATAIR-EDEM framework material M6 and quantifies three controls on the simulated angle. A funnel-pour deck (1,500 particles, Hertz–Mindlin no-slip with constant-torque rolling friction) was authored from first principles in EDEM 2024; the angle was fitted by least squares to radial-bin surface heights across eight azimuthal sectors inside a 120 mm analysis domain. The verified baseline gives δ = 12.53° ± 0.88° (CV 7.1%). Raising rolling friction from 0.12/0.01 to 0.30/0.35 (RCA–RCA/RCA–steel) moved δ to 26.73°, at least seven times the between-pour standard deviation measured across independently seeded pours (0.60°, n = 3; 0.80°, n = 2). Replacing the near-spherical three-sphere clump with a five-sphere angular template added 3.66° at High friction, replicated to a between-pour SD of 0.08°. A + 0.25 static-friction increment moved the pooled result by 0.92–1.21°, the smallest of the three effects and contrary to the ranking reported for cylindrical-discharge geometry. At least 16° of the gap to the 47° measured recycled-aggregate benchmark stays unclosed. This is a verification and sensitivity study for M6, not a completed calibration.

title: Validation of a multiscale hysteresis mechanics model to predict oily shoe-floor friction: isolating the effect of varying shoe materials
abstract: A predictive understanding of shoe-floor friction is critical to the design of footwear and flooring to prevent slip-and-fall accidents. Recently, friction models have been applied to footwear that predict friction by simulating the impact of the floor’s topography and the shoe’s viscoelastic material properties on viscoelastic energy loss. While these models have shown the effect of the floor’s topography on friction, the validity of these models to predict the impact of shoe material properties on friction is still unproven. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the validity of a viscoelastic friction model for predicting the coefficient of friction (COF) across eight different shoe materials in oily conditions. Eight shoes were produced with identical tread features but varying shoe materials. These were tested on ten porcelain floors of varying surfaces with fully characterised topography across several orders of magnitude in size. Oily COF was measured and a multiscale mechanics model was implemented to predict friction: using all length scales of topography data; systematically restricting the large- or small-scale topography features; and by using a range of scales that had been identified in prior research as optimal. The predictive ability of each method was quantified. The model performed best when small-scale topography of the floor and high-frequency material properties of the shoe were excluded. title: Frictional Behavior and Torsional Vibration Implications of Advanced Drillstring Materials: Experimental Insights from Carbon Fiber, Titanium, and Aluminum
journal: SPE Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition
abstract: Abstract Torsional stick–slip vibration continues to be one of the most destructive dynamic malfunctions in drilling operations, with a huge effect on drilling efficiency, tool life, and even operational safety. This paper presents an experimental investigation of the effect of the dynamic-to-static friction coefficient ratio (μd/μs) on torsional vibration behavior for three advanced drillstring materials: Carbon Fiber, Aluminum, and Titanium. Experiments were conducted using a scaled drilling vibration rig designed to replicate field-relevant torsional dynamics. The rotational responses at the bit were observed for μd/μs ratios of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.9 while maintaining constant top rotation speed (RPM). In addition to qualitative RPM analysis, a stick–slip severity index (SSI) was calculated for the quantitative analysis of torsional vibration intensity. Results show that increasing μd/μs ratio in all materials always reduces stick–slip severity. At low μd/μs, carbon fiber shows the highest SSI, which means severe stick–slip behavior, while aluminum shows moderate instability. Titanium exhibits the lowest SSI values and the most stable torsional response.

title: Linking Shear Tensile Strength to Signals Feedback during Friction Stir Spot Welding of Pure Aluminium Using Copper Interlayer Materials
abstract: Friction stir spot welding (FSSW) of aluminium alloys has been studied by many researchers, however FSSW using interlayer materials needs to be further researched to better understand the use of interlayer materials. In this chapter, friction stir spot welding was used to fabricate spot welds of AA1060 (3 mm thick) without and with a 0.125 mm copper interlayer material. A rotational speed and a dwell time of 527 rpm and 5 seconds were used, respectively, and the overlap area was 30 mm. The spot welds exhibited good welds visually, with the presence of some flashes. It was observed that the shear tensile strength of the spot welds fabricated without the copper interlayer material showed higher strength than those fabricated using the copper interlayer material. And this was due to the generation of low heat input, the use of a low rotational speed that led to low temperature, and the type of interlayer used (copper) that had different properties than pure aluminium (base material). The results obtained demonstrated that there is an agreement with the literature that shows the use of interlayer materials affect the resulting properties of the welds.

title: Tribocatalytic degradation of cationic dyes using Na₀.₄K₀.₁Bi₀.₅TiO₃: influence of friction pair materials and reactive species
abstract: Abstract This study explores the tribocatalytic activity of cationic dyes (Rhodamine B (RhB) and Methylene Blue (MB)) using Na 0.4 K 0.1 Bi 0.5 TiO 3 ( NKBT) as a catalyst under various conditions. The degradation efficiencies of RhB, MB, and binary (RhB + MB) dyes were examined, revealing that RhB exhibited higher degradation (~ 90%) compared to MB (~ 44%) at 600 rpm over 360 min. However, in the binary dye system, MB degraded more (~ 53%) than RhB (~ 9%), contrary to the results of individual dye degradation. The observed results may be attributed to the steric hindrance caused by the planar structure of MB molecules, which interferes with the Coulombic attraction between RhB dye and the catalyst surface, thereby reducing the degradation efficiency of RhB dye. Kinetic analysis showed rate constants of 0.00684 min − 1 , 0.00142 min − 1 , 0.00022 min − 1 , and 0.00208 min − 1 for RhB, MB, binary RhB, and binary MB, respectively. The effect of different friction pairs on RhB dye degradation was studied using polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) disc (homemade) with glass, polypropylene (PP), and PTFE beakers. The PTFE beaker-PTFE disc pair showed the highest degradation (~ 93%), followed by PP-PTFE (~ 89%) and glass-PTFE (~ 77%) at 600 rpm over 180 min. Optimal RhB dye degradation (~ 96%) was achieved in the PTFE beaker at 1000 rpm within 120 min.

title: Prediction of friction and wear performance of copper-free resin-based brake materials under multiple operating conditions based on BO-GWO-ELM
abstract: Test conditions (speed, load, and temperature) are key factors affecting the friction and wear performance of resin-based brake materials. To investigate the changes in friction and wear performance of copper-free resin-based brake materials under different conditions and their prediction methods, this paper analyzes the effects of speed and load on the friction coefficient (COF) and wear rate (WR) of the materials, and establishes various prediction models. The results show that speed has a significant impact on friction and wear performance. At 350°C and 1 MPa, when the speed increases from 360 r/min to 480 r/min, the COF decreases while the WR increases. A continuous and smooth friction film is formed at 480 r/min. When the speed rises to 540∼600 r/min, the friction film gradually breaks down. At 600 r/min, it presents an island-like distribution, and the wear mechanism transitions from abrasive wear to a combination of fatigue wear and adhesive wear. As the load increases, the failure behavior of the material intensifies. At 350°C and 600 r/min, when the load increases from 0.6 MPa to 1.0 MPa, the WR increases by 42.6%. Among the four prediction models, the ELM performs the best (with a test set R 2 of 0.8643 for the COF and 0.9161 for the WR. The BO-GWO-ELM, improved by the BO and GWO algorithms, further enhances prediction accuracy, achieving test set R 2 values of 0.9704 and 0.9652 for the COF and WR, respectively. title: Friction Stir Welding and Friction Stir Spot Welding
abstract: This book provides an overview and discussion of the current state of friction stir welding (FSW) and friction stir spot welding (FSSW) using interlayer materials to fabricate high-quality joints for specific applications, leading to the optimization of these techniques. It also discusses energy savings achieved by reducing the rotational speed of the FSW tool during material joining. Additionally, the book addresses the reduction of weld defects in the joint region and the improvement of joint efficiency. • Focuses on the use of interlayer materials in friction stir welding and friction stir spot welding • Presents case studies on the effects of using copper and brass interlayer materials during the joining of AA5083 • Reviews the background of solid-state welding techniques • Provides an overview of friction stir welding and friction stir spot welding of similar and dissimilar aluminium alloys • Discusses the reduction of weld defects in the joint region and the improvement of joint efficiency This book is intended for researchers and graduate students in materials science, welding, and materials processing.

title: Friction Stir Welding (FSW) and Friction Stir Spot Welding (FSSW)
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) is a solid-state welding technique, and friction stir spot welding (FSSW) is a variant of FSW for spot welding. These techniques are used for the welding of materials, including aluminium alloys. This chapter shows a summary of selected studies on FSW and FSSW of aluminium alloys. The successful welding of aluminium alloys using FSW and FSSW has been established, and the fabricated welds and spot welds exhibit excellent properties, including microhardness and tensile strength. The process parameters affect the microstructure evolution of the fabricated welds or spot welds and further affect the resulting properties of the welds/spot welds. The joining of aluminium alloys has been well researched, and many studies are being carried out to optimise these joining techniques. The FSSW technique leaves behind a keyhole, and a technique called refill friction stir spot welding (RFSSW) was developed to close the keyhole and the spot welds with a keyhole refilled showed different properties when compared to spot welds fabricated using conventional FSSW. However, FSSW and RFSSW of aluminium alloys need more studies to further understand the behaviour of FSS-Welds and RFSS welds of aluminium alloys when the process parameters are varied, and tools of different geometries are used.

title: The Slipping Ladder Problem with Friction
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: We model the ladder as a rigid body and assume constant friction at the contacts. After setting up the equation of motion, a non-linear ordinary differential equation, we derive the analytical solution as position-dependent velocity, i.e. the angular velocity as a function of the angle. By evaluating a numerical example, we observe that the presented model is not yet fully realistic, as the normal contact force at the wall can become negative, which requires switching to a non-smooth mechanics model. Intended as educational material for courses in applied mechanics or classical physics, this exercise bridges the gap between introductory textbook statics and advanced non-linear dynamics.

title: Pipe Friction
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Darcy-Weisbach worked to its boundaries, and where the tables stop applying A head-loss figure carried to three decimal places is a statement about a roughness value somebody assumed, and the honest output of the calculation is the width of the band that assumption opens. Every head-loss method in use resolves, after the geometry is settled, to a single assumed property of the pipe wall. The handbooks publish that property as a value for new, clean pipe of a stated material, and the line it is applied to has age, scale, joints, fittings and at least one modification nobody recorded. The arithmetic downstream of the assumption is exact and the assumption is not, so a result presented as one number conceals the only uncertainty that matters. This book works each method from the federal handbooks that publish it, recomputes every worked result across the plausible range of the roughness assumption rather than at its midpoint, and reports the band. Where the band is narrow the reader may proceed on a figure; where it is wide, and it is often wide enough to change a pump selection, the finding is the width itself. Audiences: Choosing a method and knowing what it assumes — Has two or three methods available and picks by habit or by whichever spreadsheet was inherited. Cannot say what each method assumes about the flow regime or the fluid, so cannot say when the choice stops being harmless. title: Friction and interfacial mechanics of surgical suturing: needle–tissue penetration, suture drag and friction-control strategies
abstract: Surgical suturing involves a sequence of tribological contacts that begins with needle penetration, continues through suture pull-through, and culminates in knot tightening and locking. Uncontrolled friction at these interfaces can cause tissue trauma, coating delamination, or knot slippage. This narrative review synthesises the biomechanics and tribology of the needle–tissue, suture–tissue, and suture–suture interfaces. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for studies published from January 2000 to July 2026, and studies were selected for mechanical relevance and synthesised by tribological interface. Needle insertion force is a combined response of tissue deformation, cutting and shaft friction, with attention to needle geometry, trajectory, velocity, tissue properties and force sensing. Suture drag is examined in relation to material, diameter, surface roughness, monofilament or multifilament construction, hydration, loading and pulling speed. Surface-engineering approaches, including lubricants, silicone and polymeric treatments, antimicrobial coatings, dopamine-, chitosan- and graphene-based modifications, and tissue-integrating sutures, are evaluated for friction reduction, durability, handling and knot performance. The review also discusses the transition from low resistance during passage to sufficient suture–suture friction after tightening, together with experimental apparatus, biological tissue models, finite-element methods and robotic force feedback. title: Surface Engineering Processes for Reducing Friction and Wear
abstract: Surface engineering is a key technological field that directly influences the performance, efficiency, reliability, and service life of engineering components and systems. In particular, surface modification technologies play a crucial role in reducing friction and wear, which are among the primary causes of energy losses, material degradation, and component failure across diverse sectors, including transportation, energy, biomedical engineering, electronics, and manufacturing. This Special Issue is dedicated to recent developments in tribology and surface engineering aimed at improving the wear resistance and operational performance of engineering materials and components. The published contributions address topics including the tribological behavior of metallic materials, wear mechanisms in industrial applications, the performance of coated cutting tools, and the influence of manufacturing processes and surface conditions on friction and wear. The collection also includes studies on additively manufactured alloys, multilayer-coated tools, bimetallic materials, and laser-directed energy deposition technologies for rail repair and surface enhancement. The papers presented experimental investigations and application-oriented studies that enhanced the understanding of the relationships between material microstructure, surface characteristics, and tribological performance. title: Physical and mechanical properties of rocks for their separation in friction separators
abstract: The process of separating rock material into fractions is based on the differences in the paths, velocities, or directions of their particle travel. The key parameters controlling separation are the friction coefficients when particles collide with a surface. Differences in the friction coefficients of the particles in the rock material to be separated serve as the basis for operation of the friction separators, and improving their efficiency is a pressing challenge. This article presents a study of the physical and mechanical properties of asbestos-containing products, which changes increase the efficiency of the friction separators during the separation process. The study analyzes and generalizes data from scientific, technical, and patent literature, and synthesizes the information obtained. Additionally, physical and mathematical modeling methods are employed, experimental studies are conducted, and a regression analysis is performed. The article presents data from experimental measurements of the friction coefficients, recovery (elasticity), and instantaneous friction of asbestos, peridotite, serpentinite, and ophite. A numerical experiment was performed to analyze the travel paths of the asbestos and copper-zinc ore particles using a software based on an equilibrium model of the acting forces. The results of the experiment demonstrated that a 1.5-fold increase in the kinetic friction coefficient leads to a 1.5-fold reduction in the travel range of asbestos particles for

title: A Global high-Resolution Friction Surface Dataset
abstract: Abstract Global physical accessibility analysis requires friction surfaces that are spatially detailed, transparent, reusable, and suitable for both on-network and off-network movement. We introduce the Global high-Resolution Updatable Friction Surface (GRUFS), a pair of global 30 m raster datasets representing movement cost in minutes per meter. GRUFS Foot models walking movement on roads, paths, ferries, and off-road terrain, while GRUFS Mixed models driving speeds on roads and walking movement off-road. The surfaces are generated from publicly available inputs, including OpenStreetMap transport and water features, GLAD land cover, FABDEM elevation, Copernicus GLO-30 elevation patches, and GAUL-derived country membership for road-speed assignment. The dataset is distributed as scaled integer raster surfaces with accompanying lookup tables, supporting inputs, production code, and validation materials. GRUFS is designed for accessibility analysis, facility catchment estimation, service coverage assessment, policy targeting, and scenario testing, particularly in data-scarce settings where consistent, high-resolution travel-time inputs are needed. The production workflow is designed to support annual, versioned releases as source transport and environmental data are updated, subject to available maintenance resources.

title: An associated model of Coulomb friction based on the real area of contact
abstract: Coulomb friction is a non-associated law: it contains a threshold that depends on the contact pressure, i.e. a stress that is not conjugate to any internal variable, hence it admits no dissipation potential in the sense of generalized standard materials (GSM), and the incremental frictional contact problem is not a minimization problem. In this paper, we propose an alternative friction model that retains Coulomb-like behavior while being associated and fully GSM-compatible. Key to our formulation is the introduction of a new internal variable motivated by the microscopic contact state of rough surfaces, whose evolution is driven by the plastic deformation of the asperities. Under a non-decreasing contact pressure and below a threshold pressure, the model recovers Coulomb friction up to an asperity-scale penetration depth. This depth is physically meaningful and can be calibrated to reproduce known tribology results. Under decreasing contact pressures, the model exhibits a memory effect due to irreversible plastic deformation of the asperities, whereas above the pressure threshold it yields a saturation of the frictional traction. We present both penalty and Lagrange multiplier formulations of the model. A 2D finite element implementation of the penalty approach confirms excellent agreement with the classical Coulomb predictions across two benchmark tests.

title: Lamellar–Microspine Architecture for Robust Friction on Slippery Soft Objects
abstract: ABSTRACT Robust friction on soft substrates remains challenging under wet or oil‐lubricated conditions because conventional strategies fail when faced with both interfacial lubrication and material compliance. Here we present a lamellar–microspine architecture that combines gecko‐inspired lamellar compliance with insect‐inspired microspine anchoring to address this problem. Under shear loading, the microspines penetrate progressively into soft substrates, converting sliding into anchoring and generating high friction. The lamellar backing distributes loads evenly and extends the effective high‐friction regime. As a result, the lamellar–microspine surface achieves friction coefficients above 2 in dry, wet, and oil‐lubricated conditions—up to 97 times higher than non‐spined contacts—while maintaining negligible detachment forces. The integration of this architecture into the fin‐inspired gripper demonstrates reliable grasping of soft, slippery, and hard‐to‐hold objects—including live fish—under both dry and lubricated environments, where conventional grippers slip. By linking mesoscale compliance with microscale anchoring, this work provides a general approach for controlling friction on soft, lubricated surfaces, with implications for robotic manipulation, climbing systems, and biological sampling.

title: Interface Selection Principle: The Emergent Nature of Macroscopic Friction in Plate Tectonics
abstract: The effective friction coefficient of the lithosphere–asthenosphere system inferred from geodynamic inversions (0.01–0.03) is far lower than the Byerlee laboratory rock friction value (0.6–0.85). This contradiction has remained unresolved for decades. This paper proposes the Interface Selection Principle: the system selects the interface with minimum μN among multiple candidate interfaces in the vertical direction as the actual sliding surface, making macroscopic friction an emergent property rather than a fixed rock material constant. This paper identifies three mechanisms that collectively contribute to the reduction of macroscopic resistance: Both the creep shear effect and the interface-selection effect have equivalent friction coefficients that decrease with decreasing plate velocity. Creep achieves this through the strain-rate path: the creep friction coefficient is proportional to plate velocity and tends to zero as velocity tends to zero. Interface selection achieves this through the relaxation-time path: the interface friction coefficient equals a finite baseline value plus a velocity-dependent term, which decreases with decreasing velocity but retains a finite baseline as velocity tends to zero. This framework suggests that previous melt-only explanations may be incomplete: asthenospheric friction may have been overestimated, while subduction megathrust friction may have been underestimated. title: The nirvana fallacy and the case for friction in responding to online child sexual abuse
abstract: On 3 April 2026 the European Union’s temporary exception for voluntary detection of child sexual abuse material lapsed, and for three months the alternative that perfectionist arguments rarely state became policy: to do nothing. During the previous gap, in 2020–21, reports of abuse material from the EU fell by 58%. This article names the reasoning behind such outcomes as the nirvana fallacy, which Demsetz identified in 1969 as measuring the imperfect against an ideal instead of the real alternative. Four forms recur in the child-safety debate: circumvention, false positives, categorical impossibility and the slippery slope. Each states a real issue and leaves its comparator unstated. The article reframes the measures as friction, drawing on situational crime prevention, public health harm reduction and the economics of adversarial systems, then works along the offending pathway to set out what each friction layer achieves and what it cannot. Randomised trials and field deployments on Google Search, Pornhub and the Tor search engine Ahmia.fi show warnings reducing attempted access and increasing help-seeking, while hash matching, classifiers and age assurance carry known limits alongside measured effects. The article does not propose weakening encryption, and argues that most serious objections to other controls should be treated as design constraints rather than as refusals. A comparative test of four questions applies to objections and proposals alike, along with eight recom

title: Certified neural operators for frictional contact dynamics of jointed structures
abstract: Friction in mechanical joints dominates damping in assembled structures, and predicting it depends on set-valued contact across interfaces whose manufactured topography is only partially known. Topography-resolving simulation is the most predictive route, but its cost is governed by a non-smooth contact sub-problem at every implicit time step. We prove that this sub-problem is a strongly monotone variational inequality with a single-valued, Lipschitz continuous, piecewise real-analytic solution operator, and exploit this structure in an admissible, certified, structure-preserving learned solver. A neural operator is composed with a projection onto the Coulomb cone, so every prediction satisfies the contact law exactly. Training minimises the contact-law residual; a supervised guidance term on a small reference subset is annealed to zero after the opening epochs, so the deployed surrogate is a stationary point of the residual objective alone. It warm-starts a few certified projected-Jacobi sweeps that yield a computable error bound and preserve the negligible numerical damping of the base integrator. The bound’s pessimism and cost scale with the squared condition number of the condensed operator, and a cone-invariant per-point scaling removes most of that penalty on ill-conditioned interfaces. title: Investigation of fatigue performance for friction surfacing groove repairs of high-strength aluminum alloys
abstract: Friction stir-based solid state layer deposition techniques are presumed to have significant potential for repair applications. The main advantage is mostly related to the lower heat input during layer deposition, minimizing thermal effects to the surrounding structure. This work presents the application of a friction surfacing (FS) approach for groove repair of similar material combinations of AA2024 and AA7475, respectively. Regarding the process stability, a reduction of travel speed within the groove area improves the bonding of the deposit to the subjacent structure. To further consolidate and enhance the bonding of the deposit, hybrid friction diffusion bonding (HFDB), which is a friction stir-based materials processing technique, has successfully been applied. For the optimized FS groove repair strategy, including HFDB post-processing, fatigue testing was performed, revealing an improvement of the fatigue properties compared to the grooved reference material. The AA2024 repaired grooves present mechanical properties approaching the AA2024 base material. The repair of the AA7475 grooves also led to an improvement; however, the AA7475 results stay below the respective reference material and, therefore, the improvement is less pronounced compared to AA2024. The results provide the first benchmark for fatigue properties of FS-repaired grooves and highlight this technique as a simple and efficient approach for repair at low thermal input, minimizing effects on the surroundi

title: Attraction-controlled torque organization and rotational states in frictional granular matter
abstract: In this study, we numerically investigate how interparticle attraction affects stress transmission, torque organization, and particle rotation in a two-dimensional frictional granular material. Although the attraction is a central force and exerts no direct torque on the particles, it strongly modifies the contact network and particle rotation. Attraction produces a low-rate stress state and selects the high-stress state near the shear-thickening regime of the dry system, while leaving the high-rate thickened state almost unchanged. By decomposing the shear stress, we find that the direct attractive contribution accounts for only a fraction of the total stress, while the repulsive contribution is strongly enhanced. Attraction increases the coordination number and torque amplitude and can reverse the local torque-sign correlation. At low packing fractions and intermediate shear rates, a stress-collapse state emerges with strongly suppressed torque and rotation despite a finite contact network. These results show that attraction controls macroscopic rheology through reorganization of the frictional contact network.

title: Adaptive Lateral Control of Vehicles under Abrupt and Nonuniform Tire–Road Friction
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset accompanies the research manuscript entitled Adaptive Lateral Control of Vehicles under Abrupt and Nonuniform Tire–Road Friction. The study investigates adaptive model predictive control, lateral stability coordination, and constrained wheel-force allocation under abrupt and nonuniform tire–road friction conditions. The numerical evaluation comprises 88 physical scenarios, seven controllers, and 616 simulation runs using a four-wheel Fiala tire model. A separate numerical evaluation includes 144 simulations using a Dugoff combined-slip tire model. The deposited materials are intended to support the examination and reproducibility of the numerical findings, including conditional tracking performance, controller comparisons, failure outcomes, and model sensitivity. The primary evaluation focuses on a finite deterministic scenario set. The results do not constitute experimental vehicle validation or establish general performance superiority across all friction and driving conditions. The scope of reproducibility depends on the data, configurations, and analysis or simulation code included in this release.
