title: Interface frictions: (In)tolerances and the extractive labour of repair in airport digital infrastructures
abstract: Contemporary public and corporate discourses frequently celebrate advanced automation as a seamless portal to frictionless, touchless mobility. Critical human geography, however, has long demonstrated that these computational networks remain deeply enmeshed in messy physical procedures and human agencies. This paper introduces the concept of interface friction —defined as the minor, quotidian slowdowns and subtle miscomputations that emerge where rigid software logic collides with the fluid variability of human life—to diagnose the unrecognised labour that sustains technically intolerant systems. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 88 airport frontline workers and managers at Beijing's Capital and Daxing International Airports, we trace how interface frictions systematically manifest across three relational registers of human difference: the corporeal, the procedural, and the affective. Rather than cascading into spectacular ruptures that trigger engineering overhauls or technological overhauls, these routine micro-stalls are normalised and tolerated with the help of often-unseen human efforts. We argue that the automated terminal functions by establishing an asymmetrical, extractive choreography of tolerance. When the technical boundaries of software code are reached, the system offloads the material drag of its own computational stiffness onto the stretched corporeal and affective capacities of staff (and sometimes users), who are enrolled to perform an uncompensated

title: Static Friction Measurement of Steels Under Dry and Lubricated Conditions Using An Oscillating Tribometer
abstract: For the dimensioning of press fits and screw connections, knowledge around the static friction coefficient between two surfaces is essential. Variation of the surface and the state of lubrication can change this parameter. The research in this publication presents a novel screening method for the static coefficient of friction, using an oscillating tribometer with electromagentic drive. The materials which were investigated, were two types of steels (stainless steel 1.4313 and heat-treatable steel 1.6511), combined in different ways, in dry or lubricated and also in nitrided condition.The novel test method can be used at application-near contact pressures, up to 120 MPa as used in this research. I particular the test method works with a linear increase of the stroke setpoint, starting from almost zero. As the actuator stroke increases, so do the shear forces due to elastic deformation of the components. These shear forces are perfectly measurable with the tribometer's piezo friction force transducer. Finally, the shear force exceeds the static friction and sliding occurs. High-resolution data acquisition provides insight into braking loss events and reveals the fundamental friction effects of common engineering materials at relevant loading levels.The reproducible results for the static friction coefficient enabled the authors to draw some correlations between surface hardness conditions and the static friction. The presented method and the final findings hopefully provide en

title: Friction Stir Welding of Rapidly Solidified 6082 Alloy: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties
abstract: This study investigates the microstructure and mechanical properties of friction stir welded (FSW) joints produced from AA6082 alloy fabricated by rapid solidification and hot extrusion. The base material exhibited a homogeneous microstructure with a fine average grain size of ~1.3 µm, significantly lower than the 5.5 µm measured for the conventionally processed reference material. The most favorable joint properties were obtained at a tool rotational speed of 1000 rpm. Under these conditions, the welded joint showed strength comparable to the base material, reaching 206 MPa UTS and 151 MPa YS, although with reduced ductility. EBSD analysis revealed only minor microstructural changes after welding, with the grain size in the stir zone remaining nearly unchanged at approximately 1.5 µm. These results demonstrate that the fine-grained microstructure of the rapidly solidified AA6082 alloy is largely preserved during FSW and highlight its potential for solid-state joining applications.

title: A unified model for estimation of the friction coefficient of sliding isolators by means of small-scale tests
abstract: The coefficient of friction is a key parameter for the design of Curved Surface Sliders (CSS), as it defines the hysteretic behavior of the isolator and directly influences energy dissipation, displacement capacity, and recentering capability. While full-scale testing is required by current standards to characterize the effective coefficient of friction in both prototype and quality control tests, small-scale experiments are commonly used for the characterization of sliding materials for research and development due to their cost-effectiveness and feasibility. Today, the extrapolation of small-scale results to full-scale devices remains a critical challenge. To fill this gap, this study aims to propose a methodology to quantify the coefficient of friction of full-scale isolators by means of tests performed on small-scale specimens of the sliding material. Starting from established approaches developed to account for the dependencies of the coefficient of friction on mechanical parameters such as pressure, velocity and history of motion, a unified model is proposed, together with a practical procedure for calibration its parameter through small-scale tests. The proposed unified model is a semi-empirical formulation calibrated against measured data obtained from sliding tests. Its structure is informed by general physical considerations and by the experimentally observed dependence of friction on axial pressure, sliding velocity, and dissipated energy, while its parameters are

title: Thermomechanical modeling of friction stir blind riveting for CF/PEEK–AA6061 stacks
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part B Journal of Engineering Manufacture
abstract: This study proposes an innovative thermodynamic analysis method for the friction stir blind riveting (FSBR) of carbon fiber-reinforced thermoplastics (CFRTP) and aluminum alloy stacks. The proposed model comprehensively incorporates both the viscoplastic heat generated within the sticking-affected zone of the workpiece and the interfacial frictional heat between the workpiece and the rivet. Building upon these thermal mechanisms, temperature-dependent material yield strength and friction coefficient functions were integrated into the analytical framework, thereby establishing a fully thermo-mechanically coupled model for the FSBR process. Experimental validation demonstrated good agreement between model predictions and measured values of temperature, penetration force, and torque, with maximum relative errors of 6%, 9%, and 15%, respectively. Comparative analysis indicates that accounting for viscoplastic heat primarily influences the temperature field within a localized region approximately 0–6 mm from the rivet. Neglecting viscoplastic heat sources in the numerical model leads to a significant increase in prediction errors for penetration force and torque compared to experimental data.

title: A Self-Lubricating PEEK Composite Enhanced by Microcapsules via Friction-Triggered Hydrogel Layer Formation
abstract: A hydrogel is an ideal material for lubrication, with hydrogel-filled microcapsules emerging as a promising strategy to simultaneously achieve low friction and high load-bearing capacity. The hydrogel microcapsules were prepared with porous SiO2 as the shell; polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), polyacrylic acid (PAA), tannic acid (TA), and dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine (DMPC) sol (named as PPTD sol) as one type of core material, and calcium lactate as another core material, and the two kinds of microcapsules were compounded into the PEEK matrix. During friction, the released PPTD sol and calcium lactate were cross-linked into the hydrogel through microporous extrusion and covered on the friction surface. The in situ formation of the lubricating hydrogel layer significantly improved the polymer's lubrication performance under severe operating conditions, with the friction coefficient decreased by above 82% and the one-order-of-magnitude decrease of the wear rate. The strategy is expected to become a universal solution.

title: APPLIED MODEL OF AXIAL COMPRESSION OF TRANSVERSELY ISOTROPIC POROUS CYLINDER WITH END FRICTION
publisher: N. I. Lobachevsky State University of Nizhny Novgorod
abstract: In the context of the linear Cowin – Nunziato micro-dilatation theory, the contact problem of axial compression of a finite transversely isotropic porous cylinder placed between two rigid plates moving towards each other is addressed. To account for the effect of friction, an effective integral parameter is introduced as the ratio of the equivalent tangential force to the normal force. Using physically justified approximations (linear radial variation of the radial displacement, no radial dependence of the axial displacement and micro-dilatation) together with the first-order Kantorovich method and the Lagrange variational principle, the three-dimensional boundary value problem is reduced to a system of three ordinary differential equations. The analytical solution is obtained as a sum of a rod-type solution describing the fundamental stress-strain state in the central part of the cylinder and exponentially decaying boundary-layer terms generated by the combined action of micro-dilatation phenomena and contact friction. Using cortical bone as an example, a parametric study is carried out to reveal the influence of the friction coefficient and porosity characteristics on axial distributions of displacements, stresses, and micro-dilatation. The analysis reveals that end friction restricts transverse expansion, causing “barreling” (bulging of the lateral surface), and leads to a concentration of compressive radial and tangential stresses near the ends. title: Flexible contact pendulum friction nanogenerator for harvesting blue energy for marine applications
abstract: Collecting energy from low-frequency waves is really important for the development of the ocean IoT, but traditional rigid triboelectric nanogenerators (TENG) have a high starting threshold and wear out easily, which seriously limits their use in small waves. This article proposes a swing-type triboelectric nanogenerator (RS-TENG) based on the smooth contact of natural rabbit fur, aimed at efficiently harvesting low-frequency water wave energy. This device uses rabbit fur with extremely low friction and a PVC film to create a unique, soft ’brush-style’ contact. It greatly lowers the mechanical threshold for starting vibrations, allowing the pendulum to swing smoothly and continuously even under weak excitation, while also effectively reducing material wear. By systematically optimizing parameters like the friction distance, baffle angle, and pendulum counterweight, the TENG on the RS-TENG side achieved a maximum open-circuit voltage of over 360 V, a short-circuit current of 4.5 μA, and a transferred charge of 170 nC under a 2.25 Hz reciprocating drive. With a custom energy management circuit, the RS-TENG successfully lit up an array of hundreds of LEDs in a simulated water wave environment and achieved stable self-powered closed-loop operation for a commercial digital temperature and humidity meter. This study confirms that it’s feasible to develop high-sensitivity wave energy harvesting structures using bio-based flexible materials, providing power for in-situ sensor network

title: Recent developments in friction-based recycling techniques (FBRTs) for aluminum alloy chips: a comprehensive review
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
abstract: ABSTRACT Friction-based recycling techniques (FBRTs), including friction stir extrusion (FSE), friction stir back extrusion (FSBE), shear assisted processing and extrusion (ShAPE), friction stir consolidation (FSC), continuous friction stir extrusion (CFSE), and solid stir extrusion (SSE), have attracted attention for the solid-state recycling of aluminum alloy chips. These techniques utilize frictional heat and severe plastic deformation generated by the relative motion between the tool and the chips, enabling direct recycling without remelting or separate billet preheating. Despite their rapid development over the past decade, FBRTs have not been systematically reviewed as a distinct class of recycling technologies. This paper reviews the state of the art in FBRTs for recycling aluminum alloy chips and discusses the operating principles, tool configurations, material flow behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical properties of the FBRTs. The energy performance of FBRTs and solid bonding criteria for chip consolidation are comparatively evaluated. The mechanisms governing interfacial bonding, dynamic recovery, recrystallization, and grain growth are summarized. FBRTs offer an efficient route for recycling aluminum alloy chips, cutting energy consumption by 45%–75% relative to remelting. The resulting recycled products possess mechanical properties that are comparable to, or even surpass, those of some conventionally extruded or rolled materials. Future research sho

title: Low-Friction and Lubricious Surfaces on Printed Photopolymers: Additives, Grafts, Coatings, Migration and Wear
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Low friction on a printed photopolymer is not an intrinsic material property. It is the response of a complete tribosystem comprising the printed and post-cured resin, the location and attachment of the lubricating function, the counterface, contact geometry, load, speed, motion, temperature, environment and accumulated sliding history. Bulk solid lubricants, surface-segregated additives, covalently attached brushes, deposited coatings and hydrated layers can all reduce friction, but they replenish, migrate, wear and fail by different mechanisms. This review defines a qualification architecture for low-friction and lubricious printed-photopolymer surfaces. It separates initial friction from durable lubricity; requires friction and wear to be paired with surface and counterface evidence; treats migration, blooming, leaching, transfer-film formation, coating loss and substrate exposure as time-dependent state changes; and preserves the distinction among dry, oil-lubricated and aqueous contacts. Direct evidence from photocurable vat-polymerisation composites is combined with bounded adjacent evidence from UV-cured coatings, grafted polymer brushes, hydrogel coatings and UV-cured thin films. The result is a non-compensatory framework for qualifying the intended tribosystem. No commercial formulation, universal additive loading, coating thickness, coefficient of friction, wear rate or service lifetime is established.

title: OPTIMIZATION OF WEAR RESISTANCE AND FRICTION BEHAVIOUR OF RAMIE FIBER-REINFORCED POLYMER NANO-COMPOSITES
abstract: This study investigates the tribological performance of epoxy-based hybrid composites reinforced with ramie woven fabric and organically modified montmorillonite (OMMT) nanoclay. The composites were fabricated by incorporating different concentrations of OMMT nanoclay (3, 6, and 9 wt%) into the epoxy matrix containing ramie woven fabric. The tribological behaviour of the developed composites was evaluated using a pin-on-disc tribometer under a constant sliding distance of 800 m. Experiments were conducted at different applied loads of 5, 10, and 15 N and sliding velocities of 1, 2, and 3 m/s to examine their effects on the coefficient of friction (COF) and specific wear rate (SWR). Among the investigated compositions and test conditions, the composite containing 9 wt% OMMT nanoclay exhibited the best tribological performance, achieving a minimum SWR of 0.0158 (10-3X mm³/Nm) and a COF of 0.0681 at 5N load and 1 m/s velocity. The optimum tribological conditions were further validated using Taguchi-based statistical analysis. SEM was engaged to examine the worn surfaces and identify the dominant wear mechanisms. The improved tribological performance with increasing OMMT content can be attributed to enhanced filler–matrix interfacial bonding and the formation of a protective tribofilm during sliding, which reduced material loss and friction. The findings demonstrate that incorporating OMMT nanoclay into ramie woven fabric-reinforced epoxy composites is an effective approach for d

title: Magnetic Response Behavior of Friction-Induced Surface Transformation Layer on Rails
abstract: The martensitic white etching layer (WEL) is a primary contributor to rolling contact fatigue of rails, and its in situ quantitative non-destructive evaluation remains a critical challenge in railway maintenance. This study systematically investigates the quantitative relationship between the material properties of friction-induced WELs and their magnetic flux leakage (MFL) signals. A series of rail specimens with varying WEL thicknesses and surface hardness values were characterized by standardized MFL scanning and metallographic analysis. The results reveal that MFL signal features, particularly the peak amplitude and full width at half maximum, exhibit statistically significant correlations with both WEL thickness and hardness. The peak amplitude Bpeak increases linearly with WEL thickness at a rate of 0.048 mT/µm, and the full width at half maximum (FWHM) exhibits a strong positive correlation with thickness (R2 = 0.94). A multiple linear regression model incorporating both thickness and hardness achieves a coefficient of determination of R2 = 0.87 for predicting Bpeak. Independent validation using 12 unseen test samples yields a mean absolute percentage error of 10.2% and a root mean square error of 0.80 mT. title: Orbital Friction Processing Of High Strength Steels And Alloys For PM, AM & HIP Applications
abstract: Friction welding is a well established technique used for joining materials. The latest process, developed and patented for engineering applications is orbital friction welding|processing typically used for connecting large and thick sections of metal components such as rails. The work presented here highlights the results from the machinery that is currently available, which was designed, developed, built for high tonnage output, has demonstrated that high strength sections|geometries can be joined without compromise to connections; weld region microstructures and the technology can be used to produce high integrity parts for powder metallurgy (PM), additive manufacturing (AM) and hot isostatic pressing (HIP) applications, especially when large areas, geometries are concerned. title: Characteristics of Friction Surfacing Deposit and its Potential Application for Aluminum Spot Lap Joint
journal: International Journal on Smart Material and Mechatronics
abstract: Friction surfacing is a solid-state surface modification technique capable of producing aluminum deposits with robust metallurgical bonding while reducing thermal degradation of the substrate compared to fusion-based coating methods. Nonetheless, the combined influence of consumable rod diameter and substrate surface roughness on layer formation, mechanical performance, thermal behavior, and potential application as mechanical joints remains inadequately understood. This study examines the effects of rod diameter and substrate surface roughness on aluminum layers produced by friction surfacing and assesses their suitability for aluminum spot-joint applications. AA6061 aluminum alloy served as the consumable rod, while AA1100 was utilized as the substrate. The process was executed at a rotational speed of 3300 rpm and a translational speed of 9 mm/min, with variations in rod diameter and axial load. Characterization involved measurements of bending strength, microhardness, and surface roughness. The results indicated that a 12 mm rod diameter combined with a 25 kg load yielded the highest bending strength of 203.48 MPa, attributed to stable material flow and balanced heat distribution. A lower substrate surface roughness (Ra = 1.070 µm) enhanced bending strength and hardness and facilitated a more uniform thermal distribution during deposition. title: A reference contact framework of signed distance fields for efficient frictional dynamic modeling and computation
journal: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering
abstract: The signed distance field (SDF) method provides an implicit functional representation to simplify contact detection for complex geometries. However, for deformable bodies, utilizing a static SDF defined in the reference configuration often relies on heuristic geometric approximations, leading to kinematic inconsistencies. To address such a problem, this paper presents a reference contact framework (RCF) of SDFs. It defines the frictional contact model in the reference configuration of a deformable body that ensures physical rigor within the static SDF. Firstly, a pulling-back procedure is established to correlate the spatial positions of contact points in the current configuration with their material positions in the reference configuration. Then, the work done by contact forces is formulated directly in the reference configuration, and the generalized contact forces are derived through the variation with respect to generalized coordinates. The resulting formulation of contact forces intrinsically accounts for surface distortions, maintaining variational consistency with the total Lagrangian framework. Additionally, the framework is extended to a frictional contact by incorporating the Coulomb friction model, which is reformulated through a novel definition of relative tangential displacement defined within the reference configuration, i.e. the reference tangential slip. title: Thermomechanical behaviour and microstructural evolution in friction stir spot welding of dissimilar stainless steels
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
abstract: This study investigates the friction stir spot welding of dissimilar stainless steels (430S ferrite and 304L austenite), with emphasis on the thermomechanical behaviour and microstructural evolution. The welding was performed at a tool rotational speed of 1125 rpm, plunge depth of 2.7 mm, and dwell time of 5 s. Significant grain refinement was observed in the stir zone, with reductions of approximately 75.6% in ferritic steel and 45.8% in austenitic steel, attributed to the combined effects of frictional heat and severe plastic deformation that promote dynamic recrystallization. Distinct recrystallization mechanisms were identified in the two materials: continuous dynamic recrystallization in the ferritic stainless steel, associated with dislocation rearrangement followed by progressive sub-grain rotation, and discontinuous dynamic recrystallization in the austenitic stainless steel, characterized by nucleation of new grains along prior grain boundaries. The weld interface exhibited a sound metallurgical bond without the formation of deleterious intermetallic compounds, along with partial intermixing of constituent phases. Microhardness measurements revealed a significant increase in the stir zone, rising from 189 ± 10 HV to 270 ± 14 HV in the ferritic steel and from 205 ± 11 HV to 260 ± 12 HV in the austenitic steel. This enhancement is primarily attributed to grain refinement, increased dislocation density, and a balanced distribution of high-angle and low-angle grain bound

title: Mixed double-hemivariational analysis of piezoelectric contact with multiplier-coupled nonmonotone friction
abstract: We introduce and analyze a static piezoelectric contact model for Hencky-type materials in which the nonsmooth interface response depends on the tangential displacement, the electric potential jump, and a regularized representation of the normal contact reaction through the Lagrange multiplier. This yields a genuinely multiplier-dependent double nonsmooth coupling on the contact boundary. The model is formulated as a mixed problem in which a Lagrange multiplier is associated with the unilateral Signorini-type contact constraint and, through its regularized representation, also enters the nonsmooth interface response. The resulting boundary functional is expressed in hemivariational form through Clarke’s generalized directional derivative with respect to both the primal interface variables and the regularized multiplier variable. Under standard assumptions on the constitutive operators and suitable growth, compactness, and upper semicontinuity conditions on the coupled superpotential, we prove the existence of weak solutions. The proof combines a truncation procedure, a Fan–KKM argument with a Minty-type reformulation, a uniform multiplier estimate based on an inf–sup property for the normal trace, and a weak compactness argument. We also establish a sequential stability result showing the robustness of weak solutions under perturbations of the loadings and of the foundation data. title: Corrosion and Stress Corrosion Cracking Dataset of ZE41 and AZ91D Magnesium Alloys Processed by Friction Stir Processing
abstract: This dataset contains data on the corrosion and stress corrosion cracking behaviour of ZE41 and AZ91D magnesium alloys processed by friction stir processing. It include constant-load SCC data obtained in 3.5% NaCl solution. The dataset enables comparison between base materials and friction stir processed conditions and supports analysis of corrosion resistance, SCC behaviour, time-dependent deformation, and failure characteristics of ZE41 and AZ91D magnesium alloys.

title: Particle-scale controls on friction and breakage of natural sands: Roles of morphology, stiffness, and internal defects
abstract: Particle-scale characteristics strongly influence the macroscopic frictional response of granular sands by governing contact interactions, force transmission, and damage evolution. However, the coupled effects of surface morphology, micromechanical properties, and internal defects on frictional behavior remain insufficiently understood. In this study, volcanic sand, calcareous sand, and quartz sand were investigated through consolidated undrained triaxial tests combined with scanning electron microscopy, atomic force microscopy, petrographic analysis, and nanoindentation. The results demonstrate that the frictional response of natural sands cannot be interpreted solely by surface roughness or particle stiffness. Although calcareous sand exhibits substantially higher surface mean roughness than volcanic sand, its peak-state friction angle is slightly lower, while quartz sand possesses the highest indentation modulus but the lowest friction angle. These findings indicate that morphology-induced interlocking and stiffness-related deformation resistance do not independently determine frictional resistance; instead, their contributions depend on the stability of particle contact structures during loading. Furthermore, multiscale observations suggest that natural sands may follow markedly different contact-evolution pathways depending on their particle structures: quartz sand mainly undergoes sliding, rolling, and limited surface damage; calcareous sand shows local indentation, asp

title: A boundary-coupled unified frictional hysteresis model for metal rubber under quasi-static and dynamic loading
abstract: Metal rubber (MR) contains numerous internal contact, sliding, and frictional interfaces among metallic wires, which leads to pronounced nonlinear and hysteretic characteristics under quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions. Existing hysteresis models are mostly developed for specific loading conditions and are therefore unable to uniformly describe the transition from quasi-static compressive behavior to dynamic hysteretic response in MR materials. Moreover, their capability to characterize asymmetric hysteretic behavior and equilibrium-position shifts remains limited under variations in biased mass, pre-compression, and support configuration. To address these issues, a boundary-coupled unified frictional hysteresis model (BC-UFH) is proposed in this study. Within this framework, the quasi-static frictional hysteresis (QFH) form is adopted as the baseline to identify the nonlinear elastic and frictional hysteresis parameters of MR under quasi-static compression, thereby providing the parameter basis for the subsequent dynamic extension and boundary-coupled mapping. On this basis, a dynamic frictional hysteresis (DFH) extension form is further developed by introducing a dynamic slip-softening term and a pore-gas pumping viscous damping term. By incorporating the boundary conditions of unilateral and symmetric support configurations, the BC-UFH model provides a unified description of quasi-static and dynamic responses. title: Two-Pass Friction Stir Welding of AZ31/AA1050 Bimetallic Butt–Lap Joint
abstract: Abstract This study evaluated the feasibility of friction stir welding (FSW) of AZ31/AA1050 bimetallic plates produced by explosive welding. The investigated material had a total thickness of 10 mm (5 + 5 mm) and, after milling, 8 mm (4 + 4 mm). Butt–Lap joints were produced using both a single-pass and a two-pass FSW approach. The process parameters were 1600 rpm and 150 mm/min for the AZ31 alloy, and 600 rpm and 100 mm/min for the AA1050 alloy. In the single-pass variant, a tool with a 9.8 mm pin length was used, whereas in the two-pass process, tools with pin lengths of 4.8 and 3.8 mm were applied, with penetration depths ranging from 4.0 to 4.9 mm. The investigation of the joints properties involves microhardness analysis and tensile strength tests. The joints were subjected to microstructure analysis using scanning electron (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) techniques. The results showed that the single-pass process led to excessive plasticization of aluminum, intensive material mixing, and the formation of discontinuities. The most favorable results were obtained for the two-pass variant with a penetration depth of 4.0 mm, without crossing the interfacial boundary between the layers. It was found that when the total width of the mixed zone exceeded 0.4 mm, discontinuities appeared, while values above 0.6 mm resulted in voids and joint degradation. title: The Latent Space of Noise. The Prompt as Semantic Friction: Transduction Strategies in Text-to-Image Models
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This essay investigates visual transduction in text-to-image generative models, proposing a methodological reversal: using the prompt not as a descriptive-denotative instruction but as “semantic friction” — an engineered condition for observing how generative systems select, suppress, reorganize, or literalize semantically dense material. A reflective first-person prose on contemporary noise and on Umberto Eco’s age of vision, information, and noise is administered to thirteen local and cloud-based models in a 1:1 format. Four recurring response patterns emerge: defensive transduction (aestheticizing removal), entropic transduction (collapse or historicization), conceptual transduction (metatextual decomposition), and didactic transduction (hyper-literalism and bodily somatization). Framed as a single-prompt, single-seed case study offering an exploratory grid rather than a validated taxonomy, the essay cautions against attributing algorithmic consciousness or hermeneutic intentionality to such outputs and reconsiders authorship in Generative AI Art, situating the artist’s activity between rigorous control of the computational environment and critical hermeneutics.

title: Development of a novel hybrid powder bed friction stir additive manufacturing-friction stir forging process for fabrication of AA6061 spur gear: process development, thermomechanical modeling, and process-structure-property correlation
abstract: Existing manufacturing processes often struggle to fabricate lightweight gears with reliable mechanical properties while simultaneously achieving full densification, microstructural homogeneity, and near-net-shape geometric complexity. In the present work, a novel hybrid solid-state manufacturing route combining powder bed friction stir (PBFS) additive manufacturing and friction stir forging (FSF) was developed to fabricate AA6061 spur gears from powder feedstock by sequentially integrating both processes within a single manufacturing setup. The process involved layer-wise deposition of AA6061 powders via friction-stir-assisted severe plastic deformation to form a consolidated billet, followed by friction stir forging of the billet into the final gear geometry. A fully coupled thermo-mechanical numerical model based on the coupled Eulerian-Lagrangian (CEL) framework was developed to analyze densification behavior, cavity filling, and local deformation conditions during the process. The simulation predicted complete densification of the initially less-dense powder bed and identified a billet height of ~30 mm as sufficient for near-complete cavity filling with minimal residual voids. The predicted thermo-mechanical fields revealed temperatures of ~470 to 501 °C, accumulated strain of ~0.064 to 17.5, strain rates of ~0.04 to 2 s −1 , and the resultant material flow velocity of ~1.6 × 10 −4 m s −1 to ~2.4 × 10 −3 m s −1 across the gear tooth, establishing spatially varying deform

title: Robust and Wide-Range Friction Regulation via Interfacial Bridging-Promoted Hydration Switching in Phase-Separated Gels
abstract: Abstract Interfacial friction strongly influences materials performance, but achieving controllable friction with both high robustness and wide-range tunability remains difficult. In conventional friction regulation systems based on phase separations, rigid and incompatible hydrophilic–hydrophobic interfaces often cause interfacial cracking and poor stability. Here, inspired by the toughening mechanism of cartilage, we introduce amphiphilic bridging segments between hydrophilic and hydrophobic phases to construct an interfacial bridging nanophase-separated gel (IBNSGel) for robust friction control. This design transforms the fragile phase interface into a tough bridging interphase, suppresses aggregation, promotes uniform nanophase separation, and enhances interfacial stability during hydration-induced phase separation. Owing to this bridging effect, IBNSGel exhibits synergistic surface-bulk friction switching upon hydration: the surface forms a stable hydration layer for excellent lubrication, while the bulk hardens with higher modulus and lower damping, reducing conformal contact dissipation. As a result, this gel achieves stable, reversible, and wide-range coefficient of friction (CoF) switching during hydration–dehydration, with switching ratios of 150 at the macroscale and 330 at the microscale. Based on its excellent multimedium stability and biocompatibility, this friction control material demonstrates great application potential in smart medical devices, soft robots,

title: Comparative Frictional Resistance of Conventional, Self-Ligating, and Ceramic Orthodontic Brackets with Different Archwires: An In-Vitro Study
abstract: Background The bracket-archwire interface friction affects the force for orthodontic tooth movement during sliding mechanics. The material of the brackets, type of ligation, and the thickness of the archwire can vary in resistance to the sliding action of the ligature, and may thus influence the choice of the force. Objective This study aimed to compare static and kinetic frictional resistances of conventional stainless-steel, passive self-ligating stainless-steel and monocrystalline ceramic brackets against three clinically common archwires. Materials and Methods A laboratory model with 108 bracket-wire specimens was designed as a 3 × 3 factorial experiment with 12 specimens per combination. The slots were all 0.022”. The archwires were 0.014-inch nickel-titanium (NiTi), 0.016 × 0.022- inch NiTi, and 0.019 × 0.025-inch stainless steel (SS). Standardized elastomeric modules were used to ligate the conventional metal and ceramic brackets, while the passive self-ligating brackets were tested with their built-in clips. Artificial saliva was used at 37 °C and the testing machine applied a force at 5 mm/min to the specimen: static friction was represented by the peak force required to initiate sliding and kinetic friction by the mean force during the continued sliding. The data were analyzed by two-way ANOVA and Tukey tests (α = 0.05). Results The static friction of passive self-ligating brackets (0.64 ± 0.44 N) was lowest, followed by conventional metal brackets (1.36 ± 0.57 N) a

title: Intelligent Near-Infrared-Responsive MXene-Derived Hierarchical Heterostructures for On-Demand Friction Modulation and Sustainable Robust Anticorrosion
abstract: Current research predominantly focuses on the synthesis of novel lubricants for friction reduction, with limited attention given to intelligently responsive lubricating materials adapted for complex environments. This study proposes a near-infrared responsive intelligent lubrication system based on heterostructure assembled from fluorinated graphene and MXene. A zero-dimensional and two-dimensional hierarchical system is constructed to enhance the binding between the epoxy resin and the organic framework. This system demonstrates outstanding photothermal responsiveness and self-healing properties, enabling dynamic regulation of lubrication behaviors via near-infrared irradiation. After 21 days of immersion treatment, its impedance still maintains a high level of 2.76 × 108 Ω·cm2, while the friction coefficient is reduced from 0.13 to 0.03. Notably, the system retains good stability even after undergoing 14,400 reciprocating friction cycles. When subjected to 168 h of ultraviolet irradiation, the friction coefficient only rises slightly to 0.04, which indicates better anti-UV aging performance in comparison with pure epoxy resin. This study offers a novel design approach for the development of intelligent protective materials that integrate environmental responsiveness, long-term corrosion resistance, UV resistance, and high-efficiency lubrication.

title: Metallurgical and Mechanical Property Investigation of ETP Cu Similar Hybrid Friction Welds for Nuclear Fusion Applications
abstract: The evolution of microstructure and mechanical properties in electrolytic tough-pitch (ETP) copper subjected to hybrid friction welding (HFW) was investigated. The effect of introducing a programmable brake on the flywheel’s rotation while maintaining constant friction and forging pressures was explored. The welded joints were examined through a series of investigations, including optical and scanning electron microscopy with electron backscatter diffraction, tensile and microhardness testing, followed by fractography. The optimised weld achieved the highest ultimate tensile strength (≈274 MPa), a 7.87% increase over the base material, and the greatest elongation (~22%), with ductile fractures and visible necking. The measured hardness distribution depicted higher values for the weld zone compared to the thermo-mechanically affected zone, both expressing a significant decrease from the heat-affected zone and base material due to pre-welding strain hardening existing within the copper alloy. EBSD analysis on the weld zone and thermo-mechanically affected zones revealed the presence of refined grains, with low grain orientation spread (GOS) and kernel average misorientation (KAM) values, which indicated the occurrence of dynamic recrystallisation (DRX) mechanisms during HFW. HFW was able to successfully produce ETP Cu-similar welds with 98.1% joint efficiency.

title: Optimization of Friction Stir Welding Parameters for Improving the Mechanical Properties of Aluminum Alloy Joints
journal: Journal of Renewable Energy and Smart Device
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) performance depends on the interaction among processing parameters rather than individual operating conditions. This study examined the effects of rotational speed (800, 1000, and 1200 rpm), travel speed (40, 60, and 80 mm/min), and axial force (4, 6, and 8 kN) on the mechanical properties of 6-mm AA6061-T6 butt joints. A 3 × 3 × 3 full factorial design with three reported replicates per condition yielded 81 mechanical-test observations, covering ultimate tensile strength (UTS), yield strength, elongation, and hardness. Factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) and coded quadratic regression were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 31. All three parameters showed significant main effects across the four mechanical responses (p < .001), while the Rotation × Travel interaction was significant for each response. Rotational speed exhibited the largest partial effect size for UTS (partial η² = .807). The quadratic regression models explained 72.1%–84.6% of the response variance and identified 1200 rpm, 80 mm/min, and 8 kN as the highest-predicted UTS setting among the 27 evaluated combinations, with a predicted UTS of 280.39 MPa and a calculated joint efficiency of 90.45%. These findings demonstrate the importance of considering parameter interactions when selecting FSW operating conditions, while limiting the model-based recommendation to the investigated material, tool configuration, and experimental range.

title: Topological Unification of Anomalous Fracture and Friction in Solids via Dynamic Homotopy Manifold Evolution
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Classical continuum mechanics and linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) adopt a strictly local paradigm, interpreting fracture initiation, crack propagation, and frictional slip via local stress concentration, material disorder, or inertial dynamic instability. Despite widespread success in conventional mechanical behaviors, this framework fails to explain a series of deterministic, reproducible anomalies observed in homogeneous, low-defect media: quasi-static wavy crack oscillation, spontaneous micro-branching in defect-free brittle solids, biaxial-stress-induced anomalous shift of fracture threshold, and dual-scale stick–slip on atomically flat interfaces. This work establishes a dynamic homotopy manifold evolution framework for solid mechanics. The core physical mechanism lies in quasi-static boundary constraint evolution, which continuously deforms the system’s configuration homotopy manifold, accumulates topological charge, generates finite homotopy obstructions, and eventually triggers cross-class topological reconnection. Crucially, the proposed topology does not override classical elasticity or fracture criteria. Local stress remains the fundamental dynamical threshold, while topological structures independently renormalize the effective energy barrier and select topologically admissible evolutionary paths. Closed-form mathematical definitions of homotopy manifold, topological charge density, homotopy obstruction functional, and effective topological barrier are pr

title: Structural Response of Al–Cu–Mg Alloy to Friction–Stir Processing and Solution Treatment: Effect of Initial State
abstract: Due to the severe plastic deformation introduced into the parent material during friction–stir processing (FSP), the original microstructure is often substantially replaced. As a result, it is sometimes believed that the FSP–processed microstructure is largely independent of the initial material state. While this assumption holds true for non-heat-treatable aluminium alloys, this study challenges its universality for heat–treatable alloys. Using the 2519 Al–Cu–Mg alloy as a model system, it is demonstrated that а transitioning from the initial hot–rolled state to solution–treated (W) and aged (T6) temper conditions significantly reduces the processing temperature under identical FSP parameters. This leads to substantial changes in the resulting microstructure, particularly in the precipitation pattern, thereby exerting a pronounced effect on the mechanical performance and annealing behaviour of the FSP–processed materials. It is deduced that this phenomenon was associated, at least partially, with the variations in thermal conductivity caused by differences in solute content within the aluminium matrix.

title: Study on Bonding Performance of Double-Layer Ultra-Thin Friction Course of Asphalt Pavement
abstract: ABSTRACT To reduce the material consumption and resource waste associated with conventional milling and repaving of aged ultra-thin friction courses (UTFCs), this study proposes a rehabilitation strategy in which a new UTFC is overlaid on an existing UTFC to form a double-layer UTFC and investigates its interlayer bonding performance. Interlayer shear and pull-off tests were conducted to evaluate the bonding behavior of the double-layer system. In addition, image analysis techniques, including computed tomography scanning and three-dimensional reconstruction, were used to characterize the porosity distribution and tack coat migration within the interlayer zone of double-layer UTFC structures with different surface texture depths. Owing to the inherently high porosity of UTFC mixtures, the tack coat can migrate both upward and downward through interfacial voids during specimen preparation and subsequent loading. The results indicate that the interlayer bonding performance is jointly controlled by the surface texture depth of the existing UTFC and the tack coat dosage, with the tack coat dosage exerting a more pronounced influence. The interlayer shear modulus can serve as an effective indicator for evaluating interlayer bonding quality and shows a strong correlation with both interlayer shear strength and pull-off strength. Under different tack coat dosages, an under-compacted zone with varying spatial extent consistently formed near the interlayer interface. Further analysis

title: AI Safety Technology Implementation in High-Risk Manufacturing Processes : Focusing on Implementation Friction and Acceptance Infrastructure
journal: Forum of Public Safety and Culture
abstract: This study aims to analyze the structure of implementation friction that arises as artificial intelligence(AI)-based safety technologies introduced into high-risk manufacturing processes become embedded in safety behavior and safety culture, and to derive stakeholder-specific measures for building an acceptance infrastructure that mitigates such friction. Three core analytic criteria—understand-ability, trustworthiness, and participatory capacity—together with a supplementary institutional-linkage criterion were deductively derived from the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology, trust-in-automation theory, and safety-behavior theory, and ten domestic and twelve international core studies(twenty-two in total), together with institutional and policy materials, were coded according to an a-priors code-book in a theory-driven qualitative document analysis that combines deductive coding with inductive categorization. The findings indicate that friction differs by technology type: surveillance and privacy concerns for computer-vision systems, wearing burden and bio-metric-data concerns for sensor/wearable systems, and false alarms and opacity for predictive-warning systems. Korean policy has actively supported the diffusion of smart safety equipment, but the acceptance infrastructure—prior explanation, data-use agreement, explainable warnings, false-alarm feedback, and on-site learning—remains comparatively underdeveloped. title: A Pickering emulsion strategy for low-friction and wear paraffin/epoxy phase-transition lubricating composite coating
abstract: Although the incorporation of phase-change materials (PCMs) can provide active thermal management to mitigate coating failures induced by frictional heat, the inherent softness of PCMs often limits their ability to enhance the mechanical and wear properties of epoxy-based coatings. Herein, an oil-in-water Pickering emulsion approach was employed to fabricate three types of solid-liquid phase-transition lubricating coatings, using paraffin wax (PW) as the oil phase and various nano-reinforcements (halloysite nanotube (HNT), SiO2 and TiO2) as stabilizers. This method produced composite coatings with a dense and pore-free microstructure due to its effective control over filler particle size and dispersion uniformity. The effects of emulsion content and various nanofillers on the mechanical properties, interfacial temperature, and tribological performance of the coatings were investigated. The composite coating prepared from 5 g HNT@PW Pickering emulsion exhibited a low friction coefficient (0.075) and low wear rate (9.3 × 10-7 mm3/(N·m)). Even under prolonged sliding (150,000 cycles, 5655 m sliding distance), the coating demonstrated outstandingly stable and durable friction-reduction and anti-wear performance, highlighting its potential for engineering applications. This behavior originates from the combined action of the PW solid-liquid phase transition, forming a lubricating film and reducing interfacial temperature, and the strengthening effect of nanoparticles, which improv

title: Skin-Contact Wearables Made from Photopolymers: Occlusion, Sweat, Friction, Sensitisation and Long-Term Use
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A skin-contact wearable made by vat photopolymerisation is a device-skin system, not merely a cured material. Occlusion changes hydration and barrier function; sweat changes ionic strength, pH and transport; motion produces friction, pressure and microclimate cycling; cleaning and ageing modify the surface; and residual or newly generated constituents can create irritation or sensitisation hazards. A one- time material assay under dry, static conditions therefore cannot qualify prolonged or repeated wear. This review defines a risk-based architecture for qualifying photopolymer wearables in their finished, clinically relevant use state. It freezes the print, wash, cure, finish, cleaning and ageing configuration; maps anatomical contact, duty cycle and vulnerable populations; separates irritation from sensitisation; combines chemical characterisation with occluded extraction and simulated-sweat exposure; and evaluates pressure, shear, roughness, moisture accumulation and mechanical durability as interacting but non-interchangeable evidence. Non-compensatory gates prevent favourable cytotoxicity, chemistry or mechanics from masking an unresolved dermal hazard. The result is a traceable qualification plan with predefined escalation, wear-stop and change-control rules, without prescribing a universal process window or product-specific acceptance limit. title: Solvent‐Free Dry Friction‐Enabled Self‐Stabilized Liquid Metal Micro/Nanoparticles Toward Stretchable Electronics
abstract: Liquid metal (LM) combines high electrical conductivity with fluidic deformability, making them promising for conductive inks, stretchable networks, and composite sensing materials. In practice, bulk LM is transformed into micro/nano-particles (LMPs) to improve stability and processability for composites. LMPs are typically prepared via shear, ultrasonication, or microfluidics in liquid media, requiring subsequent processing to obtain dry particles. Herein, inspired by friction-induced aggregation during cream application, a dry-state friction strategy is developed for solvent-free fabrication of LMPs. During friction, bulk LM is continuously fragmented, while freshly exposed surfaces rapidly oxidize in air to form robust shells. Unlike conventional liquids, which rapidly coalesce after shear, this structure prevents re-coalescence, yielding stable core-shell LMPs. Particle size can be tuned by adjusting friction parameters, including pressure, speed, and duration, and alkaline surface modification enables control over morphology and oxide shell thickness. The as-prepared LMPs exhibit excellent stability in air and liquid, with no corrosion of metal substrates. Incorporation into a polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP)-fructose matrix produces a sensing gel with stable electromechanical response, good durability, and degradable and recyclable characteristics. This work provides a simple route for LMPs, advancing their use in wearable sensors and soft electronics.

title: Feasibility Study on the Production of Fillet Welds with Defined Throat Thickness Using Wire-Based Corner Fillet Friction Stir Welding
journal: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
abstract: Friction stir welding of T- and corner-joint configurations is challenging due to restricted tool accessibility, complex material flow and the limited availability of material for the formation of load-bearing fillet-weld geometries. This study introduces wire-based corner fillet friction stir welding (W-CFFSW), a solid-state joining process in which filler wire is continuously transported, plasticised and supplied into the internal corner region through a rotating extrusion screw. A stationary shoulder confines and shapes the deposited material, enabling the formation of fillet welds with a defined throat thickness. Single- and double-sided fillet-weld geometries were produced in 3.0 mm thick EN AW-6082-T6 sheets using EN AW-6082 filler wire. A throat thickness of 4.5 mm was successfully generated by adapting the supplied filler volume to the targeted fillet geometry. Metallographic investigations revealed characteristic FSW microstructural zones and pronounced material flow within the weld nugget zone, while no macroscopic pores or voids were observed in the investigated cross-sections. The hardness distribution exhibited the characteristic W-shaped profile of precipitation-hardenable aluminium alloys. Bending tests showed no separation of the bonding interfaces, with cracking occurring in the adjacent sheet material rather than within the fillet welds. title: Experimental and numerical investigations on the mechanical behavior of friction stir stitch welded AA6016-T4 sheets using XFEM
abstract: Friction stir stitch welding enables short solid-state welds with good strength properties while avoiding the cost-intensive system technology associated with conventional friction stir welding. This study quantifies how the orientation of friction stir stitch welds influence the static strength of AA6016-T4 lap joints and identifies the underlying failure mechanisms. Five weld variants with an identical total weld length of 30 mm: single welds, double welds, specimens containing two weld exits or two weld starts, and a conventional friction stir lap weld reference were produced with a self-developed, robot-guided welding gun and characterized by metallography, hardness testing, tensile shear tests, and digital image correlation. The lap weld interface was additionally modeled in ABAQUS using XFEM with a cohesive segments approach. The double stitch welds reached a maximum lap shear strength of 10.73 kN, corresponding to a joint efficiency of 99.2 % relative to the base material, while single welds exceeded 84 %. The conventional friction stir lap weld reference reached only 52.4 %. The strength increase is attributed to the plunge and, in particular, the tool exit regions, which locally reduce the severity of the hook and cold-lap imperfections. Failure consistently initiated at the more pronounced hook in the weld start region. title: Analysis of the Effect of Friction Media Type on the Static Electric Charge Strength of Latex Balloons Using a Completely Randomized Design
abstract: Static electricity generated by friction has long been recognized; however, the magnitude and consistency of the electric charge produced on everyday materials such as latex balloons have rarely been evaluated quantitatively. Different rubbing materials were expected to produce different levels of static electric charge. This study aimed to examine the effect of different rubbing materials on the strength of the static electric charge generated on latex balloons and to identify the rubbing material that produced the strongest charge. The experiment employed a Completely Randomized Design (CRD) with one factor consisting of three treatment levels: human hair (P1), nylon/parachute fabric (P2), and wool/sweater fabric (P3). Each treatment was replicated five times. Each balloon was rubbed 25 times in one direction and then positioned 5 cm away from a tissue paper strip measuring 2 × 5 cm. The duration for which the tissue adhered to the balloon (seconds) was recorded and analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA). The findings demonstrated that the type of rubbing material significantly determined the effectiveness of triboelectric charge generation on latex balloons

title: Multi-Criteria Optimization of Friction Stir Welding Process Parameters: A Comparative Research and Review Analysis
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) is a solid-state joining technology whose performance depends strongly on the coordinated selection of process parameters. Tool rotational speed, traverse speed, material combination, and other controllable variables influence mechanical performance, corrosion behavior, joint quality, and process stability. Because these responses can conflict with one another, conventional single-response optimization is insufficient for many practical FSW applications. This research and review paper develops a comparative analytical framework for understanding how response surface methodology (RSM), regression analysis, multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM), TOPSIS, WASPAS, MORSM, grey relational analysis, and intelligent multi-objective optimization approaches have been applied to FSW parameter selection. Only the ten supplied references are synthesized. The analysis indicates that MCDM-oriented approaches provide a systematic mechanism for converting multiple performance criteria into an integrated decision, while RSM and regression-based methods provide stronger process-response modeling capabilities. TOPSIS and grey relational analysis are particularly useful when several competing quality characteristics must be considered simultaneously, whereas WASPAS and hybrid MCDM approaches extend the decision space through alternative weighting and aggregation mechanisms. The reviewed evidence also indicates a research gap concerning unified optimization architectures

title: Cross-compliance compactness in three-dimensional frictional contact: Matched-interface existence and implicit rate-and-state refinements
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Unrefereed mathematical candidate. Compact normal-tangential cross compliance supplies unknown-pressure incremental Signorini-Coulomb existence for smooth matched anchored bodies, without small friction. A separate theorem classifies an unrestricted dominated weak-product property, not contact existence. Prescribed-pressure rate-and-state refinements remain a distinct model. title: Microstructural evolution and tribological and corrosion performance of friction stir welded AZ91 magnesium alloy at different rotational speeds
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part L Journal of Materials Design and Applications
abstract: This study investigates the influence of tool rotational speed on the microstructural evolution, wear behavior, and corrosion performance of friction stir welded AZ91 magnesium alloy. The friction stir welding (FSW) process was carried out on a cylindrical threaded pin at rotation speeds of 700, 800, 900, and 1000 rpm, with the traveling speed held constant. The cylindrical threaded pin facilitated material flow, frictional heat generation, and dynamic recrystallization by increasing stirring. Optical microscopy results indicated grain refinement, with a decrease in grain size from 6.2 μm at 700 rpm to 4.1 μm at 900 rpm, corresponding to a reduction of about 33.9%. Further increasing the speed to 1000 rpm resulted in grain coarsening from 4.1 μm at 900 rpm to 5.9 μm, about 43.9% larger. The Scanning electron microscope (SEM) investigation showed fragmentation and rearrangement of β-Mg 17 Al 12 precipitates. The most uniform precipitates were distributed at 900 rpm, while there were much precipitation dissolution and precipitate-free regions at 1000 rpm. X-ray diffraction confirmed that the main phases are α-Mg, β-Mg 17 Al 12 , Al 8 Mn 5 , and MgZn 2 . The lowest wear depth and coefficient of friction (COF) values were achieved for the sample at 900 rpm, at about 1800 μm and 0.58–0.62, respectively. title: Process window and mechanical interlocking in friction stir welding of laser-textured Al-7075 and PEEK
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology
abstract: Polymer–metal hybrid joints are attractive for lightweight structural applications. However, their practical implementation is often limited by failure at the metal–polymer interface rather than by intrinsic material capability. To address this challenge, this work combines nanosecond laser-surface texturing with pinless Friction Stir Welding (FSW) to establish a controlled interfacial architecture in Al-7075/PEEK lap joints and systematically identify a stable, reproducible FSW processing window for reliable joint formation. Wave-shaped microgrooves are created on the aluminum surface by laser before joining to promote polymer-metal mechanical interlocking. Rotational speed, dwell time, and plunge displacement are varied, while joint integrity, groove preservation, and process stability are used as the evaluation criteria. A stable processing region was established primarily at 3000–4500 rpm, with dwell times of 2–6 s and plunge displacements of 0.1–0.2 mm, where sufficient polymer flow occurred without excessive thermal softening of PEEK or distortion of the microgrooves. Successful joints were obtained under restricted conditions at 6000 rpm, limited to low plunge displacement and short dwell time. Outside this processing window, higher rotational speed and longer dwell time were associated with PEEK over-softening and interfacial degradation, consistent with increased thermal input. title: Bargaining on the Shadow of the Law: Legal Frictions for Women Cross-Border Commuters Between Zimbabwe and South Africa
abstract: Cross-border commuting by women in low and middle-income countries remains severely under-researched, legally unrecognised, and wrongly merged into international migration data. This paper applies a four-step distributive analysis of the law to examine the legal frictions of stop and delay experienced by women cross-border commuters at the South Africa–Zimbabwe border. Drawing on qualitative fieldwork conducted in March 2025 in Musina and Johannesburg, including interviews with women commuters and civil society professionals, a focus group, border observation, and systematic legal mapping, the analysis identifies the primary norms generating frictions of stop and delay; the second-level norms from other bodies of law that compound their effects; the actors and interests the legal architecture structures; and the resulting distribution of costs and benefits. The paper makes three contributions. Methodologically, it demonstrates that the distributive analysis of the law offers mobilities scholarship a framework capable of tracing how formally neutral legal norms generate unequal outcomes across diverse groups of actors. Empirically and from a feminist mobilities perspective, it disaggregates women cross-border commuters into two analytically distinct sub-groups: documented women traders and undocumented women without capital, showing that legal costs, physical danger, and exposure to violence accumulate heterogeneously even within this category, while the benefits of crossing,

title: Friction–wear behaviour of wood–plastic composites against WC–Co under low–temperature sliding conditions
abstract: This study investigated the friction and wear behaviour of wood–plastic composite (WPC) against WC–Co under dry and low–temperature conditions using 5 min pin–on–disc tests. The effects of normal load and rotational speed on the coefficient of friction (CoF), wear rate, and worn surface morphology were analysed. The results revealed that increasing normal load and rotational speed reduced the CoF but increased the wear rate. Compared with dry conditions, low–temperature conditions reduced the CoF by 4.2–10.7% and the wear rate by 23.2–57.3%. ANOVA identified normal load as the dominant factor affecting both responses. Test environment, normal load, rotational speed, and the load–speed interaction significantly affected the CoF, whereas only normal load and rotational speed significantly affected the wear rate. Low–temperature conditions restricted HDPE matrix softening and plastic flow and improved the stability of the wood flour–HDPE interface. This reduced material adhesion, wood flour pull–out, and interfacial damage, resulting in lower CoF and wear rate. These findings provide a clearer understanding of the tribological mechanisms of WPC under low–temperature sliding conditions.

title: Characterization of residual stresses in dissimilar metal rotary friction welded pipes with and without an interlayer and dissimilar cladding
abstract: Dissimilar metal welds are critical in the energy and petrochemical sectors, where high-strength low alloy (HSLA) steels are joined to ferritic or austenitic stainless steels. Conventional arc welding requires buttering layers to prevent heat-affected zone (HAZ) embrittlement but is slow, stress-inducing, and prone to brittle intermetallic formation. Post-weld heat treatment is often impractical for large components and ineffective when materials have different creep resistances. Solid-state processes such as rotary friction welding (RFW) offer a promising alternative, minimising residual stresses through uniform circumferential heating and reduced thermal gradients. Recent experiment (RB2500036) at Engin-X on solid cylinder specimens showed that RFW significantly lowers residual stresses compared with arc welds. Introducing a dissimilar interlayer prior to RFW can confine the HAZ within the interlayer, effectively converting a dissimilar joint into a similar one, while post-buttering heat treatment (PBHT) may further enhance performance. The proposed research will extend RFW from solid cylinders to full pipe welds, examining stress development and microstructural evolution in dissimilar pipe joints, with and without interlayers or internal cladding, to assess the feasibility of RFW for industrial-scale applications.

title: Characterization of residual stresses in dissimilar metal rotary friction welded pipes with and without an interlayer and dissimilar cladding
abstract: Dissimilar metal welds are critical in the energy and petrochemical sectors, where high-strength low alloy (HSLA) steels are joined to ferritic or austenitic stainless steels. Conventional arc welding requires buttering layers to prevent heat-affected zone (HAZ) embrittlement but is slow, stress-inducing, and prone to brittle intermetallic formation. Post-weld heat treatment is often impractical for large components and ineffective when materials have different creep resistances. Solid-state processes such as rotary friction welding (RFW) offer a promising alternative, minimising residual stresses through uniform circumferential heating and reduced thermal gradients. Recent experiment (RB2500036) at Engin-X on solid cylinder specimens showed that RFW significantly lowers residual stresses compared with arc welds. Introducing a dissimilar interlayer prior to RFW can confine the HAZ within the interlayer, effectively converting a dissimilar joint into a similar one, while post-buttering heat treatment (PBHT) may further enhance performance. The proposed research will extend RFW from solid cylinders to full pipe welds, examining stress development and microstructural evolution in dissimilar pipe joints, with and without interlayers or internal cladding, to assess the feasibility of RFW for industrial-scale applications.

title: Modeling of Thermomechanical Asymmetry in Friction Stir Welding of MA2-1 Magnesium Alloy Plates Using the CEL Method
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) is a promising solid-state joining process for magnesium al-loys that avoids defects characteristic of fusion welding. In the present study, a three-dimensional, fully coupled thermomechanical model of FSW of two 3.0-mm-thick MA2-1 (AZ31B) alloy plates was developed using the Coupled Eulerian–Lagrangian (CEL) approach in Abaqus/Explicit. The constitutive behavior of the material was de-scribed using the Johnson–Cook model (A = 172 MPa, n = 0.456, m = 0.90), while contact interaction was represented by a modified Coulomb–Tresca friction law (μ = 0.40, δ = 0.60). A parametric study of 11 configurations was performed by varying the shoulder diameter R_sh (6–12 mm), pin diameter R_pin (2–4 mm), rotational speed ω (600–1200 rpm), and traverse speed v (60–180 mm/min). A functional specialization of the parame-ters was established: R_sh dominates the thermal regime (exponent +0.58 for T_peak) and the stress state (−1.67 for σ_mean); R_pin controls the width of the stirring zone (W_mix, exponent +0.88); and rotational speed ω is the key factor governing AS/RS deformation asymmetry (K_asm(PEEQ) = 1.10–1.40). Power-law regression equations were obtained for T_peak, σ_mean, PEEQ_max, and W_mix, with R² ≥ 0.95. Spatial correlation analysis confirmed the independence of the thermal and deformation zones, with r(T, PEEQ) = 0.07. title: The Role of Ultra‐Thin Passive Films and Organic Adsorbates on Aluminum Chips for a Friction‐Induced Solid‐State Recycling Process
abstract: Friction‐induced recycling is a method to recycle aluminum with a lower energy footprint than conventional methods. However, the quality of a metal–metal joint is strongly influenced by surface contamination, in particular by naturally formed oxide layers. Octadecyl phosphonic acid and methyl diphosphonic acid self‐assembled monolayers (SAMs) are deposited on aluminum chips bound for recycling in order to improve their storage stability. In addition, chips were etched with NaOH for varying amounts of time to further increase hydrophobicity through increased roughness as well as to create more binding sites for the phosphonic acids. Adsorption is confirmed via FTIR and XPS. Water contact angle measurements show the highest hydrophobicity for ODPA‐coated chips, followed by the bare substrate and MDPA coatings. As a side effect, it is also found that ODPA coatings and MDPA coatings, to a lesser extent, reduce friction within the bulk material. However, the presence of ODPA, especially in combination with etching, deteriorates the mechanical performance of the recycled product, making the removal of the molecule prior to recycling vital. Other pretreatments have next to no influence on the mechanical properties of the recyclates.

title: Thermo‐Mechanical Coupled Modeling and Experimental Investigation of Damage Evolution in Composite Structures During Friction Stir Blind Riveting
abstract: ABSTRACT Friction stir blind riveting (FSBR) is a promising joining technology for composite–metal hybrid structures; however, damage formation and evolution in composite laminates during the riveting process remain insufficiently understood. In this study, an integrated experimental and numerical approach was developed to investigate damage mechanisms in CF/PEEK–AA6061 FSBR joints. A thermo‐mechanically coupled finite element model was established using ABAQUS/Explicit to simulate the entire riveting process, including rivet penetration, material deformation, temperature evolution, and delamination propagation. The model predictions of penetration morphology, force–displacement response, temperature distribution, and damage evolution showed good agreement with experimental observations, demonstrating its capability for process and damage prediction. Combining ultrasonic C‐scan characterization, cross‐sectional analysis, and multi‐physical field evolution from simulations, the influence mechanism of rivet structures on composite damage was systematically revealed. The results indicate that rivet‐induced damage is primarily governed by the interaction between material removal behavior and thermo‐mechanical loading. Rivets dominated by frictional extrusion generate concentrated stresses and localized high‐temperature regions, leading to matrix softening and accelerated interlaminar damage propagation. title: Disentangling the assembly of the central and diffuse stellar components in galaxy clusters through dynamical friction and tidal stripping
journal: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
abstract: Abstract In galaxy clusters, it is common to conceptually distinguish the central, brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) from the more diffuse intracluster light (ICL). So far, however, this distinction has lacked a clear physical basis, confusing both theoretical and observational studies. We address this by presenting a dynamically motivated definition of the two stellar components, evaluated using cluster zoom simulations from the Three Hundred project. We start with a motivational hindcasting approach, robustly tracing stars from the centres of 107 present-day clusters back through the merger hierarchy. We find that the majority of the final BCG stellar mass is typically contributed by the central galaxies of only 3–5 progenitor haloes. Most accreted galaxies contribute no stars to the BCG, instead surviving as satellites or depositing stellar material throughout the cluster. This naturally leads to a definition of the BCG stellar population as originating from the central galaxies of the most massive infalling systems. These are delivered to the cluster centre via efficient dynamical friction and subsequently undergo violent relaxation. The ICL arises from the complementary population of stars tidally stripped from the outskirts of all infalling systems. We therefore develop a forecasting method, identifying stars in the BCG and ICL via the dynamical fates of their originating stellar systems. Applying this to 261 clusters, we find the resulting components remain spatially inte

title: Comparative assessment of secondary preheating strategies on mechanical performance and microstructural evolution in friction stir welding of AA6061-T6
abstract: Friction stir welding (FSW) of age-hardened AA6061-T6 causes localized softening due to dissolution of Mg₂Si precipitates. Secondary preheating aims to improve material flow and reduce thermal gradients, but the directional effect of heat application remains poorly quantified. This study systematically compares four thermal conditions; Room Temperature (RT), Top Heating (TH) using flame to heat materials top surface, Back Heating (BH) via backing plate and Combined Heating (CH) using top and bottom sources simultaneously during FSW of 3 mm sheets. Preheat was set at 100 °C for all methods. Experiments for all the strategies were conducted with two rotational speeds (950 and 1300 RPM) and three traverse speeds (45, 65 and 85 mm/min). RT-FSW produces the highest average ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 178 MPa with a joint efficiency of 57.6% but with high variability. TH-FSW improves average flexural strength, high average weld nugget microhardness but lowest impact toughness dropping to 2.3 J. BH-FSW produces poorest tensile performance with an average joint efficiency of 51.5%. CH-FSW observed slight reduction in UTS relative to RT-FSW, however, it provides the most favorable balance across all mechanical properties with highest ductility 11.8%, highest impact toughness 12.5 J, highest average weld center microhardness and lowest UTS variability.
