title: Polymeric Sealing Materials in Pneumatic Actuators: From Degradation Mechanisms to Failure Diagnostics and Service-Life Prediction
abstract: Polymeric sealing materials play a critical role in the reliability, efficiency, and dynamic performance of pneumatic actuators. Their long-term behavior is governed by the interaction between polymer structure, operating conditions, degradation mechanisms, tribological damage, and loss of sealing functionality. This review compares the principal sealing materials used or considered for pneumatic systems, including polyurethane (PU), thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR), hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber (HNBR), fluoroelastomers (FKM), ethylene–propylene–diene rubber (EPDM), silicone elastomers, and PTFE-based materials. Particular attention is given to thermo-oxidative aging, hydrolysis, crosslinking, chain scission, swelling, compression set, fatigue, and wear. Their selection involves trade-offs between friction, wear resistance, chemical and thermal stability, elastic recovery, compression set, and leakage performance. Material-characterization and condition-assessment methods, including scanning electron microscopy/energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (SEM/EDS), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), thermal analysis, mechanical testing, and tribological measurements, are evaluated with respect to their ability to detect material deterioration. Accelerated-aging and service-life prediction approaches are also discussed. The literature shows that no single material is optimal under all pneumat

title: Chemical Engineering Explained: Processes, Materials & Industrial Production Systems
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Chemical Engineering Explained: Processes, Materials & Industrial Production Systems serves as an open educational resource (OER) curriculum framework and foundational reference manual connecting molecular chemistry to full-scale industrial operations. Developed by Prep4Uni.Online, this module synthesizes physical transport phenomena, chemical thermodynamics, reaction engineering, and modern computational workflows. Core Pedagogical Coverage: Systems Engineering & IDEF0 Modeling: Deconstructs chemical production via Inputs (feedstocks, physical operating data), Controls (HAZOP, environmental codes, OSHA safety layers), Mechanisms (dynamic simulation, pilot facilities), and Outputs (scalable, consistent manufacturing). Reaction Design & Isothermal Kinetics: Mathematical formulation and operational analysis of Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors (CSTR) and Plug Flow Reactors (PFR), including Damköhler number scaling, residence time distributions, and Arrhenius activation kinetics. Unit Operations & Separation Processes: Multiphase mass balances, binary distillation column fraction calculations, Darcy-Weisbach hydraulic friction modeling, and thermal heat exchanger duty evaluation. Process Safety & Decarbonization: Green chemistry paradigms, zero-liquid discharge (ZLD) water remediation, amine absorption for carbon capture, and green hydrogen electrolyzer networks. Self-Assessment & Quantitative Problems: Comprehensive foundational, scenario-based, and analytical practice problems

title: 3D‐Printed Titanium Gyroid Scaffold Structure Integrated With Tough Hybrid Materials for Cartilage Replacement
abstract: A novel hybrid implant for cartilage replacement was developed by integrating a silica‐poly(tetrahydrofuran) (SiO 2 ‐PolyTHF) sol–gel derived biomaterial into a 3D‐printed titanium (Ti) gyroid scaffold. Potential applications include knee cartilage or focal cartilage replacement. The hybrid material provides a cartilage‐mimicking, low‐friction bearing surface, while the Ti gyroid structure serves as a bone anchor to enable biological fixation through bone ingrowth (mechanical interlock). Integration of the hybrid into the Ti scaffold was optimized by tailoring the tetrahydrofuran:(3‐glycidyloxypropyl)trimethoxysilane (THF:GPTMS) ratio to control gelation kinetics and shrinkage‐induced stress during sol–gel processing. This processing strategy enabled crack‐free integration of the hybrid within the Ti gyroid scaffold and promoted robust interfacial mechanical performance. The hybrid–Ti interface exhibited strong mechanical interlocking, evidenced by mechanical testing in compression, shear, and cyclic loading over a 90 day period in PBS. Tribology testing against fresh bovine cartilage revealed that the hybrid/Ti scaffold maintained a low friction coefficient against the cartilage (~0.1), comparable to native cartilage on cartilage, and significantly lower than UHMWPE on cartilage. The results highlight the hybrid/Ti gyroid scaffold as a promising solution for cartilage replacement, with advantages in mechanical performance, cartilage‐mimicking tribology, and biological integr

title: Optimization of the composition of the composite material of contact inserts for electric vehicles based on the criterion of wear resistance
abstract: The paper considers the problem of reusing spent graphite contact inserts of electric transport and improving their functional properties by modifying the composition of the composite material. Modern approaches to the formation of graphite and copper-graphite electrical contact composites, the influence of the granulometric composition, conductive and solid lubricating additives on the electrical and tribological characteristics are analyzed. The prospects for using secondary graphite as the main raw material are shown, provided that the structural integrity and electrically conductive contacts between particles are restored. The feasibility of using carbon black to form an additional conductive network, copper powder to reduce contact resistance, and molybdenum disulfide to stabilize friction and reduce wear is substantiated. It has been established that the properties of such composites are multifactorial and nonlinear in nature, therefore the choice of composition requires comprehensive optimization with simultaneous consideration of the electrical resistance, wear resistance of the insert, and the effect on the contact wire.

title: Finite Element Analysis of Drone Impact on a Rotating Aircraft Engine Fan: Sensitivity to Blade Material and Impact Velocity
journal: Modelling—International Open Access Journal of Modelling in Engineering Science
abstract: An explicit finite element study examined the sensitivity of a rotating aircraft-engine fan to blade material and drone impact velocity. A complete 20-blade rotor and a deformable, equivalent-material quadcopter were modelled in ANSYS/LS-DYNA. Ti-6Al-4V, Ti-6242 and AA2024-T3 blades were assessed at 30, 60 and 100 m/s with an initial fan angular velocity of 283 rad/s. Nine frictional simulations and one Ti-6Al-4V frictionless case at 100 m/s were evaluated using stress, equivalent plastic strain, directional displacement, erosion and energy histories. Ti-6Al-4V produced the lowest maximum blade plastic strain at each velocity; AA2024-T3 values were 11.6–26.9 times greater despite lower equivalent stress. No fan elements were deleted, whereas drone deletion occurred in every case. The maximum-history reduction in surviving-drone kinetic energy increased with velocity, but the highest velocity did not produce the largest plastic strain in every material. Including friction increased maximum plastic strain by a factor of 6.46 in the sensitivity case. The results highlight multi-blade chronology and complementary response measures within the adopted model; local impact convergence and configuration-specific experimental validation were not established.

title: Quality Management in Academic Research: A Practical Workshop and Training Materials
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Quality management in academic research does not need to mean additional bureaucracy or the implementation of a formal quality management system. Many aspects of research quality can be strengthened through relatively simple practices that make research processes more transparent, reproducible, traceable, and resilient to error. This collection contains the presentation, facilitator resources, participant materials, exercises, and supplementary teaching materials developed for a one-day interactive workshop on quality management in academic research. The workshop is designed primarily for PhD researchers and postdoctoral researchers in the biomedical and life sciences and can be adapted to experimental, animal-based, computational, and data-intensive research environments. This workshop uses practical examples and participants' own research workflows to explore where quality is created, where it can be lost, and how lightweight quality practices can be integrated into everyday research. Particular emphasis is placed on identifying strengths and vulnerabilities in research processes, improving documentation and traceability, developing usable standard operating procedures (SOPs), learning constructively from errors, and implementing improvements without creating unnecessary administrative burden. The workshop combines short conceptual inputs with participatory exercises. Participants map research processes across dimensions such as roles and responsibilities, process steps, da

title: Comparative Development of Engineering Predictive Models for the Deformation Modulus of Granular Materials Based on Triaxial Compression Data
abstract: Accurate prediction of the deformation modulus of granular materials is important for engineering analysis, but the coupled effects of material state, particle size, and frictional resistance are difficult to represent using a single empirical relationship. This study comparatively evaluates engineering predictive models using an experimental triaxial-compression database reported in a companion study accepted for publication, comprising 25 experimentally realized material states and 75 replicate deformation-modulus measurements. Five representative granular materials were used to establish the investigated property ranges. Bulk density ρ, equivalent particle diameter deq, and internal friction angle φ were used as quantitative predictors. A Protodyakonov multifactor formulation provided the engineering baseline, with R = 0.9029, R2 = 0.4481, and RMSE = 6.39 MPa. Among four predefined analytical formulations, the four-parameter multiplicative power-law Model 1 achieved R2 = 0.8769, RMSE = 3.02 MPa. The complete quadratic response-surface model provided the strongest calibration fit R2 = 0.9129, RMSE = 2.54 MPa, whereas sequential removal of the \(d_{eq}^2\) and φ2 terms produced an eight-coefficient reduced model with R2 = 0.9046, RMSE = 2.66 MPa. Leave-one-out cross-validation changed the model ranking: Model 1 provided the lowest cross-validated error \(R_{\mathrm{CV}}^2\) = 0.8304, RMSECV = 3.54 MPa, followed by the additive linear model 4.06 MPa, reduced model 4.22 MPa, a

title: Interstitial Fluid Load Support in Human Articular Cartilage: Effects of Degeneration, Loading, and Material Properties via Combined Experimental Testing and Computational Modeling
abstract: Interstitial fluid pressurization plays a key role in cartilage mechanics, as it enables load support, reduces solid matrix stress, and limits solid-solid contact, thereby minimizing wear and friction. Because direct measurement of interstitial fluid load support is challenging, our modeling approach provides a practical means to estimate it based on experimental data. While its role has been studied experimentally and computationally, the combined effects of osteoarthritis, tissue composition/material parameters, anatomical location, and loading protocols on fluid pressurization remain poorly understood, especially in human cartilage. Here, we investigate these factors and further examine the relationship between fluid load support and friction. Human cartilage plugs (n = 40), obtained from the tibia and femur, representing varying osteoarthritic levels, underwent experimental friction testing. The axial deformation of each sample observed during testing was replicated using a sample-specific finite element model to determine constituent-specific material parameters and track interstitial fluid pressure over time. The results demonstrate that interstitial fluid load support is highly dependent on the loading protocol and particularly sensitive to variations in material parameters related to the extracellular matrix, fibrillar network, and fluid flow. These findings improve our understanding of cartilage function and inform the development of cartilage-mimicking biomaterials

title: Geotechnical Investigation of Silicomanganese Slag as a Sustainable Fill Material for Reinforced Earth Retaining Wall Construction
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
first_author: C.N.V. Satyanarayana Reddy and K. Purnanandam K. Rohith Kumar
abstract: AbstractThe increasing demand for construction materials and environmental concerns associatedwith industrial waste disposal have encouraged the exploration of alternative geomaterialsderived from industrial by-products. This study evaluates the suitability of silicomanganeseslag as a sustainable fill material for geotechnical applications through a comprehensiveexperimental investigation. The physical, hydraulic, mechanical, interface and environmentalcharacteristics of silicomanganese slag were assessed through laboratory testing, includingindex properties, compaction behaviour, permeability, shear strength, soil-geotextileinteraction, earth pressure response and leaching characteristics. The results demonstrate thatsilicomanganese slag possesses favourable characteristics of a frictional geomaterial,including low unit weight, high shear resistance, good drainage capacity and satisfactoryinteraction with geosynthetic reinforcement. The material also exhibited promisingperformance in reducing lateral earth pressure, although leaching studies identified elevatedmanganese release as an environmental limitation requiring site-specific evaluation and,where necessary, containment measures. Based on the overall evaluation, silicomanganeseslag is identified as a potential alternative to conventional fill materials for selectedgeotechnical applications such as lightweight embankments, retaining wall backfills andreinforced soil structures, subject to the environmental and durability

title: Geotechnical characterization and slope stability analysis of bottom ash material using limit equilibrium and finite element methods
abstract: Lignite and coal-fired power plants produce considerable amounts of bottom ash throughout their operating lives. The safe and economic storage of enormous quantities of bottom ash generated by power plants over the medium and long term in limited areas can become a challenging engineering problem. In this study, the geotechnical properties of bottom ash material obtained from two distinct locations in the bottom ash storage areas of a thermal power plant located in Kütahya province were determined, and slope stability properties of bottom ash material were investigated. Laboratory tests were conducted to determine the particle size distribution, specific gravity, and shear strength characteristics of the investigated bottom ash material. The laboratory tests results showed that the bottom ash material mainly consists of sand-sized particles. According to the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS), the bottom ash material can be classified as silty sand (SM) and poorly graded sand (SP). Specific gravity of the bottom ash material was measured to be relatively low compared to sand, its cohesion was determined to be about zero and negligible, and its internal friction angle was determined approximately 34°. Test results showed that behavior characteristics of the bottom ash material is similar to granular soil behavior characteristics. The slope stability performance of the bottom ash material was investigated by both limit equilibrium (LE) and finite element (FE) methods. In

title: Material removal and damage mechanisms of SiC ceramics via hydroxyl surface modification
abstract: Sintered silicon carbide (SSiC) is susceptible to brittle chipping during grinding owing to its high hardness and low fracture toughness. This study proposes a hydroxyl-based surface modification strategy via the Fenton reaction using slurries containing CeO₂, SiO₂, or TiO₂ nanoparticles. Single- and double-scratch nanoscratch tests systematically evaluated material removal behavior, mechanical responses, and damage evolution of modified SSiC. The results indicate that hydroxyl radicals (•OH) generated in the Fenton system form a low-hardness oxidation-modified layer on the SSiC surface and convert free silicon phases into soluble silicates, thereby enhancing material removal characteristics. Nanoindentation results revealed increased indentation depth, reduced hardness, and more homogeneous deformation response after modification. Following SiO₂ and TiO₂ modifications, material removal transitioned from predominantly brittle chipping to a mixed brittle-ductile mode, with a substantial extension of the elastic-plastic removal regime. Notably, under TiO₂ modification, the average removal depth in the brittle regime during single scratching decreased by 56.9%, and the friction coefficient fluctuation in double-scratch tests was minimized, signifying optimal removal stability. XPS analysis revealed that Ti-OH groups on TiO₂ nanoparticle surfaces form stable coordination with Si-OH groups on SiC, producing Si-O-C transition bonds that partly suppress silicon loss. title: Recent Progress in Extrusion and Related SPD Technologies for Metallic Materials: A Review
journal: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
abstract: Extrusion is a core branch of advanced metal forming. Over the past century, it has evolved from conventional hot and cold extrusion into a diversified family of processes that now encompasses severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques. The industrial limits of these processes are governed by a small set of dominant physical mechanisms: dynamic recrystallization (DRX), which dictates grain refinement; adiabatic heating and the associated hot shortness (surface cracking), which bound the maximum usable extrusion speed; and, in porthole-die and hybrid extrusion, the pressure-temperature-time criteria that govern solid-state seam-weld integrity. This review examines metal extrusion and the closely related SPD technologies from this mechanism-oriented perspective. First, it elucidates the fundamentals governing metal flow and deformation behavior (MFDB) during extrusion, including the primary shear zone, the dead metal zone, and container-wall friction, together with the influence of material-intrinsic factors (alloy composition and initial grain morphology) and external conditions (die design and process parameters). Second, it discusses the key role of die design and manufacturing in regulating metal flow and ensuring product precision, including the application of finite element analysis (FEA) and intelligent algorithms to die optimization. The core of this review is a comparative analysis of state-of-the-art processes, organized into two kinematically distinct categories: co

title: Compression, Local Buckling and Crushing of Printed Photopolymer Structures: Material State, Architecture and Boundary Conditions
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The compressive response of a printed photopolymer structure is not a single material property. A solid coupon may exhibit elastic deformation, yielding, cracking, barreling or confinement, while a lattice can respond through strut bending, node rotation, local cell buckling, global instability, brittle fracture, progressive crushing and densification. The measured curve also depends on as-built relative density, wall and strut fidelity, skins, platen alignment, friction, aspect ratio, contact, loading rate and the definitions used for stress, strain, plateau and densification. This review defines a non-compensatory qualification framework for monotonic compression, local buckling and crushing of solid and architected vat-printed photopolymer structures. It separates base-material constitutive response from architecture-driven response, requires the tested geometry rather than the CAD model to control interpretation, and treats boundary conditions and contact as part of the experiment. Energy absorption must retain its integration limit and mass or volume normalization. Numerical models require measured geometry, appropriate material and contact laws, imperfection treatment and independent validation at another scale, cell count, relative density or topology. The primary corpus supports mechanism-resolved evaluation across rigid, tough and elastomeric systems, but not universal plateau stresses, densification strains, topology rankings, buckling coefficients or crashworthines

title: A Study on a Stitching Device for Stabilizing Sewing Material Position Through Relative Motion of a Pressing Unit
abstract: Material friction, thickness, elasticity, and three-dimensional geometry cause slippage and positional deviations during stitching. To stabilize sewing material positions, this study proposes a device that accommodates moving and stitching unit movements through relative displacement of a local pressing unit. In the prototype, lifting and horizontal return motions overlap, and contact between the returning member and a metal stopper defines the P1 endpoint. Individual stitch lengths were measured at 30 positions on five headrest specimens. At a nominal pitch of 4.5 mm, the 150 measurements yielded a mean of 4.459 mm, sample standard deviation of 0.049 mm, and coefficient of variation of 1.108%. A conventional operator-sewn specimen set to 4.0 mm yielded a mean of 4.167 mm and sample standard deviation of 0.285 mm across 33 measurements. This is a limited descriptive case comparison because nominal pitches and specimen counts differ, and equivalence in material, sewing speed, and thread tension was not confirmed. Command-to-current-position deviations were calculated from 91,118 PLC records as auxiliary axis-tracking indicators. Tester-reported dragging, jamming, and misalignment between the upper and lower layers under unsuitable pressing conditions were documented separately. title: A Step Towards Selecting the Best Material to Design a Full Piping Network for oil transport (BAPCO - ACWA Power Network)
abstract: This capstone project evaluates how pipe material selection independently influences the microscale thermal characteristics and macroscale hydraulic efficiency of long-distance light gas oil transport pipelines. Utilizing a multi-stage computational framework, two independent numerical tools ANSYS Fluent and Pipe Flow Expert were deployed to analyze four distinct pipeline wall configurations: bare API 5L carbon steel, Corrosion-Resistant Alloy (CRA)-clad Incoloy Alloy 825, internally epoxy-coated steel, and internally High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE)-lined steel. These material configurations were tested under consistent refinery-scale operating conditions across four major fluid grades: Petrol 91, Petrol 95, Kerosene, and Diesel. On a microscale level, steady-state 2D axisymmetric Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) models built in ANSYS Fluent isolated localized fluid-wall boundary thermal dynamics across a single 30-meter segment. The results demonstrate that wall material properties exert a much stronger influence on thermal resistance than fluid type. Bare carbon steel exhibited the lowest thermal resistance, allowing rapid thermal dissipation with inner-wall heat fluxes ranging from 352 to 356 W/m². Conversely, low-conductivity polymer boundaries acted as highly effective thermal barriers, with the HDPE-lined configurations drastically minimizing inner-wall heat flux down to 267–270 W/m² and reducing heat transfer per unit length. title: Towards modeling and understanding of individual and combined effects of cross-linker and STF material modifiers in UHMWPE armor fabric
abstract: This study experimentally characterizes and numerically models a novel Ultra-High Molecular Weight Polyethylene (UHMWPE) composite fabric system for armor applications. The fabric is treated with diazirine-based crosslinker and impregnated with a shear-thickening fluid (STF), composed of fumed silica nanoparticles dispersed in a polyethylene glycol medium. Specifically, to understand the individual and combined effects of the material modifiers, three material groups were tested: (i) untreated fabric, (ii) crosslinked fabric, and (iii) crosslinked fabric impregnated with STF. Puncture/piercing testing revealed that the STF-impregnated crosslinked fabric potentially absorbed 3.3 times more energy than the control fabric, while increasing the fabric mass by 68%. Flexural rigidity increased by 283% and 317% for the crosslinked and STF-treated fabrics, respectively. Next, a macro-scale quasi-static finite element model was developed through a user-defined material subroutine. A key challenge in accurately capturing the mechanical response of such composite fabrics under puncture is the identification of probe/fabric friction as well as the element deletion parameters, which are often not reliably identifiable directly from tests at the weave form of fabric. To address this, an alternative approach based on design of computer experiments and inverse parameter identification was proposed. title: Assessment of a Two-Layer Material Point Method for Three-Dimensional Water-Granular Sloshing
abstract: Molten-pool sloshing is a critical safety concern during Core Disruptive Accidents (CDAs) in Sodium-cooled Fast Reactors (SFRs), as the inward collapse of the liquid fuel may lead to energetic neutronic recriticality. The presence of solid particles further complicates the flow physics through interphase drag, particle wall friction, and granular yielding. This study assesses a two-layer Material Point Method (MPM) for three-dimensional water-granular sloshing using pure-water comparisons and four centered water-acrylic-particle configurations from the KfK 5090 experimental campaign. The two phases use superposed momentum grids with implicit drag coupling, APIC transfer for water, and ASFLIP transfer for the granular phase. Pure-water calculations examine regional pressure sensitivity and free-surface evolution in centered and offset geometries. Closure parameters are selected using the layered saturated case D1PI-1 and are subsequently held fixed for the fully mixed case D1PI-2 and the dry-annulus cases D1P-1 and D1P-2. In D1PI-1, the five reported standardized residuals have magnitudes no greater than 1.10 under the adopted normalization, although the ensemble-mean wall and center heights are overpredicted and the center rebound exhibits appreciable realization variability. The other configurations expose substantial discrepancies in wall run-up, supported water arrival, and, for the thicker dry annulus, center rebound. journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Analytical solutions and numerical verification of small-strain moduli for granular materials: From unary to binary media
abstract: The small-strain moduli are key parameters for characterizing the physical properties of granular materials and for engineering design. To investigate its variation under complex gradation conditions, theoretical derivation and simulation-based verification were conducted. In this study, the theoretical small-strain modulus equations considering the finite friction for unary media were derived. By using the contact information of contact probability, contact participation proportion, sliding proportion, and tangential stiffness reduction coefficient, the theoretical small-strain modulus equations for binary media were further derived. Numerical models of unary/binary media were created by the Discrete Element Method (DEM) to obtain the contact information and determine the specific formula parameter values. The macroscopic moduli of the samples were measured by simulated triaxial compression tests and wave velocity tests based on DEM to further verify the modulus formulas. This study reveals that all the macroscopic modulus equations can be derived from the microscopic contact information and the contact parameters can be obtained by DEM simulation. For example, the modulus formulas for unary media align well with the simulated values, whereas the formulas align well for binary media of fine‑dominated skeletons and coarse‑dominated skeletons. title: Investigation on flow and heat transfer characteristics of phase change material slurry in twisted flat tubes
journal: International Journal of Heat and Fluid Flow
abstract: Against the backdrop of intensifying global energy supply-demand imbalances, enhancing energy utilization efficiency has become a critical challenge. As a phase change material with high energy storage density, ice slurry holds significant application value in HVAC systems. This research adopts the Euler-Euler two-fluid model to conduct a numerical investigation of the flow and heat transfer characteristics of ice slurry within twisted flat tubes. The analysis focuses on the effects of the straight section length (W) and the twist pitch length (P) of the twisted flat tube cross-section on flow patterns, resistance characteristics, heat transfer performance, and the ice particle phase change process. Results indicated that a helical secondary flow forms within the twisted flat tube, with its intensity increasing as both W and P decrease. The average friction factor (f) decreases with increasing flow velocity (u), increases with rising W and ice slurry volume fraction (α), and decreases with increasing P. The average nusselt number (Nu) increases with rising W and u, decreases with increasing P, and shows a decreasing trend with increasing α. The concentration of ice particulates exhibits a monotonic decline along the streamwise path. Higher W values and lower P values promote the melting of ice particles. Finally, empirical correlations for f and average Nu are established, with prediction deviations controlled within ±10% and ±5%, respectively. This study provides theoretical

title: Finite-Element-Guided Design of Metallic and Bioresorbable Bone Screws: Linking Thread Geometry, Material Stiffness, and ACL Screw Mechanics
abstract: Abstract Bone screw fixation is governed by the thread geometry, material stiffness, contact friction, and loading path. Here, a staged finite-element workflow was used to screen bone-screw designs for bone-to-bone and ACL fixation. Two-dimensional models rapidly compared thread form, pitch, and material under axial loading and pullout displacement, while three-dimensional models evaluated diameter-pitch interactions, metallic material effects, pullout response, stress partitioning, and insertion torque. The 2D results showed radial stress attenuation and a trade-off in which V-shaped threads improved pullout but increased local stress. In 3D, screw diameter dominated the peak stress, and SS 316 and Ti6Al4 V behaved similarly within the metallic design space. Within the present modeling constraints, fine-pitch/metric threads emerged as candidate ACL designs when immediate pullout resistance is prioritized, whereas coarser buttress or square profiles appear more appropriate when reducing bone/graft stress is critical. Polymeric/composite screws should be paired with lower-stress thread profiles and validated experimentally because their lower stiffness may increase deformation risk.

title: Impact of laser modification on the contact angle and surface wettability of hydroxyapatite-coated PEEK implant material
abstract: Introduction Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) is increasingly used in dental implantology because of its biomimetic properties. However, its application is limited by bio-inertness and inherent hydrophobicity, which may affect early biological interactions. PEEK surfaces are often coated with bioactive materials such as hydroxyapatite (HA), but it remains unclear how subsequent surface modification techniques such as laser treatment affect their wettability. There is still limited data on blood surface interactions in laser-treated HA/PEEK composites. This study was designed to assess and compare the blood contact angle of HA/PEEK surfaces before and after laser modification. Materials and methods Twenty-one HA-coated PEEK discs were evaluated, with each individual disc serving as the experimental unit for contact-angle assessment. Blood contact-angle measurements were obtained from each disc before laser treatment and repeated on the same disc following laser surface modification, resulting in paired observations. Hydroxyapatite (HA) nano powder was applied to the PEEK surfaces using friction stir processing (FSP). Fresh EDTA-anticoagulated whole blood obtained from a single donor was used as the test fluid. To minimize variability, blood was collected from the same donor and venipuncture site, and all measurements were performed by the same operator under standardized conditions. Following baseline contact-angle measurement, the HA/PEEK discs were treated using an Er,Cr:YSGG las

title: An explicit dynamic material point–scaled boundary finite element coupling framework with improved hybrid contact for soil–structure interaction
abstract: Large-deformation soil–structure interaction problems involve soil distortion, evolving frictional contact, and deformable structural response, which remain challenging for conventional mesh-based approaches. This paper develops an explicit dynamic coupling framework combining the material point method with the scaled boundary finite element method. The soil domain is discretized by the generalized interpolation material point method, whereas the structural domain is represented by polygonal scaled boundary elements. For the structural solver, an explicit dynamic scaled boundary finite element formulation is established. Sector-based integration points are introduced as persistent local history points for stress update and internal-force evaluation, while consistent mass matrix is evaluated semi-analytically and converted into a lumped nodal form for central-difference integration. To model the interface interaction, a topology-aware hybrid contact algorithm uses the nearest structural boundary node only as a local search seed and treats regular surface nodes, concave and convex corners separately. Contact forces are transferred through background grid on the material point side and applied directly to the structural boundary nodes. Numerical examples reproduce structural dynamics, analytical sliding and rolling, granular collapse, and flexible retaining-wall response. The results demonstrate robust contact behaviour near evolving interfaces and corners while preserving conta

title: Evolutionary characteristics of fretting wear behaviour in stainless-steel materials for vehicle drivetrain systems
abstract: Purpose This study aims to clarify the coupled evolution of frictional hysteresis, energy dissipation, contact stiffness and surface damage in self-mated SS304 rough flat-on-flat fretting contacts. Design/methodology/approach Self-mated SS304 specimens are tested at five durations. Hysteresis loops, dissipated energy, coefficient of friction (µ), tangential contact stiffness (Kt), gross-slip stiffness (Kp), surface topography and wear morphology are analysed. An energy-dependent Bouc–Wen model is developed to describe the evolution of the hysteretic response. Findings Kp, Kt and µ generally increase with cumulative dissipated energy. Surface roughness and height distribution evolve progressively, while wear morphology develops from regular grooves to ploughing, plastic smearing, local detachment and debris redistribution. The proposed model reproduces the hysteresis response with an root mean square error of 1.2 N, Normalized root mean square error of 1.0%, R2 of 0.98 and loop-area error of 2.5%. Originality/value The study establishes cumulative dissipated energy as an effective parameter for linking frictional response, contact stiffness and surface damage and provides an energy-dependent framework for modelling the wear-induced evolution of fretting hysteresis in self-mated SS304 contacts.

title: Thermo-Mechanical Performance Evaluation Of Mechanical Seal Materials in Fire Tender Pumps Using Ansys Finite Element Simulation

title: A healthy social life and, where possible, a healthy and sustainable diet: how the social and material environments shape eating practices
journal: Qualitative Market Research An International Journal
abstract: Purpose Grounded in social practice theory, this study aims to describe the coordination of the eating practices of a socially diverse sample of individuals, half of whom have shifted toward healthier and more sustainable diets, while the other half have not. Design/methodology/approach Qualitative data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 32 individuals. Through reflexive thematic analysis, the authors examine informants’ eating practices to understand how social and material environments facilitate or hinder the adoption of healthier diets. Findings The authors’ findings indicate that changes in eating practices are shaped by coordination, asymmetric negotiation and a sense of belonging. The fragility of plant-based practices does not primarily stem from weak commitment but from a lack of infrastructural support. Individuals revert to dominant eating practices not because they lack knowledge, awareness or moral concern, but because the social and material environment privileges asymmetric coordination. Eating is fundamentally a practice of social integration. Consequently, maintaining a healthy social life frequently takes precedence over maintaining dietary consistency. Sustainable transitions will therefore succeed only when environmentally aligned practices become socially effortless, when they allow individuals to preserve belonging without friction. Practical implications Political interventions play a pivotal role in reshaping the “rules of the eatin

title: Ultrasonic Pulse Velocity in Materials Engineering: Principles, Advances, and Applications: A Comprehensive Review of UPV-Based Non-Destructive Evaluation Across Concrete, Rock, Soil, and Composite Materials
abstract: Ultrasonic pulse velocity (UPV) is among the most widely used non-destructive evaluation (NDE) techniques, offering a non-invasive, cost-effective, standardized measure of structural elastic integrity. This review synthesizes advances in UPV methodology, wave propagation modeling, and data-driven analysis across six domains: (1) thermal damage assessment in concrete, where deep-learning classifiers (GRU networks using instantaneous-frequency and spectral-entropy features) raise three-class classification accuracy from 52% to 94%; (2) wave propagation in heterogeneous concrete, where multiple-scattering models incorporating the interfacial transition zone (ITZ) and Percus–Yevick pair-correlations raise predicted attenuation from ~3 to 11–22 Np/m; (3) soil characterization across compacted, agricultural, and xanthan-stabilized soils; (4) rock mechanics, where Rheological Dynamics Theory derives Poisson’s ratio, cohesion, and friction angle from P- and S-wave velocities; (5) self-compacting and cement–slag concretes, as well as advanced concrete systems, where UPV tracks hydration, strength, and thermal degradation; and (6) ultra-sound-mediated remediation of PFAS-contaminated soils. Drawing on 55 sources (2001–2026, plus seminal 1945–1961 theory), a bibliometric analysis reveals a 2012 growth-rate breakpoint after which output accelerated more than fifty-fold. title: ANALISIS KEAUSAN DAN FRAKTOGRAFI PADA BAJA KARBON RENDAH JIS G3445 STKM 13C MATERIAL UTAMA TUBE SILINDER HIDROLIK DELIMBING KNIFE KHH S162E
abstract: This study aims to analyze wear and fractography of low-carbon steel JIS G3445 STKM 13C used as the main material for the hydraulic cylinder tube of the KHH S162E delimbing knife. The testing procedures included Vickers hardness measurement, wear testing using the Ogoshi Universal High Speed Testing method, and surface morphology observation using Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM). The results showed an average hardness value of 244.2 HV0.3 with a standard deviation of 7.90. The specific wear values of the three samples were 7.084752 × 10⁻⁶, 9.886500 × 10⁻⁶, and 1.2358125 × 10⁻⁶ mm³/mm, respectively. SEM observations revealed scratch grooves, micro-grooves, material flaking, voids, and wear particles on the material surface. These morphological characteristics indicate abrasive wear and delamination mechanisms caused by contact and friction during operation. The findings provide useful information for evaluating material conditions and supporting maintenance considerations for hydraulic cylinder tubes to improve operational reliability and service life.

title: Decoupling Initial Kinetic Impact Energy From Post Collapse Material Crushing in Forensic Investigations of High Rise Progressive Collapses
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
first_author: Mohamed Fayez. Elnagar, Structural Consultant & Certified Forensic Engineering Expert MSc, PMP, MCIArb, MASCE, MACI, M.AISC, M.ASTM, M.FIDIC, PhD
abstract: In the wake of a catastrophic high-rise progressive collapse, forensic engineers are tasked with conducting a highly critical reverse-engineering analysis to locate the exact triggering mechanism. The fundamental physical dilemma centers on the inability to mathematically decouple the kinetic energy signatures of the initial structural impact or failure event from the immense, non-linear material crushing that occurs during the subsequent gravitational collapse. As a skyscraper collapses, thousands of tons of concrete floors plunge onto lower levels, generating massive secondary impact forces, friction, and extreme localized pressures that thoroughly pulverize the core columns, shear walls, and structural connections at the base. Consequently, the physical and microscopic forensic evidence of the original design defect or construction error is buried under a highly corrupted and pulverized debris field. Current numerical simulation software can easily model the forward propagation of a collapse, but reversing the chaotic continuum mechanics of millions of fractured elements to prove whether a specific column failed due to a localized structural overload or was simply crushed by falling debris remains a severe mathematical quagmire. This lack of analytical deconvolution allows contractors and designers to challenge forensic expert testimonies, claiming that the initial failure occurred elsewhere in the structure, thereby creating a profound gap in the judicial arbitration of m

title: Weak Interaction-Driven Self-Assembly of Low-Hygroscopicity Oxidizers for Biocidal Nanoenergetic Materials with Favorable Ignition Performance
abstract: Abstract Iodine pentoxide (I2O5) features a high elemental iodine content, and the composite materials formed with nano-aluminum (n-Al) exhibit both high reactivity and abundant gas generation. However, the n-Al/I2O5 system suffers from a long ignition delay and strong hygroscopicity of I2O5. In this work, a novel iodine-rich energetic oxidizer, [C2H10N2](H2I3O9)2 (EAI-2), was designed and synthesized via weak interaction-driven self-assembly, achieving an ultralow hygroscopicity of ≤0.06% and a high iodine content of 68.26%. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction revealed that the supramolecular architecture was stabilized by cooperative halogen bonds (I···O) and hydrogen bonds (N−H···O). These cooperative interactions effectively shielded the samples from moisture adsorption. Three n-Al/EAI-2 composites were prepared via physical mixing (PM), cooling crystallization (CC), and spray antisolvent (SA) methods. Systematic characterizations demonstrated that the preparation method profoundly affected the crystal morphology, interfacial contact, and mixing uniformity of the composites. SA-n-Al/EAI-2 exhibited the most intimate interfacial contact, attributed to the rapid nucleation and constrained crystal growth during the antisolvent-induced precipitation. Consequently, SA-n-Al/EAI-2 displayed superior sensitivity performances, with an impact sensitivity of >30 J, a friction sensitivity of 108 N, and a flame sensitivity of 7.9 cm, outperforming CC-n-Al/EAI-2. title: Supplementary Materials: A reduced-order model of coral transplant unit stability under waves and currents
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: An idealized, uncalibrated model of the mechanical failure of coral transplant units under waves, currents and internal solitary waves. A unit is a planar rigid body on a rigid bed with two unilateral frictional contacts, loaded through a Morison description of near-bed wave kinematics. The library provides closed-form stability thresholds, a Moreau-Jean time-stepper with two independent event-driven reference solvers, and the figure and report pipeline of the accompanying paper.

The structure operates as a closed-loop survival system. title: Constitutive model of metal rubber material based on the design of planar lattice topological configuration
abstract: To address the significant variance in mechanical properties caused by the random inter-wire entanglement of traditional metal rubber, this paper proposes a planar lattice topological design and fabrication process with a deterministic structure. Quasi-static compression and dynamic sweep-frequency experiments demonstrate that this process overcomes the limitations of traditional methods, enhancing the consistency of hysteretic energy dissipation and the stability of dynamic vibration isolation. To reveal its micro-mechanical responses, the unit cell angle of the isosceles triangle and the array arrangement numbers are extracted as core topological parameters. By integrating the unit cell force and inter-wire dry friction mechanisms, a nonlinear constitutive model incorporating these topological features is established. Subsequently, the HB-AFT algorithm is applied to accurately resolve the displacement transmissibility. To resolve the instability within the resonance jump region, the NSGA-II algorithm is utilized to optimize the topological parameters, aiming to minimize the peak transmissibility. The result indicates that the topological parameters directly dictate the hysteretic energy dissipation and macroscopic stiffness of the metal rubber. Furthermore, the optimized topology effectively narrows the nonlinear bifurcation frequency band, suppresses the resonance peak, and significantly improves the overall vibration isolation stability.

title: Probabilistic large-deformation modelling of tunnel face collapse using random material point method (RMPM) incorporating cross-correlated random fields
abstract: Accurate prediction of tunnel collapse and post-failure ground deformation is critical for safe urban tunnelling. Conventional deterministic analyses usually assume homogeneous ground with mean properties and therefore may not capture the effects of spatially variable soil strength. This study develops a probabilistic large-deformation framework by coupling the Material Point Method with random field theory (RMPM) to simulate tunnel collapse in spatially variable soils. Cross-correlated lognormal random fields of effective cohesion, c', and effective friction angle, φ', are generated using the Karhunen–Loève expansion and Cholesky decomposition, and Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to quantify the statistics of the maximum run-out distance and maximum surface settlement. The MPM model is validated against physical model tests and other published results, showing good agreement in final collapse geometry. Results show that positive c'-φ' correlation slightly increases the mean collapse extent and amplifies response variability, whereas negative correlation has a stabilizing effect. Sensitivity analyses further show that vertical correlation length exerts a stronger influence on collapse propagation than horizontal correlation length, with smaller vertical correlation lengths tending to form stratified strength barriers that suppress upward failure development. The proposed RMPM framework provides a useful tool for probabilistic tunnel-collapse assessment under spatially v

title: Supplementary material from "Reduced water repellence as a potential cost of quiet flight adaptations"
abstract: Quiet flight allows predators such as owls to approach prey undetected. This ability evolved convergently in several nocturnal bird taxa and results from feather modifications, such as a velvet-like dorsal feather surface modification that reduces frictional noise of neighbouring feathers. Despite extensive research on the aerodynamic and acoustic costs and benefits of these feather modifications, potential functional trade-offs that could explain their constrained distribution among birds remain poorly understood. Feathers perform multiple other essential functions, including signalling, insulation and water repellence. To accomplish the latter, most feathers are highly hydrophobic owing to their hierarchical surface structure. However, the presence of velvet modifies this hierarchical surface structure and may change how water interacts with the feather surface. Here, we test whether the velvet-like feather surface modifies feather wettability. Using contact-angle measurements across 34 bird species we show that feathers possessing velvet microstructures had a significantly lower contact angle compared to feathers lacking this structure (i.e. respectively CA = 126° and CA = 141°) but remained overall hydrophobic (CA > 90°). This reveals a previously unrecognized physical consequence of the velvet feather surface and suggests that adaptations for acoustic stealth have previously overlooked costs that may lead to ecological and evolutionary constraints.

title: Silver Ion Implantation into Orthodontic Stainless-Steel Materials: Physicochemical Characterization and In Vitro Microbiological Evaluation
abstract: Fixed orthodontic appliances create retention sites for bacterial biofilm, increasing the risk of white spot lesions and periodontal complications. Silver ion (Ag) implantation offers a potential solution by conferring antimicrobial properties while preserving mechanical integrity. This study evaluated the physicochemical properties, Ag release, biocompatibility, and antibacterial efficacy of AISI 301 stainless-steel orthodontic brackets (Ormco Bios) modified by silver ion implantation using a Pulsed Filtered Cathodic Arc Vacuum System. Physical and micro-structural surface characterizations—including SEM/EDS, interferometric roughness analysis, contact angle measurements, nanoindentation hardness testing, and friction coefficient determination (under dry and saliva-lubricated conditions)—were conducted directly on the modified brackets. In compliance with international testing standards requiring defined geometric areas, AISI 301 flat samples of same chemical composition and microstructure were used to quantify Ag release in artificial saliva (cumulative silver ion release in artificial saliva was quantified via ICP-MS over time, with measured concentrations corrected for the volume extracted at each sampling interval), as well as to perform in vitro biological (human fibroblast cytocompatibility) and microbiological assays against seven bacterial strains (Streptococcus mutans, Streptococcus gordonii, Lactobacillus salivarius, Lactobacillus acidophilus, Porphyromonas gingiva

title: Effect of Commercial Halloysite Nanotube Grade on the Tribo‐Mechanical Performance and Structural Evolution of Polytetrafluoroethylene Composites
abstract: ABSTRACT The aim of this work was to establish how the grade of commercial halloysite nanotubes affects the structure, mechanical properties, and tribological behavior of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) composites. Three grades of halloysite, ANT 811, ANT 1108, and ANT 3810, differing in phase composition and textural characteristics, were used as fillers at 1, 2, and 5 wt.%. The addition of 5 wt.% ANT 811 halloysite, which had the highest specific surface area and the smallest crystallite size, reduced the wear rate by 100% compared to initial PTFE, from (496 ± 32) × 10 −6 to (1.2 ± 0.6) × 10 −6 mm 3 /(N·m), while a low coefficient of friction of 0.20 was maintained. The degree of crystallinity increased from 64% for initial PTFE to 73% for the ANT 811 composite. These improvements were achieved at the cost of reduced ductility. The elongation at break decreased by 55%, although it remained 9 times higher than that of the composite with ANT 3810. FTIR spectroscopy, XPS, and SEM revealed that the halloysite particles acted as a solid lubricant at the initial stage of friction and then initiated the formation of a secondary tribo‐layer enriched with tribo‐oxidation products. The resulting composites can be recommended as anti‐friction materials for dry sliding units.

title: Antiderivative approach to radiative free convection past a vertically raised surface in a porous material with entropy analysis
abstract: This study investigates free convective heat and mass transfer over a vertically raised surface embedded in a fluid-saturated porous medium subjected to Rosseland-approximated radiative heat flux, for the case of constant wall heat and mass flux ( \(n=1/3\) ). An antiderivative (Von Kármán integral) approach is used to reduce the governing boundary-layer equations to closed algebraic relations for the boundary-layer-thickness ratio, local Nusselt number, and local Sherwood number. The governing parameters are the buoyancy ratio N , the Lewis number Le , and the radiation parameter Rd . At the reference point \(N=0\) , \(Le=1\) , the method is calibrated against the classical similarity solution of Lai and Kulacki (giving \(Nu/Ra_x^{1/2}=Sh/Ra_x^{1/2}=0.6777\) ); away from this point the closed-form predictions are compared against the benchmark to within the deviations reported in Table. Across the tested range \(Le\in [1,100]\) , the Nusselt number is found to fall by roughly a factor of 3 while the Sherwood number rises by more than an order of magnitude, reflecting the disparate diffusion regimes captured by Le . Velocity, temperature, concentration, entropy generation, and Bejan-number profiles are analysed for varying N , Rd , and Le , together with skin friction, Nusselt, and Sherwood numbers.

title: Reorienting Indigenous Heritage for Socioenvironmental Justice
abstract: Abstract This article presents a study of the archaeological ruins of Tiwanaku and Quilmes in the south-central Andes as spaces of equivocation at the intersection of diverging human–nature and past–present ontologies. Drawing on multisited archaeological ethnography, the research reveals the underlying struggles for Indigenous heritage rights and self-determination through discursive–material juxtapositions, frictional materialities, and multiple temporalities. Three lines of inquiry are examined: (a) the modern–colonial origins of dominant configurations of heritage rights in the Andes, (b) the failures of development projects aimed at the “rehabilitation” of native technologies and knowledge, and (c) the pluriversal becoming of Indigenous heritage from the ruins of multicultural development. The findings offer a critical counterpoint to rights-based narratives and consent-seeking approaches that objectify heritage and communities within hegemonic conservation and development regimes. Alternative forms of political subjectivity and socionatural configurations enable an assessment of the entangled environmental and decolonial dimensions of heritage, indigeneity, and rights.

title: Study of mask handling in a plasma etching chamber
abstract: Different from the wafer, photomask during the mask process the mask backside (quartz side) will become the front side when the mask is used for lithography, therefore mask backside stamp mark or scratch control during the process step was one of the important criteria for mask quality control. Mask handling in a plasma etching system is unique, the handling device not only takes responsibility for loading the mask but also needs to consider anti-corrosion, thermal stability, and anti-friction material properties. In this paper we introduce some studies of mask handling in a plasma etching chamber, different materials combination handling components and different shapes handling components were tested, after thousands of times mask load/unload with thousands of plasma RF hours treatment some assembles handling components shown good performance some assembles not. Based on the experiment results we will summarize crucial factors to design a handling device for the plasma etching chamber.

title: Fabrication of Bifunctional UHMWPE Composites With Self‐Lubricating and Self‐Repairing Capabilities via Core‐Shell MSNs ‐ PFPE @ PEW Particles
abstract: ABSTRACT In mechanical systems, the energy dissipation and wear caused by friction usually lead to the failure of materials during their service life, thereby driving the demand for polymer composite materials with both tribological properties and self‐repairing capabilities. Studying polymer composites with self‐lubrication and self‐repairing functions is an effective approach. Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) was infused into the micropores of mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) and polyethylene wax (PEW) was used to encapsulate the oil‐carrying particles to prepare MSNs‐PFPE@PEW with a core‐shell structure, which was combined with ultra‐high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) as a filler to prepare UHMWPE/MSNs‐PFPE@PEW composites. The material possesses both self‐lubricating and self‐repairing properties. Compared with pure UHMWPE, the friction coefficient and wear rate of the composite material supplemented with 10% MSNs‐PFPE@PEW can be reduced by 72.22% and 60.47%, respectively, and 59.74% of the wear damage and 60.47% of the scratch damage can be repaired. PFPE migrates to the friction interface under the action of load and friction heat during the friction process to form a friction transfer film, which plays a lubricating role. PEW undergoes a phase change upon heating treatment, which is able to fill in the damage on the surface of the composite material, and play a role in repairing it. This study provides a new idea for the development of self‐lubricating and self‐

title: Why ice is so slippery
abstract: We simulate nanoscale ice--glass friction from first principles and upscale it by modelling frictional heating. Nanoscale simulations alone overestimate friction and miss its velocity dependence. Frictional heating warms the contact toward the melting point, thickening the premelting film tenfold and cutting its viscosity a hundredfold; friction drops with velocity, matching experiment. Premelting forms the film without sliding or heating, but its slipperiness hinges on frictional heating, as Bowden and Hughes proposed in 1939, without melting. Snow, other materials and coatings remain open.

title: Introduction to Solid-State Welding Techniques
abstract: The welding of similar or dissimilar materials involves the utilisation of joining techniques to fabricate welds with excellent properties. There are many solid-state welding techniques, including explosive welding, forge welding, and friction stir welding. These joining techniques have been utilised to join numerous materials, including aluminium, copper, and titanium. These welds are fabricated without the materials to join reaching their melting points; the joints are fabricated in a solid state. This chapter presents details on selected solid-state welding techniques and further presents some studies in which these techniques were used for the welding of various materials, such as aluminium. Solid-state welding techniques have been used to join materials that are difficult to join using conventional welding techniques. Some of these joining techniques, such as friction stir welding (FSW) and friction stir spot welding (FSSW), were developed a few decades ago and need to be investigated further, and that will lead to expanding their applications in many sectors, such as marine and aeronautics.

title: Atom-scale contributions to nanofriction response in transition metal dichalcogenides
publisher: Beilstein Institute for the Advancement of Chemical Sciences
abstract: We investigate the nanoscale friction behaviour of MX 2 monolayers (M = Mo, W; X = S, Se) on Au(111) and Ag(111) substrates with silicon tip using classical molecular dynamics simulations with machine-learning-based force fields. This approach enables an accurate description of tip-surface interactions and friction mechanisms at the atomic scale. We observe a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence of the friction force on the applied normal load, indicating a breakdown of Amontons's law at the nanoscale. Analysis of lateral force signals and their spatial Fourier transforms reveals the coexistence of multiple sliding modes, including longitudinal sliding, lateral slip, and zig-zag motions. We show that the overall friction response is governed by the relative contributions of these motions. While the qualitative features of friction are largely substrate-independent, both the magnitude of friction and the balance between sliding modes depend sensitively on the substrate-monolayer combination. In particular, Au/MoSe 2 /Si exhibits significantly reduced friction due to suppression of lateral slip motion. Our results indicate that the method is broadly applicable for probing nanoscale friction in related heterostructures.

title: Monitoring the Technical Condition of Gearboxes in High-Power "Kirovets" Tractors Using Telematics Systems
journal: Sel skohozjajstvennaja tehnika obsluzhivanie i remont (Agricultural Machinery Service and Repair)
abstract: The article addresses the problem of improving the operational reliability of gearboxes in high power Kirovets tractors (series K 701–K 7M) through instrumental monitoring of the load on hydro clutch couplings — the main life determining component of the transmission. An analysis of gearbox component reliability, the evolution of friction materials and lubricant compositions, and the distribution of tractor operating time across various agricultural operations is presented. It is shown that the traditional accounting of operating time in engine hours does not reflect the actual load on individual units. A prototype monitoring system developed by specialists of the FSBSI FNAC VIM is described; it is based on Galileosky 7x telematics terminals and integrates gear engagement counters, a flow meter, and sensors for monitoring clutch disc slippage. The feasibility of transitioning to the advanced Galileosky 10 platform is substantiated: it supports CAN FD, offers an increased number of analog inputs, provides a significantly larger non volatile memory capacity, and enables flexible programmable diagnostic logic. The proposed solutions are shown to comply with the requirements of GOST 20793 2023 and GOST 35318 2025 regarding online monitoring of technical condition and operating time accounting using onboard control systems.

title: Topological Reconfiguration in Sheared Granular Assemblies: Non-Dissipative Mechanism and Its Irreversible Characteristics
abstract: Granular materials exhibit pronounced macroscopic irreversible deformations during shearing, which mainly contributes to frictional sliding dissipation in the conventional thermodynamic frameworks. This study aims to investigate the non-dissipative microscopic mechanisms governing macroscopic irreversibility of granular materials. Using DEM, a series of biaxial shear and reverse loading simulations are conducted on dense granular assemblies with different friction coefficients. The results show that continuous topological reconfiguration occurs through the transformation from lower-order to higher-order meso-loops, eventually reaching a statistical steady state at the critical state. Accompanying this topological evolution, elastic energy at contact level is continuously stored and released, providing a persistent non-dissipative energy exchange that sustains continuous shear alongside primary frictional dissipation. Based on the reverse loading analysis, topological reconfiguration is intrinsically irrecoverable, causing part of the free energy to remain locked within the reconfigured contact network as irrecoverable free energy. Meanwhile, another portion of the recoverable free energy is irreversibly dissipated through friction during unloading. Together, these two components constitute the irreversible free energy. The evolution of irreversible free energy with interparticle friction is consistent with those of the critical frictional dissipation and macroscopic volumetri

title: Modelling of single-asperity ploughing in aluminum sheet metal forming
abstract: In sheet metal forming, there are direct interactions between tool and workpiece asperities in boundary lubrication regimes. Under these conditions, the friction force results from ploughing of hard tool surface asperities through softer workpiece material and shearing of the boundary layers which form on workpiece and tool surfaces. To predict friction, it is important to understand these two frictional mechanisms. The boundary-layer shear strength was characterized experimentally and incorporated into finite element simulations of a single-asperity ploughing model. These simulations were validated using single-asperity ploughing experiments. After validation, additional simulations with a wider range of asperity geometries and contact conditions were conducted. Results show boundary-layer shear dominates for blunt asperities where the ratio of asperity height to its radius in the sliding direction is small. As this ratio increases, the contribution of material deformation to friction becomes dominant. Current results show that the assumption that friction is a simple additive contribution of these two mechanisms is inaccurate for relatively sharp and wide asperities. For ploughing aligned with the major radius of elliptical asperities, the height to major radius ratio has the strongest influence on the friction response. title: Bayesian inversion of rate-and-state parameters from stable velocity step experiments on Quartz Gouge close to instability
abstract: SUMMARY Accurate determination of rate-and-state friction parameters from experiments is crucial for physics-based modelling of the earthquake source. In this study, we develop a Bayesian inversion framework based on a spring-slider model of the experiment to infer rate-and-state frictional properties from stable velocity-step experiments of a fine-grained quartz gouge that is close to instability. The inversion framework infers frictional parameters with superior precision to conventional methods based on nonlinear least squares. We identify that logarithmic sampling of the characteristic slip $D_{\rm RS}$ is an essential step for accurate inversion. Testing the same gouge material under the same effective normal stress but different pore pressure additionally shows that the presence of pressurized pore fluids changes the inferred rate-and-state properties of the gouge material by increasing rate-and-state parameters a, b and $D_{\rm RS}$. The Bayesian inversion framework provides a valuable tool for inferring accurately rate-and-state parameters of realistic gouge materials close to instability, with a small and quantifiable range of uncertainty in cases where the steady-state behaviour quantified by $a-b$ can be constrained independently. title: Investigation on tribological properties of PETG with integrated PTFE inserts
abstract: The parts and components produced from polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) using additive manufacturing techniques require improvements in tribological properties, which represent a significant scientific and technical challenge. The high coefficient of friction and susceptibility to wear of PETG restrict its use in functional parts that operate under sliding conditions. This study, therefore, proposes coaxially integrating cylindrical polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) inserts measuring 3 or 6 mm in diameter into 3D printed PETG structures. PETG samples were fabricated using fused deposition modelling and tested under various normal loads (50 – 150 N) at a sliding velocity of 0.2 m/s to evaluate their tribological properties. The experimental results demonstrated that the PTFE inserts reduced the coefficient of friction by up to 68 % (from 0.57 – 0.64 to 0.18 – 0.24) compared to pristine PETG. Samples with a 6 mm insert exhibited the best performance, with a coefficient of friction ranging from 0.18 to 0.24 and up to 75 % wear reduction. PETG serves as a structurally strong matrix, while the PTFE inserts impart excellent anti-friction properties through transfer-film formation. Thermomechanical analysis verified the stability of the materials in the range from 40 to 80 °C. title: Ring-shear test data of garnet sand used for analogue modelling in the experimental tectonics laboratory at GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, Potsdam
abstract: This dataset provides friction data from ring-shear tests on garnet sand used in analogue modelling of tectonic processes as a rock analogue for “strong” or “high density” layers in the earth’s upper crust (e.g. Klinkmüller et al., 2016). According to our analysis the material shows a Mohr-Coulomb behaviour characterized by a linear failure envelope. Peak, dynamic and reactivation friction coefficients of garnet sand are µP = 0.83, µD = 0.61, and µR = 0.73, respectively (Table 5). Cohesion of the material ranges between 20-120 Pa. The material shows a no significant rate-dependency. The data presented here are derived by ring shear testing using a SCHULZE RST-01.pc (Schulze, 1994, 2003, 2008) at HelTec, the Laboratory for experimental tectonics at the Helmholtz Center Potsdam – GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam, Germany. The RST is specially designed to measure friction coefficients µ and cohesions C in loose granular material accurately at low confining pressures (<20 kPa) and shear velocities (<1 mm/sec) similar to sandbox experiments. In this tester, a granular bulk material layer is sheared internally at constant normal stress σN and shear velocity v while shear force and lid displacement (corresponding to density and volume change ΔV) are measured continuously. For more details see Klinkmüller et al. (2016).

title: Effect of carbon morphology on the wear resistance of aluminum-carbon composites
journal: International Conference on Mechanical Engineering, Materials and Automation Technology (MMEAT)
abstract: Aluminum-based materials are widely used in overhead transmission line conductors and related components, but they are prone to friction and wear under complex service conditions, which affects their service reliability. To improve their wear resistance, Al₄C₃/Al composites, aluminum-coated graphite/Al composites, and carbon powder/Al composites were prepared by a melting and casting method. The friction and wear behaviors of pure aluminum and the three composites were investigated using an Rtec tribometer, combined with analyses of metallographic microstructure, X-ray diffraction (XRD), three-dimensional wear scar morphology, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The results show that all three carbon morphologies improved the friction and wear properties of aluminum-based materials to some extent. Among them, the aluminum-coated graphite/Al composite exhibited the best friction-reducing and wear-resistant performance, with the volume wear rate decreasing from 4.63×10⁻³ to 2.46×10⁻³ mm³·(N·m)⁻¹. This improvement was attributed to the good dispersion of aluminum-coated graphite in the aluminum matrix and the solid-lubricating effect of graphite during friction. In contrast, local agglomeration weakened the wearreducing effect of carbon powder, while Al₄C₃ particles acted as hard abrasive particles, resulting in limited improvement in wear resistance. title: EFFECT OF CARBON FIBERS AND NANOSIZED ZINC OXIDE ON THE STRUCTURE AND PROPERTIES OF PTFE-BASED COMPOSITES
abstract: The structure, physical-mechanical, and tribological properties of polytetrafluoroethylene-based composite materials modified with mechanically activated short carbon fibers (CF) and nanosized zinc oxide (ZnO) were investigated. The aim of this work was to determine the effect of a binary CF/ZnO filler on the structure, physical-mechanical, and tribological properties of PTFE. The composites were produced by cold pressing at a pressure of 50 MPa followed by sintering at 375±5 °C. The carbon fiber content was 1, 5, and 10 wt.%, while the nanosized ZnO content was 1 and 2 wt.%. The properties of the materials were studied using mechanical testing, pin-on-disk tribological testing, X-ray diffraction analysis, scanning electron microscopy, and FTIR spectroscopy. It was found that the combined introduction of the fillers makes it possible to preserve the offset yield strength of the composites at the level of neat PTFE and to significantly improve their wear resistance. The combined filling changes the supramolecular structure of the polymer, increases the degree of crystallinity up to 79 %, and promotes the formation of secondary structures on the friction surface. The best combination of properties was obtained for the composition PTFE + 5 wt.% CF + 2 wt.% ZnO, for which the mass wear rate decreased by a factor of 631 compared with neat PTFE at a coefficient of friction of 0.24. According to FTIR spectroscopy, oxygen-containing groups are formed on the surface of the composites

title: How Electrical Arcing Governs Wear and Performance in Current-Carrying Pantograph Contacts
abstract: The pantograph–catenary system serves as the core power supply device, ensuring stable operation of high-speed trains, and its contact interface represents a typical current-carrying friction system, where the introduction of electric current significantly complicates the wear mechanisms. The coupling effect of mechanical wear and electrical wear exacerbates damage to and degradation of carbon strip materials, while electric arcs induced by unstable contact states directly regulate the tribological characteristics and electrical conductivity of the friction pair. To investigate the current-carrying friction and wear behavior of carbon strips under the dominant effect of electric arcs, this study simulated the irregularity conditions of contact wires, observed the evolution characteristics of electric arcs, and systematically analyzed the effects of test current and contact load on the damage characteristics and current-carrying performance of the contact pair. The results indicate that arc morphology exhibits differentiated characteristics across friction cycles, with significant fluctuations in arc intensity. Regarding the friction coefficient, under a contact load of 25 N, the friction coefficients corresponding to currents of 0 A, 40 A, and 80 A are 0.378, 0.242, and 0.335, respectively; under a contact load of 50 N, the corresponding values are 0.432, 0.180, and 0.209, respectively. Peak, dynamic and reactivation friction coefficients of corundum sand are µP = 0.75, µD = 0.59, and µR = 0.67, respectively (Table 5). Cohesion of the material ranges between 20-90 Pa. title: Finite element modeling of oblique impacts of softballs
abstract: Abstract This study involved a finite element (FE) analysis of softballs for sliding and gripping oblique impacts across a range of angles and velocities. A temporal friction model was implemented that incorporated independently measured static and dynamic coefficients of friction. Normal impacts were used to calibrate material parameters to match ball stiffness and coefficient of restitution within 4% of experimental results, while oblique impacts were used to validate the friction model. The FE results were evaluated through comparisons with experimentally measured angular velocities, linear and rotational energy, and normal and tangential impact forces. Ball inhomogeneity was found to be important, where the model’s angular velocity was 13% and 3% higher than experiment for a homogeneous and inhomogeneous ball, respectively. Compared with constant-friction models, the temporal friction model reduced the mean normalized root-mean-square error in predicted angular velocity by 29% across gripping and sliding impacts and for the first time described both sliding and gripping behavior. Normal and tangential impact forces were within 2.5% and 6.1% of experimental measurements. The FE softball model demonstrated good agreement with experimental data, showing that ball mass distribution and temporal friction are important to describe shear deformation under oblique impacts.
