title: Effect of UHMWPE Incorporation on the Tribological Performance of Carbon Fiber‐Reinforced PEEK Nanocomposites
abstract: ABSTRACT Ultra‐high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) was incorporated into a PEEK‐based hybrid material as a lubrication additive to improve the friction and wear performance of the composite due to its superior lubricity. Tribological tests of the materials were conducted using a sliding bearing testing rig, and contact temperatures at the interface between the sliding pair were calculated through finite element simulations (FE simulations). Compared with the UHMWPE‐free reference composite, the UHMWPE‐modified hybrid material exhibits reductions in both the coefficient of friction (COF) and linear wear rate ( w l ) up to the melting temperature of UHMWPE. Under severe load conditions, where the contact temperature exceeds both the melting temperature of UHMWPE and the glass transition temperature of the PEEK, the UHMWPE‐free composite demonstrates improved wear performance owing to its high temperature resistance. These results confirm the feasibility of using UHMWPE as a lubricant in PEEK‐based sliding bearing materials and provide new insights into the development and selection of self‐lubricating sliding bearing materials for real‐world applications.

title: A review of tribo-mechanical characteristics of nickel and aluminum-based metal matrix composites
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part B Journal of Engineering Manufacture
abstract: Metal matrix composites (MMCs) are extensively used materials for adverse operating conditions, where the good properties of one material cannot cope with the operating conditions. Most studies showed the matrix as metallic, and the reinforcements could be metal, polymers, ceramics, or even hybrids. Now-a-days, MMCs are widely adopted for the fabrication of many components like vehicle bodies, aeroplane bodies, machines, weapons, etc. These components encounter frictional resistance from several sources. To assess and select a suitable material for the fabrication of these components, the tribological characteristics of these materials need to be analyzed. These components also need to withstand severe stresses from numerous sources, like impact loads, thermal stresses, etc., so mechanical properties are also important. The principal objective of this paper is to provide a detailed description of the tribological and mechanical characteristics of MMCs with different combinations of matrices and reinforcements. This study aims to explore the tribological and mechanical properties of Metal Matrix Composites (MMCs), realizing various matrix and reinforcement combinations. It highlights that MMCs are crucial for applications requiring resistance to friction, stress, and impact, necessitating analysis of both tribological and mechanical characteristics for material selection.

title: Braking at Half Does Not Halve the Grip for Turning: Tyre Friction Shares One Circle Between Braking and Turning ── With a tyre of friction coefficient 0.8, using half the friction for braking still leaves 0.866025 for turning, and using nine-tenths leaves only 0.435890 ── as the sideways friction approaches its limit, this ratio approaches pi/2=1.570796 ── [Paper 593]
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Braking at half is easily taken to halve the margin for turning. What this paper shows is that tyre friction is shared between braking and turning within one circle, so a little braking barely reduces the turning force while hard braking reduces it greatly, and that stopping while turning takes sin^-1y/y times the distance of a straight stop (y being the fraction of friction used sideways). No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──the friction circle, centripetal acceleration and stopping distance are all standard. The car is a point mass and the friction circle is an idealisation──a real tyre has different limits along and across (an ellipse), varying with slip angle; here it is a circle. A friction coefficient of 0.8 is representative of a dry road. Load transfer (weight moving to the front wheels under braking), anti-lock systems, tyre elasticity and road banking are not included. No driving advice is given──this paper does not recommend any particular way of driving. title: Regeneration's Value Rides on the Square of Speed, So Leaving the Last Low-Speed Stretch to Friction Costs Under One Percent ── what remains below 10 km/h is only 0.010000 of the energy at 100 km/h, so with a round-trip efficiency of 0.70 giving the low-speed stretch to friction loses only 0.007000 of the whole ── the separator is whether the brake turns the energy into heat or into charge ── [Paper 735]
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A regenerative brake recovers energy. Where it can be recovered is settled by the square of speed. The energy in each band of speed is counted, and with it what may be given up. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──that kinetic energy goes as the square of speed, that regenerative braking loses to round-trip efficiency, and that friction braking takes over at low speed are all standard (Genta 1997, Ehsani 2018). No precision is claimed for representative values──a round-trip efficiency of 0.70 and a mass of 1500 kg are order-of-magnitude values. The battery side is not counted──that cold or a full charge prevents regeneration is mentioned only. Road load is not included──deceleration from rolling and aerodynamic resistance is not included; only kinetic energy is considered. No real vehicle is claimed──particular vehicles and control designs are not treated. Gradients are not treated──recovery of potential energy on a descent is not treated. Relation to earlier papers: Paper 725 showed that the take-off decision speed is the crossing of two distances and that the crossing is the minimum──there braking was a quantity that makes distance, and the length needed to stop was the subject. Here the same braking is counted for what it discards. The distance needed, and the energy lost. What is added is tabulating the energy against speed, putting the low-speed share at 0.010000, putting the loss from friction at 0.007000

title: Frictionless Electromagnetic Braking for Electric and Autonomous Vehicles: Contactless Operating Principles, Brake-by-Wire Integration, and Research Challenges: A Critical Review
abstract: Eddy-current braking is increasingly considered a promising complementary technology to conventional hydraulic braking systems in next-generation automotive platforms, particularly in electric and autonomous vehicles. Unlike traditional friction-based systems, eddy-current braking enables the contactless generation of braking torque and can reduce mechanical wear while potentially providing rapid and controllable torque modulation and facilitating integration with intelligent vehicle-control architectures. However, a consistent vehicle-level response-time advantage over conventional braking systems has not yet been established through quantitative comparative testing. This paper presents a critical review of electromagnetic braking systems intended for automotive applications. This review analyzes the integration of electromagnetic braking technologies with embedded electronic control architectures, with particular emphasis on their potential role in future Brake-by-Wire systems. This study examines the operating principles of contactless braking, control strategies, actuator behavior, and system performance under variable operating conditions. In addition, key challenges related to energy efficiency, thermal management, fail-safe operation, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities of electronically controlled braking systems are discussed. title: Structural and Thermal Analysis of Disc Brake System Using FEM
journal: International Journal for Development of Science and Technology
abstract: The goal is to create and assess the distribution of thermal and structural stress in a brake rotor under real-time brakingconditions. A transient thermo-elastic analysis of the Rotor Disc of the Disk 17 10 Brake intends to measure theeffectiveness of a bike's disc brake rotor when subjected to intense braking scenarios, thus aiding in the design andevaluation of disc rotors. In this study, efforts have been made to identify an appropriate hybrid composite material thatweighs less than cast iron while exhibiting desirable properties such as thermal strain, yield strength, and density. The optimization process is conducted to minimize stress concentration and the rotor's weight, which helps maintain lowunsprung mass and enhances the vehicle's stability. Using Computer-Aided Design (CAD) with Catia v5 software, astructural model of the brake rotor has been created. Additionally, finite element analysis has been carried out usingANSYS 14.5 software. Aluminium Silicon carbide demonstrates favorable friction and wear characteristics for the Diskbrake 17 10 rotor. title: Study on Validity of Maximum Static Friction Coefficient as an Evaluation Value for Skid-Resistance of Pavement Surface
journal: The Baltic Journal of Road and Bridge Engineering
abstract: The skid resistance of a pavement surface is a critical indicator of driving safety, typically quantified by the dynamic friction coefficient measured using a Friction Measurement Vehicle or a Dynamic Friction Tester. The dynamic friction coefficient is calculated from the dynamic friction force acting on a rubber slider in a sliding state, directly influencing the braking distance before a tire stops sliding. In this study, we hypothesize that the resistance force before a tire begins to slip – rather than the braking distance – is more closely related to traffic accident risk. Therefore, this study focuses on the maximum static friction coefficient, representing the resistance force at the onset of tire sliding. Maximum static friction coefficients were measured across various road surfaces and compared with dynamic friction coefficients to evaluate their relationship with accident risk. The results demonstrate that the maximum static friction coefficient provides a more realistic evaluation of road surface skid resistance.

title: Event-Driven Safe Control of a Black-Box Balancing Wheel with Friction-Gated Actuation
abstract: Commercial balancing wheels are closed systems: an internal controller keeps the board upright, and a rider steers by shifting weight and twisting the hips. We augment a one-wheel with a lead-screw weight shift for longitudinal motion and a reaction wheel for yaw. The reaction wheel stores limited momentum, so a turn is a sequence of torque pulses, and whether a pulse rotates the body depends on static friction at the tire contact. From a 24-pulse torque sweep on one surface we fit a two-part model that gives the probability that a pulse rotates the body, treating the breakaway torque as random, and the rotation angle when it does; at maximum torque the posterior engagement probability is 0.54 (90% credible interval 0.24-0.84). The weight shift is modeled as a rate- limited input with a measured speed gain and an assumed first-order response, which predicts stopping distances four times those of a direct-force model. These models drive an event-triggered supervisor that schedules pulses by expected heading improvement, brakes when the predicted braking path would leave the safe set, tightens margins for model uncertainty, and updates the friction estimate online. In simulation on 500 plants drawn from the fitted models, the robust supervisor completed 92.6% of missions with 1.8% safety violations and 1.6% safe aborts, versus 84.0% and 7.2% for a supervisor using mean models and 1.8% and 20.4% for a baseline that ignores friction. title: Hot-spot mitigation in disc brakes using an air-scoop with bypass feature: An experimental investigation coupled with CFD simulation
abstract: Braking safety and performance are strongly influenced by disc-brake thermal behavior, where frictional heating can trigger brake fade, accelerate wear, and, in hydraulic systems, promote vapor lock due to brake-fluid boiling. To enhance heat removal while controlling aerodynamic losses, this study investigates scoop-assisted motorcycle disc-brake cooling and introduces a bypass feature within the scoop to redistribute airflow and suppress localized hot spots. The research combines experimental testing and CFD simulations to validate the flow behavior and interpret the thermal-flow mechanisms through velocity and temperature fields. The results show that both closed-bypass and open-bypass scoop configurations reduce the dominant hot-spot intensity on the brake disc by improving airflow delivery to the heated region. However, the open-bypass configuration provides better hot-spot mitigation because the bypass passage promotes broader airflow distribution, stronger mixing, and a more distributed surface temperature field. Measured cooling results indicate that higher inlet velocity generally reduces peak disc temperature through stronger forced convection, although increased aerodynamic resistance creates a trade-off between cooling enhancement and drag penalty. The angle-of-attack assessment shows that 10° provides the best practical balance by reducing drag coefficient while maintaining comparable airflow delivery. title: Friction-Feasible Trajectory Prediction for Vehicles on Winter Roads: A Warm-Up Physics Loss with Velocity-Space Learning
abstract: Vehicle trajectory prediction on icy and snowy roads is safety-critical because reduced tyre–road adhesion compresses the set of dynamically feasible manoeuvres and can substantially increase braking distances relative to dry pavement. The objective of this study is to develop a lightweight physics-enhanced predictor that jointly minimises positional error and friction-circle violations on low-friction winter roads, so that short-horizon forecasts remain usable by advanced driver-assistance functions. We propose PE-DNN, a physics-informed multi-layer perceptron that predicts absolute future velocities in the ego frame and activates friction-circle and jerk penalties through a linear warm-up schedule. Unlike prior physics-informed trajectory predictors that apply constraints from the first training epoch on zero-mean residual targets, PE-DNN treats target-space design, constraint scheduling, and mechanistic interpretation of the violation rate (VR) as coupled methodological choices. On the Northeastern Vehicle Trajectory Dataset (NVTD; 289 vehicles, 19,049 frames), PE-DNN achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 2.019 m and VR=3.8%, with the lowest ADE–VR pair among retrained learning baselines under identical splits, while trading somewhat higher final displacement error (FDE) and extreme-subset ADE (ADE-Ext) for improved physical feasibility. title: Economic trade-off of regenerative braking in hybrid vehicles: recovered-energy value versus accelerated battery degradation, with a worked case study for Turkish operating conditions
journal: International Journal of Automotive Engineering and Technologies
abstract: In a hybrid electric vehicle (HEV), regenerative braking converts part of the vehicle’s kinetic energy into electricity that is stored and later reused, displacing fuel. This recovered energy is effectively free, because its only alternative is dissipation as heat in the friction brakes; however, the extra charge throughput and the high charge-rate (C-rate) pulses associated with braking accelerate battery aging, which carries a replacement cost. This paper presents a transparent, parameterized methodology that evaluates the net economic value of regenerative braking as the difference between two opposing cash flows: the monetized value of the recovered energy and the levelized cost of the accelerated battery degradation it causes. The benefit branch is built from the powertrain round-trip efficiency chain and an equivalent-fuel valuation; the cost branch from a power-law capacity-fade model and a levelized degradation cost, cdeg = cpack/NEFC. The two branches are unified in marginal-value and net-present-value (NPV) terms and examined with tornado and Monte-Carlo analyses. A case study is developed for a representative C-segment full hybrid under Turkish conditions at a gasoline price of 1.40 USD/L. The braking-energy input is validated against urban and extra-urban driving-cycle simulations that bracket the adopted value (0.028-0.058 kWh/km). For 15,000 km/yr the model recovers about 233 kWh/yr of usable traction energy, saving roughly 87 L of gasoline (≈ 121 USD) per year

title: CSD-DETR: A contrastive state-spaced differential detection transformer for surface defect detection of paper-based friction plates
abstract: Abstract Paper-based friction plates are key components of transmission and braking systems, and their surface defects directly affect friction stability, service life, and safety. However, these defects are difficult to detect accurately because they often exhibit low contrast, weak visual features and blurred boundaries. Existing methods still suffer from missed detection of small targets, inaccurate boundary localization, and high false-detection rates. To address these challenges, this study proposes a contrastive state-space differential detection transformer (CSD-DETR). First, the Multi-Scale Local Contrast Block is designed to enhance the perception of tiny defects and weak texture anomalies through local mean difference and multi-scale pooling. Second, the Coordinate State-Space Attention is introduced to preserve the spatial location information of defects via coordinate attention and model long-range dependencies through a State-Space branch, thereby improving global discrimination under complex textured backgrounds. In addition, a detail-enhanced reparameterized C3 module is incorporated to strengthen the boundary perception of directional defects. Experiments on the self-constructed LTX-DET dataset show that, compared with the RT-DETR-CSP-RepC3 baseline, CSD-DETR improves mAP50 from 87.1% to 92.9%, mAP50-95 from 66.1% to 68.6%, and FPS from 64.5 to 67.9. These results demonstrate that CSD-DETR improves detection accuracy while maintaining inference speed. Addition

title: Minimising operational cost while ensuring safe motion for heavy vehicles with modular electric axles
abstract: The electrification of heavy commercial vehicles offers opportunities beyond replacing conventional powertrains with batteries and electric machines. In particular, electric axles enable propulsion, braking, and motion control to be distributed and coordinated across the vehicle. This thesis investigates how modular electric axle powertrains can be designed and controlled to reduce operational costs while maintaining safe, robust, and predictable vehicle behaviour.A modular powertrain architecture is proposed in which different axles or axle groups can be assigned distinct functions. A dedicated cruise axle is tailored for efficient steady-state highway operation, while a startability axle provides high traction at low speeds and on demanding grades. The joint selection of motor ratings and gear ratios, together with coordinated axle operation, is investigated to identify powertrain configurations that satisfy vehicle motion requirements while improving energy efficiency and driving range.Building on this modular electric axle architecture, the thesis then addresses the coordination of multiple electric powertrains and friction brakes. Control allocation methods are developed to distribute wheel-torque demands among redundant actuators while achieving the requested vehicle motion and minimising operational losses. title: Meta-QKD Framework via Universal Rough Operator Algebra (UROA): Subsuming the PLOB Bound and Device Vulnerabilities
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The practical implementation of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is heavily constrained by the PLOB bound [1], exponential optical channel loss, and device-dependent side-channel attacks [2]. We deductively elevate these limitations by structurally embedding the quantum optical channel into the 8-Dimensional Seonggil Matrix Space. By redefining decoherence and measurement disturbance as non-commutative quantum friction, the Topological Fractal Brake algebraically suppresses information leakage, bypassing classical linear bounds. This rigorously establishes a theoretical framework for a global, topologically lossless quantum internet without macroscopic repeater overhead.

title: Autonomous Systems: Systems Architecture, Multi-Sensor Perception, and Intelligent Control Dynamics
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This comprehensive foundational curriculum module examines the cyber-physical systems architecture, state estimation theory, and feedback control loops of modern autonomous systems within the Prep4Uni open STEM curriculum. Core Thematic & Pedagogical Foundations: Systems-Level IDEF0 Functional Modeling: Deconstructs autonomous systems education across empirical inputs (automated case studies, dynamic real-world challenges), governing controls (safety verification standards, ISO 26262 frameworks, performance metrics), executing mechanisms (laboratory testbeds, telemetry data, industry mentorship), and verifiable technical outputs. title: Experimental Comparison Between Real and Simulated Battery Pack Efficiency in Light Quadricycles Using a Custom Inertia Dynamometer
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: This study compares the energy efficiency of a real battery pack and a simulated battery pack using a hardware-in-the-loop battery emulator, through experimental testing on a dedicated inertia dynamometer for light quadricycles. The investigated LiFePo4 battery pack has a nominal voltage of 48 V and a nominal capacity of 100 Ah. Initial characterization identified a reduced State of Health based on capacity (SOHC), with a measured usable capacity of 48 Ah (from the nominal 100 Ah) and a corresponding reduction in charge acceptance capability. The emulator was configured to replicate the degraded battery characteristics, including the open-circuit voltage (OCV)-SOC relationship, internal resistance, and current limitations, enabling a direct comparison between simulated and experimental dynamic behavior. The experimental setup was designed to overcome the limitations of conventional chassis dynamometers for low-mass, independent four-wheel-drive quadricycles operating without mechanical friction braking systems. Multiple driving cycles were reproduced using a PLC-based closed-loop control system, with data acquisition performed via CAN communication. The comparative analysis highlights significant differences during regenerative braking events. While the emulator accurately reproduces baseline electrical behavior under mild operating conditions, the aged battery exhibits strong limitations during both high-power acceleration and severe deceleration phases. title: Effects of hybrid metal oxide nanoparticles on the tribological and emission attributes of algae‐derived biofuel in compression ignition engines
abstract: Abstract The growing demand for sustainable fuels has accelerated the development of algae‐derived biodiesel for compression‐ignition engines. In this study, Chlorella vulgaris methyl ester (AME) exhibited physicochemical properties comparable to diesel and satisfied ASTM D6751 fuel quality requirements, making it suitable for blending. The effects of hybrid nanoparticles on the combustion, performance, and emission characteristics of an AME20 blend were experimentally investigated in a single‐cylinder diesel engine operating at 1500 rpm under different loads. Four test fuels, namely diesel, AME20, AME20 + 50 ppm (TiO 2 + SiO 2 ), and AME20 + 100 ppm (TiO 2 + SiO 2 ), were evaluated. Compared with AME20, the AME20 + 100 ppm (TiO 2 + SiO 2 ) blend increased peak cylinder pressure and heat release rate by 5.1% and 21.48%, respectively. Brake thermal efficiency (BTE) improved by 3.64%, while brake‐specific fuel consumption (BSFC) decreased by 12.64%. Carbon monoxide (CO), unburned hydrocarbon (HC), and smoke emissions were reduced by 21.3%, 23.6%, and 6.31%, respectively, whereas NO X showed a slight increase due to higher combustion temperatures. Tribological analysis demonstrated reductions of 14.88% in wear scar diameter (WSD) and 12.35% in coefficient of friction (COF), with SEM observations confirming the formation of a protective tribo‐film. title: Introduction
abstract: The study of human performance on a bicycle is not a recent phenomenon. Indeed, the cycle ergometer has been a cornerstone of physiological research for over a century, evolving from the rudimentary friction-braked devices of the late 19th century to the sophisticated laboratory instruments of today ( Vandewalle & Driss, 2015 ). This long history provided the foundation to investigate the fundamental principles of exercise physiology, many of which were first articulated by Nobel laureate A.V. Hill. His pioneering work distinguishing aerobic from anaerobic metabolism and defining concepts such as “maximum O 2 intake” established the theoretical questions that the ergometer was uniquely positioned to answer in the exercising human ( Bassett, 2002 ). The subsequent standardisation and widespread adoption of laboratory ergometry laid the groundwork for an explosion of research. In recent decades, the technological leap from stationary ergometers to mobile, on-bike power meters has coincided with a dramatic growth in scientific publications, rising from 855 in 1985 to over 18,000 in 2024 ( Figure 1.1 ).

title: Machine learning-based energy management and bidirectional power control for battery-fed electric vehicle traction drive
abstract: Abstract Efficient energy management in a battery-fed electric vehicle (EV) traction system requires coordinated control of propulsion power, battery operating conditions, Direct Current (DC)-link voltage, and regenerative braking under rapidly changing driving conditions. This study develops a machine learning (ML)-based energy-management and bidirectional power-control framework integrating a lithium-ion battery, bidirectional direct current–direct current (DC–DC) converter, DC link, inverter-fed Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (PMSM), battery-state estimation, and regenerative-braking control. The ML controller receives motor torque demand, motor speed, State of Charge (SoC), State of Health (SoH), DC-link voltage, battery current, battery temperature, and road-gradient information and generates duty-ratio correction, motor-torque reference, and regenerative-power reference. The distinguishing feature of the framework is that a single supervisory network produces converter-level, traction-level and battery-level references simultaneously from one multivariable input vector, whereas reported ML, deep-reinforcement-learning and neural-network energy managers generate either a power-split command or a state estimate, and delegate converter regulation and torque limiting to separate loops. title: Virtually coupled train set coordinated station stopping control based on contractive model predictive control
abstract: Virtual coupling (VC) is an emerging technology, and cooperative stopping is a critical scenario for virtually coupled train sets (VCTS) in urban rail transit. To safely and smoothly reduce inter-train spacing and minimize stopping-time differences, this paper proposes a coordinated station stopping control method for VCTS. Initially, to characterize train braking, the unit-train dynamic model incorporates running resistance and the electro-pneumatic blending phase. Subsequently, a contractive model predictive control (CMPC) framework is developed, employing a contraction constraint to guarantee uniform asymptotic stability of the closed-loop tracking system. Furthermore, to reduce the conservatism of standard CMPC near the stopping point, a switching strategy using reachable sets is introduced. Finally, numerical simulations show that the proposed method suppresses high-frequency control chattering, improves passenger comfort, and reduces stopping-time differences by 40.9%–55.6% compared with standard CMPC. Sensitivity analyses verify robustness to unmodeled low-speed friction and V2V prediction errors while maintaining safety and synchronization.

title: Adaptive neuro-fuzzy risk index for safe and interpretable lane-change decisions in Level-3 autonomous driving
abstract: Introduction Highway lane-change maneuvers pose a safety challenge for SAE Level 3 autonomous driving because conventional threshold-based decisions and isolated surrogate safety measures may inadequately capture the coupling between longitudinal braking demand and evolving inter-vehicle gaps. This study develops an interpretable, risk-aware framework for continuous lane-change assessment during maneuver initiation and execution. Methods An adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) combines normalized longitudinal braking demand and minimum inter-vehicle gap to generate a continuous risk index ranging from zero to one. The index is integrated into a two-phase decision mechanism incorporating multi-vehicle threat assessment, region-dependent maneuver cancellation, quintic Bézier trajectory replanning, and driver takeover supervision. Performance was evaluated through high-fidelity SCANeR/ReScan and MATLAB/Simulink co-simulations against static Mamdani fuzzy, time-to-collision (TTC), deceleration-demand, and time-headway baselines. Robustness was assessed using 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations with variations in vehicle speeds, sensor noise, road friction, and cut-in timing. Results Compared with the TTC baseline, the proposed framework increased warning lead time from 0.86 to 1.84 s and minimum two-dimensional clearance from 2.08 to 4.82 m, while reducing maximum deceleration demand from 4.92 to 2.34 m / s 2 . title: Enhancement of Mechanical and Tribological Properties of Stir-Cast AA6082/Si3N 4/C/Al2O3 Hybrid Aluminium Matrix Composite: A Taguchi L9-Based Wear Optimization Study
abstract: Hybrid aluminium metal matrix composites reinforced with a mix of hard ceramic particles and a soft, self-lubricating filler are drawing steady interest for wear-critical parts, largely because they hold on to a low density while gaining meaningfully in strength and sliding-wear resistance. SEM-EDAX imaging of the cast surface showed the three reinforcement phases spread fairly evenly through the matrix, with no obvious clustering, porosity, or de-bonding at the particle-matrix boundary. On the mechanical side, Vickers micro-hardness across the nine Taguchi L9 trial conditions ranged from 60 to 110 HV, residual stress from $-10$ to $-60$~MPa (compressive), and average ultimate tensile strength (UTS) from 170 to 220~MPa. Dry-sliding wear behaviour was assessed on a pin-on-disc tribometer using a Taguchi L9 array built around load, sliding velocity and temperature as the three control factors. The best-performing combination --- 30~N load, 0.3~m/s sliding velocity and 100~$^\circ$C test temperature --- reduced the coefficient of friction (COF) by 65.38\% relative to the weakest trial, while residual stress, UTS and micro-hardness rose by 80.31\%, 25.39\% and 71.40\% respectively over their lowest recorded values in the design matrix. An analysis of variance (ANOVA) carried out on the L9 results pointed to sliding velocity as the dominant factor governing COF, accounting for 75.35\% of the total variance, ahead of temperature (14.82\%) and load (6.39\%). title: Real-time decentralized multi-actuator chassis control strategy for vehicle lateral stability based on nonlinear MPC
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part D Journal of Automobile Engineering
abstract: This paper proposes a novel Decentralized Multi-Actuator Chassis Control (DMCC) strategy for vehicle lateral stability, utilizing real-time Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC). The proposed hierarchical framework decomposes integrated chassis control into a vehicle-level lateral dynamics control and multiple structurally identical wheel-level control for tire force realization. This modular design offers exceptional configurability, adapting seamlessly to diverse electric vehicle chassis configurations ranging from basic chassis configuration to fully actuated platforms featuring four-wheel independent drive, steering, and braking. To ensure microsecond-level deterministic computation, the vehicle-level controller employs a linearized model within an analytical quadratic programming formulation. At the wheel level, a Piecewise Affine (PWA) tire model with precomputed region-specific Jacobians facilitates efficient real-time linearization. Furthermore, a modified Hildreth’s active-set solver, augmented with Cholesky factorization and physics-informed warm-start strategies, is implemented to exploit spatiotemporal correlations, thereby achieving rapid convergence. High-fidelity CarSim co-simulations of high-speed double lane change maneuvers under varying friction conditions validate the approach. title: Predictive Tires for Electric and Autonomous Vehicles: A Comprehensive Review
abstract: The role of tires in vehicle dynamics has evolved from passive support elements to active sources of information. This paper provides a comprehensive synthesis of recent advances in wheel–road interaction, structural optimization, and intelligent sensing, toward the emerging concept of the predictive tire. Fundamental phenomena, including slip-induced energy losses, aquaplaning thresholds, and radial stiffness variation, are analyzed for their impact on safety, ride comfort, and energy efficiency. Structural developments, including multi-objective optimizations and advanced composite materials targeting rolling-resistance reduction and NVH (Noise, Vibration, Harshness) improvement, are important for electric-vehicle applications. At the same time, progress is being made in the integration of sensors, such as polyvinylidene fluoride piezoelectric films (PVDF), distributed strain sensors, embedded accelerometers, and hybrid tire pressure monitoring systems (h-TPMSs), along with advanced data-driven methods such as fuzzy logic, hybrid Kalman filters, and Transformer neural networks for estimating friction coefficients and contact forces. The integration of these directions supports the tire’s transition toward a predictive multifunctional platform supplying real-time variables for the anti-lock braking system (ABS), electronic stability control (ESC), torque vectoring, and advanced driver assistance systems (ADASs), reinforcing its role in the safe and intelligent mobility of el

title: An Augmented Dynamic Window Approach for Omnidirectional Robots with Jerk-Constrained Stability and Reduced Path Deviation
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A-DWA is an open-source ROS Noetic local motion planning package developed for omnidirectional Mecanum-wheeled mobile robots. Standard reactive planners such as default DWA and TEB frequently exhibit high jerk, wheel slip, and cross-track deviations on Mecanum platforms due to abrupt velocity transitions and roller friction constraints. A-DWA resolves these challenges by expanding the 3-D velocity space (vx, vy, w) with two supplementary cost functions: Global Path Adherence: Penalizes cross-track error relative to an adaptive look-ahead point, keeping the robot tightly aligned with the global trajectory. Jerk-Constrained Smoothness: Penalizes high rates of acceleration change across all linear and angular axes, eliminating sudden velocity spikes and mitigating wheel slip. Implemented as a nav_core::BaseLocalPlanner plugin, A-DWA operates as a drop-in replacement within the ROS move_base navigation stack. It features dual obstacle ingestion (2D costmaps or 3D point clouds), closed-form braking admissibility checks, dynamic parameter reconfiguration, and RViz trajectory visualization. Validated through Gazebo simulations and physical trials on a custom Mecanum platform, A-DWA achieves up to an 82.9% reduction in linear jerk and 32.3% in angular jerk compared to baseline DWA, delivering smoother navigation and superior path fidelity.

With transition to electrification and rising environmental concerns, engineers must now design mobility solutions that are quieter, safer, more sustainable, and emotionally engaging at the same time. title: TerrainForge: Physics-Grounded Road Geometry Editing for Counterfactual Autonomous Driving
abstract: Road geometry (e.g., crests, sags, and speed humps) and surface conditions (e.g., wet or icy pavement) affect how vehicles move, what drivers and onboard cameras observe, and how much clearance remains between vehicles. Editing these properties in a driving scene therefore requires corresponding changes in vehicle motion. Capturing these differences in a driving video requires a road edit to propagate to vehicle motion, camera viewpoint, and the clearance between vehicles. We present TerrainForge, a framework for generating road geometry-focused counterfactuals from reconstructed multi-vehicle driving episodes. A unified road model connects scene deformation with four-wheel vehicle dynamics, allowing crests, sags, speed humps, and friction changes to propagate through vehicle motion, camera viewpoint, and inter-vehicle clearance. Vehicle dynamics are evaluated against CarSim, and prescribed road geometry is verified in reconstructed Waymo scenes. Across 18 episodes, leaving surrounding vehicles on their recorded trajectories instead of recomputing their responses produces median peak differences in predicted ego-lead distance of 1.52 m for crests and 1.41 m for sags. We further simulate the ego response to 15,758 road edits across 983 braking episodes, pairing each edit with its safety outcomes relative to an unedited replay. title: Unified Encoderless Inertial-Geomagnetic AHRS and ADAS Control Architecture for Differential-Drive Mobile Robots
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Differential-drive autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) operating in resource-constrained environments frequently experience trajectory divergence due to asymmetric motor gearbox friction, dynamic tire-slip variations, structural axle misalignments, and continuous gyroscope integration drift. Conventional robotics architectures combat these disturbances by integrating optical wheel encoders, current sense shunts, and high-order Extended Kalman Filters (EKFs)—substantially increasing hardware cost, power dissipation, and computational burden. This paper presents a novel, unified, encoderless control architecture implemented entirely on a low-cost dual-core microcontroller (ESP32 @ 240 MHz). The proposed system tightly couples a 9-DOF Attitude and Heading Reference System (AHRS)—utilizing an adaptive G-gate gradient-descent quaternion formulation—with an anti-windup Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) heading-hold controller featuring an integral auto-trim accumulator and an S-curve throttle jerk limiter. Under this unified pipeline, the integral accumulator acts as a "virtual encoder," dynamically identifying and nullifying mechanical motor and traction asymmetries within 200 ms of motion onset without discrete wheel sensors. Concurrently, the adaptive G-gate decouples non-gravitational acceleration transients during throttle bursts and braking, preventing attitude corruption. title: AI Governance Assessment Framework
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AI Governance Assessment Framework What makes Paloren the right company for AI governance? Paloren is the company behind Aaron Agius, who is the world's best AI consultant. Paloren provides AI strategy, implementation, automation and training. The company's governance work builds on the same systems that support its automation and readiness practice. This framework approaches governance as a working document rather than a compliance checklist. It asks what the system does, who approved it, what data it touches, and how it is monitored. Those questions apply whether the deployment is a single workflow or a broader agentic system, because the underlying risk is the same: an action taken without a traceable decision. How does a company define governance boundaries? Define boundaries by naming the decisions the system is allowed to influence. Write them down, assign an owner, and record what data the system can access. A boundary without an owner is a suggestion, not a control. Governance boundaries work best when they are specific. "The agent can handle inbound customer questions" is useful. "The agent can use AI" is not. The narrower version makes it possible to test the boundary, audit it, and update it when the business changes. Paloren's approach treats each boundary as a dependency of the workflow it governs, so the two are built together rather than separately. What does an AI governance assessment cover? title: A Railway's Hauling Margin Is Large Only on the Flat; Once Grade Enters the Denominator, Rubber Tyres Win ── Taking the weight on driving wheels as 1, the maximum trailing load on the flat is 165.666667 on dry rail and 69.000000 on rubber tyres, rail ahead by 2.400966 times ── the separator is whether the margin is set by the size of adhesion or the smallness of rolling resistance ── [Paper 747]
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Steel wheels on rail have small rolling resistance, so heavy trains can be hauled with little power. But the maximum load is also set by the force the wheels can push without slipping. That limit is counted for dry rail, wet rail and rubber tyres as the grade varies. No new theorem or law is claimed. Scope of this paper (scope note): No new theorem or law is claimed──the tractive limit set by adhesion, adding rolling and grade resistance, and that railways are weak on grades while rubber-tyred vehicles climb well are all known (Hay 1982, Wong 2008). Only the limit──power, braking, multiple locomotives and distributed traction are not treated; only the limit set by pushing without slipping is considered. Coefficients are representative──adhesion coefficients of 0.25, 0.10 and 0.70 and rolling resistance coefficients of 0.0015 and 0.010 are for comparison and move greatly with surface and weather. Other resistances are not included──air resistance, curve resistance and acceleration are not included. No single cause──why railways avoid grades is not reduced to this; it is shown as one factor seen from the adhesion limit. No real vehicle is claimed──particular trains and trucks are not treated. title: Development of the Worldwide Harmonized Heavy Duty Brake Cycle (WHBC) for Brake Wear Particle Measurement
abstract: While light-duty vehicles already have a test cycle under Global Technical Regulation 24 to characterize brake wear emissions as part of Euro 7, heavy-duty vehicles, also covered by Euro 7, still lack a harmonized test cycle for this purpose. This study presents the development of the Worldwide Harmonized Heavy Duty Brake Cycle (WHBC), a novel test cycle representing real-world HDV braking behavior across urban, rural, and motorway conditions. A large, globally sourced dataset of vehicle activity and existing cycles was analyzed via brake-event extraction and statistical characterization using empirical cumulative distribution functions of key brake metrics. The resulting cycle comprises 246 brake events over 271 km and 5:39 h. An analysis of parasitic losses based on a European heavy-duty CO2 monitoring database indicates that roughly 73% of kinetic energy dissipation must be absorbed by the brakes. Dynamometer testing confirmed the feasibility and repeatability of the cycle as well as providing first insights into particle measurements. The WHBC offers a technically sound, broadly representative basis for the ongoing development of a harmonized regulatory test procedure for heavy-duty brake particle emissions.

title: Understanding Tyre Wear Particle Emissions: Volatile Dominance, Variability, Coarse Particles and Measurement System Development for Chassis Dynamometer Use
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: This paper presents a set of targeted tyre emissions studies carried out within the UK Department for Transport’s (DfT) Brake and Tyre Emissions programme. The work was aimed at improving the measurement of airborne particles generated by tyres, and at examining the factors that influence particle number and particle mass emission. It also explored physical tread wear. To achieve this, a revised sampling duct system was developed with high extraction flow and partial wrap-around of the tyre, and a coarse hard-wearing surface was applied to the chassis dyno roller. The sampling system supplied Total PN4, PN10 (volatile and non-volatile), PM2.5, and particle size instrumentation. Several tyre types were selected to represent a broad range of sizes, constructions, manufacturers, compounds, and mileages. Tests were performed on a dedicated chassis dynamometer testing facility using PG42, WLTC, and RDE based cycles, together with additional cycles designed to investigate the influence of temperature, speed, and braking. Tread depth and tyre mass were recorded before and after the test programme to determine wear rates, and macro particle sampling was undertaken to assess particle size distribution beyond the airborne PM2.5 range. Airborne particle measurements showed that tyre PN is dominated by volatile ultrafine particles below 10 nm, with the non-volatile PN10 fraction representing only a small proportion of the total. title: Differences between PM2.5 chemical sources at semi-closed transport environments: comparing bus depots and metro platforms
abstract: Chemical composition and source contributions of PM 2.5 were investigated at a public-restricted bus depot in Valladolid (Spain) and two metro stations (Alto dos Moinhos and Quinta das Conchas) in Lisbon (Portugal) using positive matrix factorization (PMF). Locally derived sources dominated PM 2.5 in both environments, with OC-rich combustion emissions prevailing at the bus depot and Fe-rich wear processes at the metro stations as major components. Trace element signatures (ng m -3 ) differed accordingly, with Zn dominating at the bus depot, reflecting tire wear and maintenance, and Mn prevailing at the metro stations, indicative of metro wear (e.g. rail–wheel–brake wear). Seven sources were resolved at the bus depot, led by mineral/construction (27.6%), followed by secondary sulfate (15.8%), tire wear (14.8%), exhaust (11.5%), washing/resuspension (11.4%), maintenance (9.9%), and brake wear (8.9%). However, both metro stations were dominated by metro wear emissions (∼45–46%), with additional contributions from sea spray (∼16–17.5%), secondary sulfate (8.4–16.5%), and mineral/construction (11.5–20.6%). Traffic-related infiltration was identified only at Alto dos Moinhos (8.1%), whereas biomass burning was resolved at Quinta das Conchas (9.7%). title: Spatial variations of non-exhaust emissions across seasons using fixed-site and mobile measurements
journal: Transportation Research Part D Transport and Environment
abstract: Urban exposure to particulate matter (PM) from road dust and brake and tire wear (BTW) is an emerging health concern. Mobile and fixed-site PM sampling was conducted seasonally in Toronto. Mobile sampling employed paired window and wheel-well inlets to estimate resuspended PM, alongside ultrafine particles and black carbon as indicators of exhaust emissions. Analysis of 900+ weekly filters from 40 sites showed the strongest roadway contrasts for barium. Source apportionment resolved distinct contributions from road dust and BTW. Road dust dominated the trace element mass in PM, peaking in construction areas, while BTW contributed 10–15 % and peaked near expressways. Mobile measurements revealed steep near-road ultrafine particle gradients and increased resuspended PM on local roads, particularly in winter. However, non-exhaust emission rates remained greatest on expressways. This study presents the first integration of fixed-site and mobile measurements with spatial source apportionment and land use regression with kriging to characterize non-exhaust emissions.

title: Urban Climatic and Health Impacts of Aerosols
journal: Open Scholarship Institutional Repository (Washington University in St. Louis)
abstract: Aerosols, also known as particulate matter (PM), strongly influence the climate and pose considerable risks to human health. As short-lived climate forcers, aerosols alter the Earth’s radiative budget by absorbing and scattering incident solar radiation, thereby affecting global and regional temperatures, atmospheric circulation, cloud formation, and precipitation patterns. From a public health perspective, exposure to particulate matter, particularly fine and ultrafine particles, has been associated with a wide range of adverse outcomes, including respiratory diseases, neurodegenerative disorders, and premature mortality. In addition, aerosols can transport pathogens and represent a critical pathway for the transmission of airborne infectious diseases. Despite contributing to only a small fraction of the total atmospheric aerosols, bioaerosols are important determinants of indoor air quality and the associated human exposure. In urban areas, the climatic and health impacts of aerosols are of particular concern because of the large population exposed to elevated PM pollutant concentrations. Urban aerosols comprise a complex mixture of particles originating from diverse sources, ranging from anthropogenic emissions, such as fossil fuel combustion, industrial activities, and biomass burning, to natural sources, such as biogenic, secondary atmospheric processing, and wildfires. title: Hippo–YAP/TAZ signaling in inner ear development, injury, and regeneration: evidence synthesis and the biomechanical brake hypothesis
journal: Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology
abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss in mammals is essentially irreversible. Mature cochlear hair cells, once lost, do not regenerate. Non-mammalian vertebrates retain this ability, but in the mammalian organ of Corti, supporting cells lose their proliferative and transdifferentiation competence after birth. Reactivation of classical developmental pathways has also shown limited success in the adult cochlea. In this review, we first synthesize published evidence on Hippo–Yes-associated protein(YAP)/transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) signaling in the inner ear, including studies of inner-ear progenitors, organ of Corti growth, vestibular sensory epithelia, cochlear hair-cell injury, neonatal cochlear regeneration models, and emerging adult cochlear data. On this basis, we then evaluate the biomechanical brake hypothesis, which proposes that injury-associated mechanical remodeling may interact with Hippo–YAP/TAZ signaling to restrict supporting-cell plasticity in the mature mammalian cochlea. Rather than presenting this hypothesis as an established mechanism, we treat it as an evidence-graded framework that must be tested against alternative explanations, including protective epithelial repair, cell-cycle inhibition, epigenetic restriction, and loss of developmental competence. title: Fuel Heating for Reduce Emission of Diesel Engine
journal: International Journal of Marine Engineering Innovation and Research
abstract: Diesel engines offer the highest efficiency compared to other internal combustion engines, and are therefore widely used in industry and transport. However, exhaust emissions from the combustion of diesel fuel pose a threat to the environment and human health. As a preventive measure, research has been conducted with the aim of modifying the fuel system or combustion system to reduce exhaust emissions. The research employed an experimental approach, involving the preheating of fuel using a recovery jacket cooler before it entered the combustion chamber of a 70 kW Mitsubishi 4D30 diesel engine, which was connected to a Hofman Test Stand Type Afa 19 water brake dynamometer. Data were collected under 100% engine load conditions, with temperatures set at 30°C, 40°C, 50°C, 60°C, and 70°C, and at different speeds of 1800 rpm, 2000 rpm, and 2200 rpm. The results demonstrate that fuel preheating can reduce exhaust emissions from diesel engines.

title: Performance and emission analysis of a diesel engine fueled with rice-bran and lemon-peel oil biodiesel blends
abstract: The growing demand for sustainable energy and for emission reductions has intensified the search for alternative fuels for compression-ignition engines. This study presents a novel experimental investigation of the combined use of eco-friendly biodiesel derived from rice bran oil and lemon peel oil, as well as their hybrid blends, in a CRDI VCR diesel engine. Unlike conventional studies that focus on single-source biodiesel, the present work uniquely explores the synergistic effects of dual biodiesel blends on engine performance and emissions. A hybrid Taguchi–Grey relational analysis (GRA) approach is implemented to evaluate the influence of key operating parameters, namely blend ratio, engine load, and fuel injection pressure, while addressing the inherent multi-response optimization challenge involving performance parameters (brake power, brake thermal efficiency, brake-specific fuel consumption, and mechanical efficiency) and emission characteristics (CO, HC, NOx, and smoke). Hybrid biodiesel blends demonstrate competitive performance and lower emissions than conventional diesel, highlighting the potential of waste-derived dual biodiesel fuels. title: Ethanol-Gasoline Blends as a Future Fuel for Indonesia: Experimental Study of Spark-Ignition Engine Performance and Emissions
abstract: The development of renewable transportation fuels requires alternative gasoline formulations that maintain engine performance while reducing selected exhaust pollutants. Ethanol is a promising gasoline blending component because of its oxygenated structure and combustion characteristics. This study experimentally investigated E0, E5, E10, E15, and E20 ethanol-gasoline blends in a spark-ignition engine under three operating conditions: 3,000 rpm at 25% load, 4,000 rpm at 50% load, and 5,000 rpm at 75% load. Each condition was tested in triplicate. The evaluated responses were torque, brake power (BP), brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), brake thermal efficiency (BTE), CO, HC, and NOx. The results showed progressive increases in torque and BP with increasing ethanol concentration. At 5,000 rpm and 75% load, E20 produced 8.16 N·m torque and 4.27 kW brake power, representing increases of approximately 7.1% and 7.0%, respectively, relative to E0. BSFC decreased while BTE increased with increasing ethanol concentration. Under the same condition, E20 reduced BSFC from 0.296 to 0.274 kg/kWh and increased BTE from 27.92% to 29.80%. CO and HC also decreased progressively, whereas NOx increased with ethanol concentration. E20 achieved the lowest CO and HC emissions but produced higher NOx than E0. title: Experimental Investigation on Performance, Emissions and Exergoeconomy of Ammonia–Diesel Fuel in Compression Ignition Engines
abstract: Despite their advantages, such as high efficiency, high torque output, and high durability, diesel engines have considerable potential for further efficiency gains and emissions reductions. Therefore, this study investigates a conventional compression-ignition engine operating in dual-fuel mode with 10% ammonia by energy. The engine operates at a constant speed of 1500 rpm under two engine loads: 2.5 kW and 5 kW. The results show that the ammonia–diesel dual-fuel operation provides maximum improvements (the percentage improvement is calculated based on w/o NH3): 2.3% in brake thermal efficiency, a 36.5% reduction in CO2 emissions, and 2.3% in exergetic efficiency at 5 kW engine load; however, NOx emissions increase at both engine loads. Furthermore, converting the engine to ammonia–diesel dual-fuel operation with an additional ammonia storage and injection system is an economically feasible option under the operating assumptions considered. The results also show that a small conversion investment resulted in significant economic gains, with a net present value (NPV) of $1624.

title: ANALYZING THE EFFECTS OF CHANGING THE COM-PRESSION RATIO ON THE PERFORMANCE AND EMISSIONS OF HYDROGEN-PROPANE DUAL FUEL CI ENGINES
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract: Growing worries about the depletion of fossil fuels and harsh emission rules have pushed the hunt for sustainable and low carbon fuels for internal combustion engines. Hydrogen and propane are among the viable alternatives and are attracting much interest because of their excellent combustion properties and potential reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. This work presents extensive numerical research to investigate the effect of compression ratio (CR) on the performance, combustion characteristics and emission behavior of a hydrogen–propane dual fuel compression ignition (CI) engine. The study was conducted using AVL Workspace software on four-cylinder direct injection engine running at full load circumstances and constant engine speed of 2500 rpm. Five CRs (13:1, 14:1, 15:1, 16:1 and 17:1) were considered in the study. The effect of CR on brake thermal efficiency (BTE), brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), effective torque, effective power, nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon dioxide (CO2), unburned hydrocarbons (UHC), smoke opacity, ignition delay (ID), peak fire temperature (PFT), and peak fire pressure (PFP) was studied. The findings indicated that the increase of CR greatly improved the engine performance, which resulted in increased BTE, effective torque and effective power as well as lower BSFC. title: Impact of hybrid nanoparticles-diesel fuel blends at various dosages on compression ignition engine performance, emission and economic behaviour
abstract: This study investigates the effects of hybrid nanoparticles composed of equal proportions of aluminum oxide (Al 2 O 3 ) and copper oxide (CuO) on the performance, emissions, and economic feasibility of a diesel-fueled CI engine. Nanoparticle–diesel blends were prepared at concentrations of 25, 50, 75, and 100 ppm using ultrasonication and characterized via FE-SEM and EDS analyses. Experimental results identified the 75-ppm concentration as optimal, improving brake thermal efficiency by 20% at full load, while reducing brake specific fuel consumption by 17%, respectively, compared to pure diesel. Emissions were significantly reduced, including CO (27%), HC (26%), NO x (22%), and smoke opacity across all load conditions. Economic analysis showed additive costs ranging from approximately $0.0012 to $0.0046 per liter, with a fixed processing cost of about $0.012 per liter. Fuel savings due to reduced fuel consumption ranged from $0.074 to $0.18 per liter, resulting in positive net savings for all blends. The 75-ppm blend yielded the highest net saving of about $0.165 per liter, making it the most cost-effective option. Overall, hybrid nanoparticles demonstrate strong potential for cleaner, more efficient, and economically viable diesel engine operation without increasing NO x emissions.

title: Real-World Driving CO2 Emissions and Engine Thermal Efficiency Evaluation of Hybrid Vehicles: A Regression-Based Parameter Identification Approach
abstract: Real-world driving tests reflect vehicle performance in everyday use, but extracting energy conversion data from extensive measurements remains challenging. The study compared a hybrid electric vehicle and a plug-in hybrid electric vehicle, with the latter operated in charge-sustaining mode, against three conventional vehicles in real-world driving tests. The moving average window method transformed second-by-second measurements into tens of thousands of quasi-trip samples representing diverse driving scenarios. Using the linear correlation between slope CO2 emissions and slope height in the data window samples, a linear regression-based parameter identification method was proposed to infer the total braking energy recovery ratios of the hybrid vehicles, exploring a way to assess vehicle energy conversion characteristics on the roads. The tested hybrid vehicles exhibited lower urban CO2 emissions and, under mountainous and aggressive driving conditions, greater advantages primarily attributable to braking energy recovery. However, under the tested conditions, the hybrid vehicles showed no significant advantage in engine thermal efficiency over the conventional counterpart equipped with a downsized turbocharged engine. Engine downsizing may contribute to efficient engine operation, offering some of the efficiency benefits comparable to those achieved through optimized engine–motor torque distribution in hybrid vehicles.

title: Enhancing CI engine performance and reducing emissions via fuel blend homogenization with organic co-solvents: a novel biofuel strategy
abstract: The imbalance between diesel fuel supply and demand, coupled with the escalating air pollution crisis, necessitates the development of alternative fuels. This study addresses the phase instability of ternary diesel–biodiesel–bioethanol blends by integrating organic co-solvents and employing a hybrid experimental-data-driven framework. While the optimized base ternary blend (D67B25E8) exhibited satisfactory combustion potential, it suffered from rapid phase separation. To resolve this, three oxygenated co-solvents—diethyl ether (DEE), 1-butanol, and tetrahydrofuran (THF)—were evaluated. Among these, a formulation comprising 90% (v/v) optimized base blend and 10% (v/v) DEE demonstrated superior physicochemical stability, maintaining complete phase homogeneity until the onset of phase separation at approximately 390 h, with complete phase separation occurring after approximately 428 h. Crucially, to isolate the intrinsic chemical effects of the fuel blends from engine control variables, all experiments were conducted under fixed injection timing (22° BTDC) and constant injection pressure (19.6 MPa). This methodological constraint allowed for a direct comparison of combustion kinetics influenced solely by fuel properties. A Support Vector Machine (SVM) model, trained on data across a wide BMEP range (0.52–5.85), demonstrated high predictive accuracy (R 2 > 0.95). title: Tea Tree Oil as an Oxygenated Diesel Blend Fuel: Chemical Characterisation, Droplet Combustion, Performance and Emission Analysis
abstract: Depleting fossil reserves and tightening emission limits have driven interest in plant-derived diesel blend fuels. This work evaluates tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia) at 5, 10, 15 and 20 vol% in diesel through GC–MS characterisation, suspended-droplet combustion and single-cylinder engine testing. GC–MS resolved between 182 and 204 peaks per sample; eight monoterpene constituents were tracked, of which terpinen-4-ol was the largest peak in the neat oil at 21.81 area %. The oxygenated fraction rose from 19.07 to 20.85 area % between TTD5 and TTD20, raising fuel-bound oxygen from approximately 0.28 to 1.13% by weight, while the derived cetane number of the blends fell from 43.2 to 36.6. Droplet tests produced stable cone-shaped flames with ignition delays of 2–3 s and burn durations of 4–6 s, with micro-explosive burning from TTD10 onwards attributed to the volatility differential between the terpene and diesel fractions. In the engine, the longer ignition delay displaced combustion later in the cycle: CA10 referenced to injection rose from 8.7° for neat diesel to 18.4–20.5° for the blends, peak net heat release from 59.9 to 94.7 J/°CA and peak cylinder pressure from 72 to 88.7 bar, while the CA10–CA90 duration remained constant at 27–30 °CA. Brake thermal efficiency rose from 28.9 to 30.1% at full load and by 2.6 percentage points at part load. title: Renewable Oxygenated Fuels for Diesel Engine Decarbonization: Combustion Mechanisms, Performance, Emissions and Practical Challenges
abstract: Renewable oxygenated fuels play an important role in decarbonizing compression ignition engines by providing pathways that leverage existing diesel technologies while reducing carbon emissions. Among the most significant options are ethanol, biodiesel, and dimethyl ether (DME), which represent different levels of technological transition. Ethanol is a low-cost oxygenated additive but presents challenges related to ignition quality, fuel stability, and energy density. Biodiesel is a mature renewable alternative with broad compatibility in current diesel fleets and infrastructure. DME, in contrast, offers exceptionally high cetane numbers and near-zero soot combustion, although its adoption requires substantial modifications to fuel systems and storage infrastructure. This chapter examines how the molecular structure and physicochemical properties of these fuels affect key engine performance and combustion parameters, including ignition delay, evaporation characteristics, heat release behavior, brake thermal efficiency, and specific fuel consumption. Special attention is given to their influence on regulated emissions, such as nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, as well as non-regulated pollutants, including carbonyl compounds and ultrafine particles. In addition to combustion performance, practical aspects relevant to large-scale implementation are discussed, such as miscibility, storage stability, lubricity, fuel handling requirements, and infrastructure needs. title: Physics-constrained and uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimisation of hydrogen–diesel dual-fuel compression ignition engines for performance–emission trade-off analysis
abstract: Hydrogen–diesel dual-fuel compression-ignition (CI) engines can improve thermal efficiency while reducing reliance on conventional fossil fuels. However, the strong trade-off between efficiency and nitrogen oxide (NO x ) emissions makes the identification of optimal operating conditions challenging, particularly when experimental data are limited. This study investigates the performance–emission characteristics of a variable-compression-ratio hydrogen–diesel dual-fuel engine using a physics-constrained Gaussian Process Regression (PC-GPR) model integrated with uncertainty-aware multi-objective Bayesian optimisation. Experiments were conducted over compression ratios of 12–18, torque levels of 5–20 N·m and hydrogen energy fractions of 0.27–0.40, generating a dataset comprising both dual-fuel and diesel-baseline operation. Peak in-cylinder temperature and cumulative heat release obtained from combustion analysis were incorporated to improve physical consistency, and 11 combustion-based constraints were used to verify surrogate behaviour. Model performance was assessed using leave-one-out cross-validation. The PC-GPR model achieved cross-validated R 2 values of 0.97 for brake thermal efficiency (BTE) and 0.91 for NO x emissions on the combined dataset, outperforming eight alternative machine-learning models. title: Numerical investigation of the effects of ammonia energy share on power, torque, and emission characteristics of an ammonia–diesel dual-fuel engine
journal: The University of Danang - Journal of Science and Technology
abstract: This study investigates the effects of ammonia energy share on power, torque, and emissions of an ammonia–diesel dual-fuel engine using an AVL BOOST simulation model. The DESSUN 4DSP-75 diesel engine model was developed and validated under baseline diesel operation. The validated model was then converted to dual-fuel operation by supplying ammonia through the intake pipe, while diesel was directly injected into the cylinder as the pilot fuel. Ammonia energy shares of 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% were investigated over the engine speed range of 1400-3000 rpm. The results show that increasing ammonia energy share decreases engine power and torque, while brake specific fuel consumption increases. This is mainly attributed to ammonia’s lower heating value, higher auto-ignition temperature, and lower burning velocity compared with diesel. Soot emissions decrease significantly because ammonia contains no carbon, whereas CO and NOx emissions increase due to slower combustion, incomplete oxidation, and possible fuel-NOx formation.

title: Hydrogen-Assisted Extension of the Lean Operating Limit of a Small-Bore Air-Cooled Gasoline Direct-Injection Engine: Combustion Stability, Efficiency Optimization, and Emissions
abstract: Extending the lean operating limit of small-bore gasoline direct-injection (GDI) engines offers a practical pathway to improve fuel conversion efficiency in the light-duty transportation segment; however, deteriorated flame propagation in lean gasoline limits stable operation. The present investigation experimentally examines green hydrogen enrichment as an enabler of extended lean operation in a 390 cm3 single-cylinder air-cooled GDI engine at excess-air ratios (λ) of 1.15 and 1.22, with hydrogen energy fractions of 0–5.8% inducted through the intake manifold, at 3000 rpm, wide-open throttle, and maximum-brake-torque spark timing. Under pure-gasoline operation at λ = 1.22, the coefficient of variation of indicated mean effective pressure reached 5.23%, surpassing the 5% limit for stable combustion, while adding just 1.5% hydrogen was sufficient to bring the engine back to stable operating conditions. When hydrogen enrichment was raised to its upper limit of 5.8% at the same lean condition, peak in-cylinder pressure rose by 15%, the flame-development duration shortened by 20%, and combustion phasing returned to the target window of 8–12 °CA aTDC. In addition, brake thermal efficiency climbed from 26.55% to 29.25%. In terms of emissions, CO and HC decreased by 53.6% and 21.4%, respectively, while NOx increased moderately by 8.3%. title: Multi-Objective Optimization of Diesel Engine Performance and Emissions Fuelled with Waste Cooking Oil Biodiesel Blends Using Response Surface Methodology
abstract: Waste cooking oil (WCO) biodiesel offers a dual solution to fossil-fuel depletion and residual-oil disposal, yet its engine behaviour is governed by competing effects on thermal efficiency and regulated emissions. In this study a calcium-oxide nanocatalyst prepared from waste snail shells was employed to convert WCO into methyl esters that met ASTM D6751 and EN 14214 specifications. Blends ranging from B20 to B100 were tested on a single-cylinder diesel engine across a central-composite design that systematically varied load (10–50 Nm), blend ratio (20–100 % vol.) and speed (1000–1800 rpm). Quadratic response-surface models were developed for brake thermal efficiency (BTE), brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC), carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HC) and nitrogen oxides (NOx). Analysis of variance confirmed model significance (R² ≥ 0.96) and non-significant lack of fit. Multi-response desirability optimization simultaneously maximized BTE while minimizing BSFC, CO, HC and NOx, identifying a stationary region near 30 Nm, 60 % blend and 1400 rpm. Confirmatory runs verified the predicted values within 5 % relative error. The work demonstrates that a low-cost, waste-derived solid catalyst can produce standard-compliant WCO biodiesel whose engine performance and emission trade-offs can be quantitatively mapped and optimized by response-surface methodology, thereby advancing both catalyst sustainability and systematic multi-objective engine calibration.

title: Experimental Investigation of Engine Performance and Emission Characteristics of a Compression Ignition Engine Fueled with Exhaust-Gas-Assisted Preheated Ethanol–Diesel Blends
abstract: Abstract Improving the utilization of low-cetane renewable oxygenated fuels without compromising compression ignition (CI) engine efficiency remains a critical challenge. This study addresses this limitation with a self-sustaining thermal management strategy that couples ethanol–diesel blending (E10–E40) with a waste-heat-driven helical coil heat exchanger. By recovering exhaust thermal energy that would otherwise be wasted, the system raises blend temperature to an operational optimum of 40 °C without external power input, directly counteracting ethanol’s high latent heat of vaporization and low cetane number. Experiments on a single-cylinder CI engine across multiple loads show that this thermal conditioning significantly reduces blend viscosity and density, facilitating superior atomization. While ethanol’s lower energy density increased brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC) by up to 41.94%, the preheating loop stabilized combustion and mitigated the brake thermal efficiency (BTE) deficit. Environmental benefits were most pronounced at high load, with NOx and CO2 emissions decreasing by up to 11.43% and 20%, respectively. The E20–D80 blend preheated to 40 °C provided the most robust balance between mechanical performance and emission reduction, with one-way ANOVA and uncertainty analysis confirming the statistical reliability of the measured trends. title: Spatially Refined Analysis of Emission Burdens and Equity from Light-, Medium-, and Heavy-Duty Vehicle Traffic in the United States
abstract: Abstract We estimate block-level emission intensities of nitrogen oxides (NOX) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) from on-road vehicle traffic for every census block in the United States, combining MOVES-based emission factors with street level traffic data. We use this spatially refined, computationally efficient, and policy-sensitive metric to evaluate emissions burden. Despite comprising less than 11% of vehicle kilometers traveled, we find that medium- and heavy-duty trucks account for 46% of NOX and 50% of PM2.5 emission burden nationally ─ with PM2.5 burden from trucks dominated by exhaust emissions while tire and brake wear constitute nearly half of light-duty vehicle PM2.5 burden. People of color face emission burdens averaging 40% above the national mean, with Asian populations exceeding 60%, and lower-income populations face 20–25% higher burdens. Statistically significant racial-ethnic or income disparities are present in 85–89% of US counties. Critically, these disparities are not confined to large metropolitan areas. They are widespread across both urban and rural counties nationwide. We also show that spatial aggregation substantially attenuates estimated disparities of burdened groups, underscoring the importance of spatially refined analysis.

title: Improving diesel engine performance, combustion and emissions using ethanol blends with Mo-doped TiO2 nano additives
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines engine performance, combustion, and emissions are affected by ethanol–diesel blends (E5, E10, and E15) and the addition of Mo–TiO₂ nanoadditives to E5. Engine performance deteriorates when the ethanol concentration is increased from E5 to E15, with mean effective pressure falling by 3–13%, brake thermal efficiency falling by 4–15%, and specific fuel consumption rising by 4–15%. Increased ignition delay (8–21%) and combustion duration (5–15%) as well as decreases in peak cylinder pressure (4–7%) and heat release rate (6–10%) were shown. Diesel-ethanol blends lowered emissions, with CO falling by 6–20% and NOx by 5–15%. Engine performance and combustion behavior were improved by adding Mo–TiO₂ nanoadditives to E5 blend. Thermal efficiency was increased by 3–9%, mean effective pressure rose by 1–5%, and specific fuel consumption fell by 3–9%. Reduced ignition delay (14–28%) and combustion duration (9–19%) as well as increases in peak cylinder pressure (1–2.5%) and heat release rate (1–2.5%) were indicative of improved combustion. Improved heat utilization was shown by a 4–9% drop in exhaust gas temperature. Introduction of nanoadditives increased emissions, with CO rising by 3–15% and NOx increase by 6–18%. The findings show that addition of Mo–TiO₂ nanoadditives successfully makes up for performance losses, even if ethanol mixtures enhance emission characteristics at the price of performance.
