title: Injection Parameter Optimisation in Biodiesel-Fuelled Variable Compression Ratio Engines: Interactions Governing Combustion, Performance and Emissions
abstract: Biodiesel is an accepted renewable replacement fuel for conventional petroleum diesel‚ but its higher viscosity and lower volatility and heating value make biodiesel blends impractical in a single compression ratio engine․ Variable compression ratio removes that constraint by allowing the compression ratio to be used as an experimental variable‚ and adding a variable to injection pressure and injection timing․ This review concerns thirty-four experimental and theoretical research frameworks published between 2008 and 2025 using biodiesel and biodiesel-oxygenate blends in variable compression ratio and parameter-controlled compression ignition engines‚ including diethyl ether‚ dimethyl carbonate‚ higher alcohols including n-butanol and n-pentanol‚ other oxygenated ethers and cetane improvers in addition to the biodiesel blend․ Each study is characterized by the fuel scheme‚ the engine configuration‚ the controlled and response variables․ Quantitative data is reported only for those studies whose results were verifiable in the original publication․ In both of the studies‚ there was a correlation between increased compression ratio and reducing carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon emissions‚ and increasing NOx emissions․ Increased compression ratio and injection pressure improved brake thermal efficiency and reduced specific fuel consumption․ As a general trend‚ moderate quantities of diethyl ether decreased NOx and CO emissions while increasing total HC emissions․ A mixture of dimet

title: SulfoChar as a Novel Nano-Biochar Additive for B20 Biodiesel Blends: Enhancing Combustion and Reducing Exhaust Emissions
abstract: While biodiesel blends offer renewable alternatives to conventional diesel, mitigating their nitrogen oxide (NOx) penalties and optimizing combustion typically requires synthetic or metallic additives. This study introduces SulfoChar, a sulfonated walnut-shell nanobiochar functionalized with sulfonic acid (–SO3H) groups, as a novel, surfactant-free fuel-borne additive for B20 (20% biodiesel/80% diesel) blends. Synthesized via pyrolysis and subsequent functionalization, the nanobiochar was characterized using FTIR, SEM, and EDS, exhibiting excellent colloidal dispersion in the fuel matrix for over 30 days without chemical stabilizers. Engine evaluations were conducted at additive concentrations of 30, 60, and 90 mg/L under full-load conditions across 2900–3300 rpm. Experimental data revealed a distinct decoupling of optimal emission and performance dosages. The maximum concentration (90 mg/L) provided the highest environmental benefits, yielding peak reductions of 48.4% in carbon monoxide (CO) and 17.4% in NOx relative to the baseline B20. Conversely, mechanical output peaked at the lowest dosage (30 mg/L), which increased brake power by up to 19.3% at 2900 rpm. Surface map analysis indicated a balanced operational regime at 40–50 mg/L and 3000–3100 rpm. title: Comparative effects of B4C and h-BN nanoparticles on the performance and emissions of a diesel engine fueled with a rapeseed biodiesel blend
abstract: This study compared B 4 C and h-BN nanoparticles separately added at 25, 50, and 100 ppm to a 50:50 rapeseed methyl ester diesel blend (B50). A single cylinder, air cooled, direct injection diesel engine was tested at 2000 rpm under five brake loads (1–3 kW). Fuel thermal conductivity, BSFC, BTE, CO, CO 2 HC, and NO X emissions, smoke density, EGT, and noise level were evaluated. Relative to D100, B50 increased load averaged BSFC, NO X , and EGT by 13.65%, 12.52%, and 6.24%, respectively, while reducing BTE, CO, HC, smoke density, and noise level by 7.79%, 15.41%, 9.84%, 31.87%, and 0.657 dB(A), respectively. Among the nanoparticle enriched B50 fuels, B50BN50 yielded the lowest BSFC and highest BTE, reducing BSFC by 4.66% and increasing BTE by 4.22% relative to B50. B50BN50 exhibited the highest measured mean thermal conductivity, reaching 0.282 W m⁻ 1 K⁻ 1 at 35 °C, corresponding to a 43.15% increase relative to the nanoparticle free B50 blend. B50BN100 produced the largest CO and HC reductions, ranging across loads from 34.78% to 50.00% and from 24.56% to 39.24%, respectively, relative to B50, and lowered load averaged noise level by 1.621 dB. B50BC50 provided the greatest load averaged smoke density reduction (24.15%). However, nanoformulations increased load averaged NO X emissions by 4.28–16.18% relative to B50.

title: Speed-Resolved experimental and CFD evaluation of a Low-Power Intake-Air ionization retrofit for diesel combustion and emission control
abstract: A low-power intake-air ionization attachment was experimentally and numerically evaluated as a retrofit strategy for diesel-engine performance and emission control without fuel reformulation or engine modification. A single-cylinder compression-ignition engine was tested under baseline and staged ionized-air conditions at 300–1500 rpm, with five repeated measurements at each operating point. Each negative-ion module operated at a fixed 12 V DC input (<1 W per module) with device-rated values of approximately −9.5 kV DC high-voltage output, 1.2 x 10 13 ions s −1 negative-ion production, and 1.9 x 10 12 ions cm −3 at a 2.9-cm reference distance. The staged strategy activated one to five modules as speed increased. At the fully load-matched 1500-rpm condition, brake power and torque remained 1.94072 kW and 12.35 N m in both modes, while fuel mass-flow rate decreased from 2.34 x 10 -4 to 2.25 x 10 -4 kg s −1 . Using an LHV of 42.5 MJ kg −1 , BSFC decreased from 0.4341 to 0.4174 kg kW -1 h −1 and brake thermal efficiency increased from 19.51 % to 20.30 %. Across the speed range, mean exhaust-gas temperature decreased by 6.8–19.8 °C and CO, HC, and NO x analyzer concentrations were lower under the staged ionization-ON condition. Crank-angle-resolved in-cylinder pressure and ion-current signals were measured, and apparent net and cumulative heat release were derived from the pressure trace. title: Water-in-diesel emulsion fuels: A comprehensive review of formulation, combustion performance, emission characteristics, and technological advances
journal: Energy Sources Part A Recovery Utilization and Environmental Effects
abstract: The need for cleaner and more efficient combustion in compression ignition engines has driven the search for alternative fuels; in this respect, water-in-diesel (W/D) emulsions have been identified as a promising, ready-to-use option. This review presents the influence of W/D emulsion fuel technology on engine efficiency and emissions, along with recent developments aimed at overcoming its limitations, drawing conclusions from over 120 research studies conducted over the last three decades. The underlying principle of W/D emulsions is the micro-explosion effect, in which dispersed water droplets undergo explosive vaporization, enhancing fuel atomization and air–fuel mixing, thereby improving combustion. There is a consistent and considerable decrease in two major emissions: nitrogen oxides (NOx reduction by 15–50%), primarily due to heat absorption by water vapor, which lowers peak flame temperatures, and particulate matter (PM reduction by 20–60%), resulting from enhanced combustion efficiency. However, a trade-off exists in the form of a slight increase in brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC), which is 5–20% higher on a mass basis (and comparable on an energy basis) and, under low-load operating conditions, potentially elevated emissions of carbon monoxide (CO by 10–45%) and unburnt hydrocarbons (HC by 8–52%). title: Optimization of TiO₂-based Water–Diesel Emulsified Fuel for Engine Performance and Emission Characteristics using Soft Computing Approaches
publisher: Science and Engineering Research Support Society
abstract: Water–diesel emulsified fuels (WDEF) have emerged as practical drop‑in solutions for compression‑ignition engines, owing to micro‑explosion–assisted atomization and charge cooling that collectively suppress NOx and smoke without drastic hardware changes. Here, titanium dioxide (TiO₂) nanoparticles are dispersed into a stable WDEF to catalyze oxidation and buffer oxygen, improving combustion quality. A Taguchi L9 design is used to study load, injection pressure, and injection timing; responses include brake thermal efficiency (BTE), NOx, and smoke. An Adaptive Neuro‑Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) is trained for response prediction, and Multi‑Objective Particle Swarm Optimization (MOPSO) delivers Pareto‑optimal operating points balancing efficiency and emissions. Across tests, TiO₂‑WDEF raises BTE (≈10–12%) and lowers NOx (≈15–25%) and smoke (≈20–30%) versus neat diesel. The ANFIS model attains high predictive fidelity (R² ≳ 0.95) and residuals close to normality, while MOPSO exposes clear trade‑offs among objectives and recommends settings that meet practical constraints. The workflow demonstrates a reproducible pathway for data‑driven optimization of nano‑emulsified alternative fuels.

title: Hong Kong Traffic Emissions and Volumes, 2003–2023: Road-Link NOx and PM2.5 Data with Hourly Profiles
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset provides Hong Kong traffic emission data and traffic volumes for the whole road network from 2003 to 2023. It contains reconstructed road-segment-level nitrogen oxide (NOx) and fine particulate matter (PM2.5) emissions, together with hourly traffic volumes for eight vehicle classes. For each year, the data describe an annual-average 24-hour traffic and emission profile across the modelled road network in Hong Kong. The reconstruction combines historical traffic counts, hourly traffic profiles, camera-derived vehicle-class proportions, and traffic-speed observations. Machine-learning models estimate missing traffic components on unmonitored road links. Hourly traffic volumes for each vehicle class are combined with speed-dependent EMFAC-HK emission factors to calculate emissions. District- and year-specific calibration factors are applied to traffic volumes and emissions to address spatial and temporal prediction biases. The dataset covers motorcycles, private cars, taxis, light goods vehicles, heavy goods vehicles, light-duty buses, heavy-duty buses, and franchised double-decker buses. Data are distributed as 21 annual CSV files, each compressed in a separate ZIP archive. Each file contains road identifiers, road-link geometries, and hourly traffic volumes and emissions by vehicle class. Traffic volumes are expressed as vehicle counts within each hourly interval. title: Node-aware spatiotemporal carbon tracing and carbon-responsive control of electrified railways for emission reduction and tertiary reserves
abstract: The decarbonization of electrified transportation reshapes the interaction between power systems and mobile energy loads. As a key component of this sector, electrified railways draw large, geographically distributed traction loads whose emissions are governed by the power system’s spatiotemporally varying carbon intensity (CI). However, existing carbon tracing methods typically use spatially uniform emission factors, obscuring nodal carbon intensity (CI) differences. Consequently, long-distance trains cannot perceive or exploit spatial carbon heterogeneity when allocating traction power along their routes. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a unified framework that transforms heterogeneous railway fleets into active, carbon-responsive resources within the power system. First, a node-aware spatiotemporal carbon tracing method integrates Power Transfer Distribution Factors (PTDF) with dynamic train-node mapping, enabling real-time quantification of the nodal carbon intensity (NCI) experienced by mobile loads. Building upon this, a two-stage hierarchical coordinated control strategy is formulated, embedding dynamic NCI signals into an online receding-horizon predictive controller to achieve joint carbon minimization and tertiary reserve. The controller autonomously executes spatiotemporal load shifting by dynamically regulating traction and braking power to avoid high-carbon zones while maintaining schedule adherence. title: Combustion phasing and emissions trade-offs of hydrogen-enriched methane in a spark-ignition engine: Fixed spark timing versus MBT-optimized ignition
abstract: This study experimentally investigated how hydrogen enrichment and spark timing jointly govern combustion, performance, and emissions in a spark-ignition engine fueled by different methane–hydrogen blends under fixed boundary conditions (11:1 compression ratio, 1500 rpm, 25% load). Methane was blended with hydrogen at different hydrogen fractions (HF) ranging from 20% to 80% by volume, and two ignition strategies were compared: (a) fixed spark timing of 30 °CA before top dead center (BTDC) for all fuel blends and (b) blend-specific optimized ignition timing (OPT-IG), selected by progressively retarding the spark until the crank angle at 50% mass fraction burned (CA50) fell within the adopted 5–10 °CA after top dead center (ATDC) near the maximum brake torque (MBT) window. The cycle-resolved in-cylinder pressure was measured and used to compute the heat-release rate (HRR) and mass fraction burned (MFB) profiles, from which the combustion phasing metrics CA10, CA50, and CA90 were extracted. Under a fixed 30 °CA BTDC timing, increasing HF accelerated flame development and shortened the main burn, advancing CA50 and shifting the peak pressure and heat release toward top dead center (TDC), which reduced brake efficiency and elevated NOx emissions. Additionally, volumetric efficiency decreased from 72% at HF20 to 65% at HF80, indicating a distinct charge-displacement penalty at high hydrogen content. title: Multiobjective Optimization of Performance and Emission Profiles in a WCO–Butanol‐Fueled RCCI Engine: An RSM‐Based Investigation of EGR and Injection Duration Interactions
abstract: ABSTRACT This investigation develops a multiobjective optimization framework for Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines utilizing a butanol, waste cooking oils–biodiesel, and diesel ternary blend. Moving beyond traditional parametric sweeps, the study employs Response Surface Methodology in conjunction with a Face‐Centered Central Composite Design to systematically decode the coupled influences of Injection Duration (ID), exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) rates, and engine load on combustion dynamics. Statistical validation via analysis of variance ensures high predictive fidelity, offering a robust mapping of the dual‐fuel reactivity landscape. Experimental results initially identified a peak brake thermal efficiency (BTE) of 32.0% at high‐load conditions (16 kg); however, this point exhibited significant NO x penalties. To reconcile the performance‐emission trade‐off, a multiobjective optimization was executed using desirability functions. The global optimum was identified at 5.68°CA ID, 13.58% EGR, and 6.66 kg load, yielding a predicted BTE of 23.73% and NO x emissions of 809.2 ppm. At this Pareto‐optimal point, NO x was reduced by 35% compared with baseline diesel through thermal dilution and reactivity stratification. The model was validated through confirmatory experiments, with a maximum error of 1.89%, confirming that the RCCI strategy offers superior environmental‐performance trade‐offs at midload conditions for sustainable, low‐carbon propulsion.

title: Ultra-high compression ratio as a key enabler for pure ammonia spark-ignition engines: Flame propagation and emission formation
abstract: The pure ammonia spark-ignition (SI) strategy has emerged as a promising solution for ammonia-fueled engines owing to its simplified system architecture and reduced control complexity. This study investigates flame propagation and pollutant formation of pure ammonia SI mode in a modern multi-cylinder heavy-duty engine equipped with an ultra-high compression ratio (CR) of 24:1 through combined experiments, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and chemical kinetic simulations. Stable pure ammonia combustion is experimentally achieved over a broad load range at a constant engine speed of 1500 rpm. A pronounced two-stage heat-release behavior is observed, indicating that the late combustion process is increasingly influenced by enhanced chemical reactivity under ultra-high-CR conditions. The first-stage heat release is dominated by turbulent flame propagation, whereas the second-stage heat release is associated with accelerated oxidation of the residual NH 3 /air mixture, with a possible contribution from localized autoignition. Owing to ammonia’s intrinsically low reactivity, early flame kernel development exhibits strong sensitivity to local charge motion. Increasing engine load shortens the combustion duration, enabling the brake thermal efficiency (BTE) to exceed 43%. Although NH 3 slip decreases with increasing load, it remains relatively high (∼8000 ppm), mainly due to incomplete oxidation and near-wall quenching. title: Impact of the fuel injection phase on the combustion and emission performance of a heavy-duty diesel micro-pilot ignition high pressure direct injection natural gas engine
abstract: Greenhouse-gas and pollutant regulations are driving heavy-duty truck engines toward higher efficiency and lower emissions. Diesel micro-pilot ignition high-pressure direct injection (HPDI) natural gas engines offer high thermal-efficiency potential, but the effects of wider diesel-natural gas injection timing combinations, especially larger injection overlap, remain insufficiently clarified. This study experimentally investigates a heavy-duty six-cylinder diesel micro-pilot HPDI natural gas engine at its economic operating point (1300 r/min, 1400 N·m). Based on a well-established dual direct-injection platform, four natural gas start-of-injection (NSOI) timings and nine diesel start-of-injection (DSOI) timings for each NSOI were tested to evaluate the effects of NSOI, DSOI and the diesel-natural gas injection interval (DNI) on combustion, performance and emissions. The results show that advancing NSOI or retarding DSOI increases the premixed natural gas fraction, strengthens combustion and improves brake thermal efficiency (BTE). The maximum BTE of 46.5% was obtained at NSOI = 18.8°CA BTDC and DSOI = 12.7°CA BTDC, corresponding to DNI = 6.1°CA and 1.7% higher than the base injection mode. Compared with the base injection mode, the compound injection mode shortened the main combustion period by up to 19°CA. title: Performance, Emission, Energy, and Exergy Assessment of Gasoline–1-Decanol, Gasoline–DIPE, and JP-8 Fuels Toward Sustainable Two-Stroke UAV Propulsion
abstract: This study experimentally investigates the performance, emission, energy, and exergy characteristics of six fuels in a two-cylinder, air-cooled, two-stroke unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) engine, using neat gasoline (G100) as the reference fuel. The test matrix comprised G100, neat JP-8, gasoline–1-decanol blends containing 10 and 20 vol.% decanol (G90D10 and G80D20), and gasoline–diisopropyl ether blends containing 10 and 20 vol.% DIPE (G90E10 and G80E20). Experiments were conducted at shaft speeds of 3250, 3750, 4500, 5250, and 6250 rpm under matched speed–load conditions. Fuel consumption, exhaust-gas temperature, excess-air ratio, gaseous emissions, and first- and second-law thermodynamic performance were evaluated. The inclusion of G100 enabled the effects of the oxygenated additives to be quantified directly. At 5250 rpm, G90E10 reduced BSFC by 0.73% relative to G100 while increasing energy and exergy efficiencies by 1.69% and 1.61%, respectively. G80E20 produced larger reductions in brake-specific CO and HC emissions, 6.63% and 14.58%, respectively, and increased energy and exergy efficiencies by 2.43% and 2.27%, respectively, although both DIPE blends increased NOx. In contrast, increasing the decanol fraction increased BSFC and reduced thermodynamic efficiency relative to G100 despite moderate reductions in CO. title: Multi-objective optimization of combustion, performance, and emission characteristics of diesel–MTBE–SiO2 fuel blends in a single-cylinder diesel engine using response surface methodology
abstract: The growing need for cleaner and more efficient diesel engine operation has increased interest in oxygenated fuel additives and nanoparticle-based fuel strategies. This study experimentally investigated the effects of methyl tert -butyl ether (MTBE) and silicon dioxide (SiO 2 ) addition on the combustion, performance, and emission characteristics of a single-cylinder compression-ignition diesel engine using response surface methodology (RSM). The experiments were conducted at 1800 rpm, considering engine load (8.24–24.72 Nm), MTBE ratio (5–15 vol%), and SiO 2 concentration (50–150 ppm) as input variables. A face-centered central composite design (CCD) comprising 18 experimental runs was employed, and second-order regression models were developed for the investigated responses. Model adequacy was assessed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and related statistical criteria. The results showed that engine load was the dominant factor influencing the investigated responses, particularly the performance and emission characteristics. Increasing engine load increased indicated mean effective pressure (IMEP) and indicated thermal efficiency (ITE) while decreasing brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC), but resulted in higher nitrogen oxides (NO x ) emissions. Moderate MTBE concentrations of approximately 9–11 vol% and SiO 2 concentrations of approximately 90–110 ppm were associated with favorable performance responses. title: Surrogate-Assisted Multi-Objective Optimization of Engine-Level Pneumatic Assistance for Arctic Diesel Generators
abstract: Diesel generators remain indispensable for supplying reliable electricity in isolated Arctic microgrids, where harsh environmental conditions, high fuel transportation costs, and stringent emission requirements motivate improvements in engine performance and environmental sustainability. This study proposes and validates a unified, surrogate-assisted tri-objective optimization framework to calibrate the engine operation of a pneumatically assisted CAT 3516 diesel generator under representative Arctic conditions at Raglan Mine, Canada. The optimization focuses on engine-level pneumatic assistance, while compressed air generation, storage, and distribution are outside the scope of the study. The framework integrates high-fidelity Diesel-RK simulations, adaptive Sobol sampling, Gaussian Process surrogate modeling with predictive uncertainty, global sensitivity analysis, deterministic multi-objective optimization, SIMUS-based Pareto ranking, and independent high-fidelity validation. We optimized three engine-control variables (start of injection, compressor pressure ratio, and fuel mass per cycle) simultaneously to maximize brake power while minimizing brake-specific fuel consumption and NOx emissions. The surrogate models achieved coefficients of determination exceeding 0.97 for brake power, brake-specific fuel consumption, and peak cylinder pressure, while the NOx surrogate reached an R2 of 0.82. title: Exploring dual-fuel operation in direct injection diesel engines: an experimental study with blends of acacia biodiesel and hydrogen
abstract: Rising interest in low-carbon compression-ignition fuel strategies has motivated the co-induction of hydrogen with biodiesel blends. This study experimentally investigates a single-cylinder, four-stroke, direct-injection diesel engine fueled with Acacia biodiesel–diesel blend (ABD20) and hydrogen induction at 5 and 10 L/min. The corresponding hydrogen energy shares are 8.3% and 15.4%, designated as ABD5H2 and ABD10H2, respectively. The test fuels were compared with neat diesel and ABD20 over the investigated brake mean effective pressure range. Hydrogen induction reduced hydrocarbon, carbon monoxide, and smoke emissions relative to ABD20. At higher loads, ABD10H2 reduced smoke opacity by up to 20.45%, decreased brake-specific fuel consumption by up to 30%, and increased brake thermal efficiency by up to 1.0% relative to ABD20. Peak heat release rate and peak in-cylinder pressure increased by 3.46% and 4.76%, respectively. Hydrogen addition also increased NOx emissions, primarily because of the higher combustion temperature and faster heat release. Overall, ABD10H2 provided improved fuel economy and reduced smoke emissions compared with ABD20, demonstrating the potential of hydrogen enrichment for low-carbon diesel-engine operation.

title: Optimal driving assignment strategies for plug-in hybrid electric heavy duty trucks
abstract: The transportation sector faces critical challenges in reducing CO 2 emissions, particularly from heavy-duty trucks (HDTs), which account for 25% of transportation-related emissions. Plug-in hybrid electric (PHE) HDTs offer a sustainable solution for long-distance freight, yet optimizing their battery management under variable route conditions such as topography, load, and speed constraints remains a complex problem. This study addresses this challenge through an integrated route-aware optimization framework for PHE HDTs. The framework combines route and elevation data, a power-constrained speed–acceleration estimator, regenerative braking, charging opportunities, and a Cellular Genetic Algorithm for Multiobjective Optimization (MOCell) to determine the driving-mode assignment between the electric motor and the internal combustion engine. A deterministic constructive heuristic, GreenRoute, is also included as a baseline for assessing the benefits of multi-objective optimization. Validation across three long-haul routes (Cádiz-Madrid, Madrid-Donostia, Paris-Berlin) demonstrates significant improvements: MOCell achieves up to 9% greater electric range and 17.5% lower emissions compared to the heuristic GreenRoute. For instance, on the Cádiz-Madrid route, MOCell reduces emissions by 5.7% and increases electric range by 4.6% when en-route charging is not considered, with further gains (6.6% and 4.1%, respectively) when charging is included. title: The Application of Waste Coal Fly Ash as a Support for a Heterogeneous Catalyst for Biodiesel Production and a Comparison with the Engine Characteristics Using a Homogeneous Catalyst
abstract: Abstract Coal fly ash is a waste product of coal-fired boiler combustion. The fly ash consists of fine glass microspheres with a relatively large surface area. This study aims to synthesize catalysts using waste coal fly ash as a support and calcine them with alkaline catalysts. Fly ash with a large surface area was synthesized using sodium methoxide to prepare a heterogeneous catalyst, which was then used to transesterify palm oil to produce biodiesel. Subsequently, engine performance and exhaust emissions from biodiesel combustion were evaluated. The experimental results indicate that biodiesel prepared with the heterogeneous catalyst exhibited lower fuel consumption and brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC) than biodiesel prepared with the homogeneous catalyst, and it had a higher brake thermal efficiency. The emission concentrations of CO, CO2, and NOX are higher in biodiesel produced with homogeneous catalysts, whereas the O2 emission concentration from biodiesel prepared with a heterogeneous catalyst is lower than that of homogeneous biodiesel. Moreover, the biodiesel produced using a heterogeneous catalyst consisting of coal fly ash containing sodium methoxide appeared to have a lower excess air ratio and heating value, while exhibiting a higher exhaust gas temperature and fuel/air equivalence ratio. Using waste coal fly ash to synthesize a heterogeneous catalyst improves biodiesel properties, thereby advancing the circular economy.

title: Enhancement of compression ignition engine characteristics of waste transformer oil-derived biodiesel via an Ag 3 PO 4 /Ag/TiO 2 –carbon nanocomposite and performance prediction using an artificial neural network approach
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part E Journal of Process Mechanical Engineering
abstract: The objective of this study is to enhance the compression ignition engine characteristics with a waste transformer oil biodiesel dosing Ag 3 PO 4 /Ag/TiO 2 –carbon nanocomposite as a fuel additive with 80% diesel, 20% waste transformer oil, and nanocomposites of 500, 1000, and 1500 ppm. This analysis revealed that up to 1000 ppm of the nanocomposite, the synergic effect improved the brake thermal efficiency, peak cylinder pressure, and peak heat release rate by 11.5%, 3.6%, and 4.5% than diesel at 100% load. It also reduced the brake-specific fuel consumption, carbon monoxide, unburned hydrocarbon, and smoke emissions by 9.5%, 18%, 18.3%, and 20% respectively, alongside increased nitrogen oxide emission by 26.6%. Further increasing the concentration of the nanocomposite leads to a decline in the characteristics of the engine. To determine the optimal blend, the numerical optimization has been done using the approach of artificial neural networks (ANNs). Furthermore, the ANN model exhibited high prediction accuracy with a correlation coefficient ( R ) close to unity (0.99–1.00), showing strong agreement between the experimental and predicted results, and effectively identified the optimal nanocomposite concentration of 1000 ppm. Additionally, the integration of experimental analysis with ANN-based optimization to identified 1000 ppm as the best-performing nanocomposite concentration among the investigated cases.

title: Experimental Analysis of Jatropha Oil in An Automobile Stumpy Limited Temperature (ASLT) Engine
journal: International Journal of Advances in Engineering and Management
abstract: This study experimentally investigated the performance of an automobile stumpy limited temperature (ASLT) automobile diesel engine fitted with a ceramic-coated cylinder head, in which a coating of 600-micron thickness was applied to the inner portion of the cylinder head, fuelled with Barbados/Jatropha oil at normal and preheated temperatures under varied injection pressures and injection timings. The experimental performance analysis evaluated brake thermal efficiency, exhaust gas temperature, and volumetric efficiency at various values of brake mean effective pressure (BMEP), while exhaust emissions of smoke and oxides of nitrogen (NOx) were recorded at the same BMEP values. Combustion characteristics at the peak-load operation of the engine were acquired using a TDC encoder, a pressure transducer, a console, and a dedicated pressure–crank-angle software package. Throughout the performance analysis, the conventional engine (CE) exhibited deteriorated performance, whereas the SLT engine exhibited improved performance with the biofuel at the manufacturer’s recommended injection timing of 27° bTDC and an injection pressure of 190 bar. Relative to the CE operating on pure diesel, the performance of both engine versions improved with advanced injection timing and at higher injection pressure. The optimum injection timing was 32° bTDC for the CE and 29° bTDC for the SLT engine under CJO operation, and the peak brake thermal efficiency increased by 7% in comparison with pure diese

title: Integrated energy–exergy modeling and fleet-level decarbonization potential of dual-fuel LPG/diesel engines validated using AVL-BOOST
abstract: Retrofitting conventional diesel engines for LPG/diesel dual-fuel operation offers a near-term decarbonization option for fleets that cannot yet transition to full electrification. This study develops an integrated engine-to-fleet framework that combines AVL-BOOST-based combustion modeling, experimental validation, energy–exergy analysis, emission trade-off assessment, and fleet-level CO₂ mitigation. The model was calibrated and validated on two representative platforms, a common-rail AVL 5402 engine and a mechanically injected D1146TI engine, using brake torque, specific energy consumption (SEC), in-cylinder pressure, combustion phasing, and gaseous and smoke emissions. The predicted torque and SEC showed high agreement with experiments, with MAPE below 5%, R² values of 0.992 and 0.948, respectively, and peak-pressure deviations below 3%. At LPG substitution ratios of 20–30%, brake power was maintained, SEC remained near the diesel baseline, exergy efficiency increased by 1.5–2.8%, and smoke decreased markedly, although NOx, CO, and HC remained sensitive to combustion phasing and low-load mixture oxidation. Fleet-scale analysis indicates that 30% retrofit penetration at an average 25% LPG substitution ratio can reduce TTW CO₂-equivalent emissions by approximately 6–9%; the corresponding WTW benefit remains dependent on the upstream LPG supply pathway. The framework provides a physics-informed basis for evaluating LPG/diesel retrofit as a transitional decarbonization pathway.

title: Experimental and statistical investigation of MgO ‐assisted microalgae biodiesel–hydrogen dual‐fuel combustion in an RCCI engine
abstract: Abstract In Reactivity‐Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) operation, hydrogen was inducted through the intake manifold as a low‐reactivity fuel (LRF), whereas microalgae biodiesel‐diesel blends enriched with magnesium oxide (MgO) nanoparticles were directly injected into the combustion chamber as high‐reactivity fuel (HRF). This study explored a unique tri‐fuel combination consisting of microalgae biodiesel, magnesium oxide nanoparticles (25 and 50 ppm), and hydrogen (5 and 10 L/min). The experimental investigation was conducted at varying loads with different blends to evaluate engine performance, combustion characteristics, and emission characteristics. The results showed that the blend B20D80 + 50 ppm MgO + 10 lpm H 2 achieved the highest brake thermal efficiency, increasing from 29.5% to 33.8%, represented as 14.58% increase, along with a decrease in brake‐specific energy consumption from 6373 kJ/kWh to 6027 kJ/kWh, corresponding to a 5.43% reduction compared with diesel. The improved combustion performance can be attributed to the enhanced oxidation of biodiesel, the catalytic activity of MgO, and the high flame speed of hydrogen, leading to notable reductions in hydrocarbons (HC), carbon monoxide (CO), carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), and soot emissions. However, NO x emissions increased due to the higher in‐cylinder temperatures. Combustion analysis further indicated increased in‐cylinder peak pressure and heat release rate, from 65 to 75 bar and 63 to 74 J/°CA, respectivel

title: Effect of Milk Scum biodiesel addition and hydrogen energy share on the performance of reactivity‐controlled compression ignition engine
abstract: Abstract Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines are a promising way to decarbonize the internal combustion engine industry. Despite this extensive literature covering dual‐fuel setups, a critical knowledge gap persists regarding the steady‐state combustion behavior of highly specific, waste‐derived oxygenated lipids when paired directly with carbon‐free LRFs. To address this gap, the current study focuses on the waste‐to‐wealth principle of utilizing Milk Scum biodiesel and mineral diesel (as a High‐Reactivity Fuel) and hydrogen (as an LRF) to achieve the minimum carbon‐based emissions. Experimentally, performance and emissions were measured using a constant‐rpm diesel engine with a compression ratio of 18, fuel injection pressure of 500 bar, fuel injection time of 23 bTDC, and common‐rail direct‐injected (B10, B15, and B20) and port‐injected hydrogen (0.077 and 0.121 kg/h) at 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% engine loads. The measurements indicate that the RCCI optimality (0.121 kg/h H 2 , B10 blend) achieved a maximum Brake Thermal Efficiency of 31.2% and 10–15% lower Brake Specific Fuel Consumption under high‐load conditions. Moreover, this hydrogen‐enriched RCCI mode achieved average reductions in CO, HC, NOx, and smoke emissions of 24%, 27%, 35%, and 40%, respectively. Interestingly, while the overall experimental matrix yielded an average NOx reduction of 35%, the optimum RCCI B10 configuration at 100% load inhibited peak NOx formation by more than 60% compared

title: Research review on vehicle energy recovery technology for energy savings
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part C Journal of Mechanical Engineering Science
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of the research progress in vehicle energy recovery technologies. It synthesizes regenerative braking systems, with an in-depth exploration of their control strategies and efficiency optimization schemes, alongside regenerative suspension systems—covering both hydraulic and electromagnetic pathways—and waste heat recovery systems. Furthermore, the study analyzes passive aerodynamic energy recovery in vehicle platoons, focusing on the variations in aerodynamic drag and their positive impact on energy recovery. Aerodynamic drag reduction during platooning is specifically defined as “passive energy recovery.” By efficiently recovering braking kinetic energy, suspension vibrational mechanical energy, and vehicle waste heat, while leveraging aerodynamic optimization, various forms of energy dissipated during conventional vehicle operation can be converted into usable electrical power. This integration significantly enhances overall energy efficiency, extends driving range, and reduces carbon emissions. Finally, the paper provides an outlook on future research directions, emphasizing that the collaborative optimization and intelligent control of multi-source energy recovery systems are pivotal to advancing the sustainability of green transportation.

title: Thermally constrained hydrogen utilization in compression-ignition engines via reduced-order digital-twin Pareto calibration
abstract: Hydrogen enrichment can improve compression-ignition (CI) engine fuel-conversion performance, but its practical use is constrained by pressure-rise, peak-pressure, emissions, and component-temperature limits. This study develops a thermally constrained reduced-order digital-twin framework for identifying safe-beneficial hydrogen utilization in a mildly boosted direct-injection CI engine. A crank-angle thermo-combustion model with hydrogen-dependent burn phasing and duration modifiers is coupled to a transient six-node thermal network. Four calibration variables—injection-timing shift, air–fuel ratio (AFR), hydrogen blend fraction, and base load—are sampled at 1600, 2000, and 2400 rpm to train speed-specific surrogates for brake thermal efficiency, brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), nitrogen oxides (NO x ) proxy, peak pressure, peak wall temperature, and peak pressure-rise rate. Feasibility is imposed using limits of 10.8 MPa, 4.9 bar/deg, and 660 K for peak pressure, pressure-rise rate, and peak wall temperature, respectively. Principal thermo-performance surrogates achieved R 2 = 0.992–0.998, while pressure-rise-rate and gated NO x models achieved R 2 = 0.972–0.975 and 0.945–0.976, respectively. Hydrogen enrichment increased brake thermal efficiency and reduced BSFC, but intensified NO x tendency, pressure-rise, and wall-temperature loading, especially under richer/high-load operation. The safe-beneficial envelope expanded under leaner operation and compressed rapidly a

title: From black waste to liquid fuel: Advances in tire pyrolysis oil for diesel engines
abstract: Waste tires, a source of “black pollution,” pose a significant environmental threat due to their non-biodegradability and massive landfilling nature. Pyrolysis has emerged as a sustainable pathway for turning these tires into valuable products, particularly tire pyrolysis oil (TPO). This review summarizes the current advancements in TPO production and purification methods, reactor technologies, physicochemical characterization, co-pyrolysis with biomass, and its implementation in diesel engines, accompanied by its detailed combustion, performance, and emission attributes. Combustion studies indicate that TPO blends exhibit a prolonged ignition delay (5–8 °CA) along with higher heat release rates (70–80 J/°CA) and increased peak cylinder pressures (58.2–74 bar) compared to conventional diesel, potentially leading to knocking at higher blend ratios, which can be mitigated through optimized compression ratio, injection timing, or the use of suitable additives. Performance analysis reveals that although TPO generally exhibits lower efficiency than diesel, blending it with biodiesel and diethyl ether significantly enhances engine performance, with diethyl ether reducing brake specific fuel consumption and biodiesel improving brake thermal efficiency to levels comparable with conventional diesel. Emissions remain a major challenge for the practical utilization of TPO, as low blend ratios (≈ 5–20% TPO) generally exhibit CO, HC, and smoke emissions comparable to diesel fuel, whereas

title: Develop optimal ignition timing models as multivariable functions for diesel-LPG blends combustion in a diesel engine
abstract: Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) is increasingly utilized as a partial substitute for conventional diesel to improve combustion efficiency and diminish harmful emissions. This study focuses on improving the efficiency of diesel-LPG blends in a stationary single-cylinder diesel engine by investigating and establishing their optimal ignition timing functions under various variables such as engine load, combustion duration, and LPG proportion in the fuel blend. The AVL BOOST software was applied to simulate the brake-specific fuel consumption of diesel-LPG blends with LPG energy substitution ratios of 0%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40% at combustion durations of 80, 100, and 120 crank angle degrees (°CA) and under two engine load conditions of 60% and 90%. The simulation results were validated by experimental studies on pure diesel combustion in the engine. Results indicate that increasing the LPG substitution ratio retards the optimal ignition timing for minimizing the fuel consumption, whereas increasing the combustion duration advances it. Quantitatively, each 10% LPG substitution results in a reduction of approximately 3 °CA in optimal ignition timing, while for every 20 °CA increase in combustion duration, the ideal ignition timing advances by 3–5 °CA. These two variables exhibit independent linear relationships with the ideal ignition timing, with the impact of the LPG substitution ratio slightly dominating that of combustion duration. The predictive models are determined to be essen

title: Experimental and machine-learning based investigation of second generation juliflora biodiesel blended with dimethyl carbonate and CoCr 2 O 4 nanoparticles in a compression ignition engine
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part C Journal of Mechanical Engineering Science
abstract: Improving the efficiency and emission characteristics of biodiesel fueled CI engine remains challenging due to limitations in fuel reactivity and combustion behavior. This study investigates the combined effect of dimethyl carbonate (DMC) and cobalt chromite nanoparticles on engine performance and emissions, supported by machine learning-based prediction. Experiments were carried out on a single-cylinder diesel engine using five fuel blends including diesel, J20, J20D10, J20D10C50, and J20D10C100 across the full load range. The J20D10C100 blend delivered the highest BTE of 29.67%, showing improvements of 13.57% over diesel and 20.78% over the J20 blend. Brake specific fuel consumption decreased to 0.375 kg per kWh, corresponding to reductions of 5.44% and 6.38% compared with diesel and the J20 blend. At full load, CO decreased from 0.53% to 0.454%, HC reduced by 14.6%, and nitrogen oxides decreased from 1070 ppm to 990 ppm. Smoke opacity showed a reduction from 67.21% to 65.19%. Among the predictive models, gradient boosting achieved the highest accuracy with an R 2 of 0.965, followed closely by random forest with 0.964. The results confirm that the proposed fuel formulation enhances engine performance while reducing emissions, which supports reliable predictive modeling.

title: Machine Learning-Assisted optimization of acetylene Dual-Fuel combustion using Copper oxide (CuO) Nano-Enhanced waste Plastic Oil in Compression Ignition (CI) Engine
abstract: In this study, an experimental and machine learning-assisted investigation was conducted on a modified single-cylinder direct-injection Compression Ignition (CI) engine operating in acetylene dual-fuel mode using copper oxide (CuO) nanoparticle-enhanced waste plastic oil (WPO) blends. The proposed approach integrates waste-to-energy fuel utilization, catalytic nano-additives, high-reactivity gaseous combustion, and data-driven predictive modelling within a unified sustainable combustion framework. Experimental investigations were performed using WPO10 and WPO20 blends containing 50 and 100 ppm CuO nanoparticles under acetylene flow rates of 5 and 10 LPM. Among all tested fuel combinations, A5WPO10Cu100 exhibited the best overall performance, achieving a maximum brake thermal efficiency of 33.12 %, corresponding to an 8.27 % improvement over diesel, together with a 21.03 % reduction in brake specific energy consumption. The optimum fuel also reduced HC, CO, and smoke opacity by 41.46 %, 47.62 %, and 43.58 %, respectively, while A10WPO10Cu100 produced the highest combustion intensity with a peak heat release rate of 68.9 J/°CA, maximum cylinder pressure of 90.5 bar, and minimum ignition delay of 8.75 °CA, indicating enhanced premixed combustion and catalytic oxidation. Although NOx emissions increased under higher acetylene induction due to elevated combustion temperatures, the overall combustion efficiency and emission trade-off were significantly improved. To further establis

title: Research on the Green Development of Port Mechanical and Electrical Equipment under the "Dual Carbon" Strategy
abstract: After the goals of carbon peaking and carbon neutrality were put forward, the pressure of emission reduction in the shipping industry has been accelerated to transmit to ports, and the green and low-carbon transformation of mechanical and electrical equipment has thus become an important starting point for the implementation of emission reduction. This paper reviews the carbon reduction practices of typical ports at home and abroad, and examines the application effects and bottlenecks of core technologies from four directions: new energy power machinery, braking energy recovery, multi-energy complementary systems, and ship shore power. Analysis shows that port decarbonization is entering a new stage of multi-technology collaborative integration, and the supply side, the energy use side, and the management side need to exert force simultaneously; the policy dividends, market traction, and technology iteration during the transformation window period bring both opportunities and challenges. Based on this, the paper puts forward suggestions on connecting with policy tools, tackling core technologies, unifying standards and norms, and implementing whole-life-cycle digital management of equipment, for reference in the green upgrading of ports.

title: IMPACT OF CHANGES IN THE TECHNICAL-OPERATIONAL PERFORMANCE OF HYBRID VEHICLES AS A PARTIALLY DECARBONIZED TECHNOLOGY ON END-OF-LIFE TREATMENT WITH REGARD TO ENVIRONMENTAL REQUIREMENTS
journal: Scientific Journal of Silesian University of Technology Series Transport
abstract: This article examines how changes in the technical and operational characteristics of hybrid vehicles, as an intermediate step in transport decarbonization, affect end-of-life treatment from an environmental standpoint. Life-cycle assessment and multifactor regression modeling are applied to evaluate the influence of traction battery capacity, battery chemistry, regenerative braking intensity and powertrain type on the integral end-of-life impact coefficient. The results show that BEVs carry an end-of-life burden approximately 3.5 times lower than PHEVs, while increasing battery capacity, though reducing in-use CO₂ emissions by up to 50%, proportionally raises recycling complexity and chemical load on processing facilities. The findings substantiate the need for standardized battery designs, regulatory end-of-life risk indicators, and integrated state-of-health monitoring to ensure safe and efficient processing of electrified vehicles.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT AND OPERATING WINDOW IDENTIFICATION FOR HYDROGEN-ASSISTED LEAN COMBUSTION CONTROL
abstract: Hydrogen-assisted lean combustion represents a promising approach for improving the environmental performance of spark-ignition engines while maintaining high energy efficiency. This study presents an environmental assessment and operating window identification of a gasoline direct injection engine equipped with hydrogen port fuel injection under lean and ultra-lean operating conditions. Hydrogen energy shares ranging from 0% to 40% were investigated with respect to brake thermal efficiency, combustion stability expressed by the coefficient of variation of indicated mean effective pressure (COV IMEP), and gaseous emissions including carbon monoxide (CO), unburned hydrocarbons (HC), and nitrogen oxides (NOₓ). The results show that hydrogen enrichment improves thermal efficiency, significantly reduces CO and HC emissions, and extends the stable lean-burn operating range beyond λ = 2.0. Furthermore, ultra-lean operation contributed to the suppression of NOₓ formation while maintaining stable combustion. An integrated environmental evaluation identified a favourable operating window corresponding to hydrogen energy shares of approximately 30–40%, where the best balance between efficiency, emission reduction, and combustion stability was achieved. The identified operating conditions provide a valuable basis for the future development of advanced combustion control and fuel injection management strategies aimed at minimizing environmental impacts.

title: Effect of High-Energy Ignition and Spark Plug on Combustion and Fuel Economy of a Dedicated Hybrid Engine
abstract: High exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) rates in dedicated hybrid engines (DHEs) cause combustion instability and fuel economy degradation. This study investigates a 2.0L turbocharged DHE with a high-tumble combustion system optimized by computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation. At the brake thermal efficiency (BTE) operating point (2750 r/min, brake mean effective pressure [BMEP] 11 bar), engine bench tests evaluated the effects of three ignition energy levels (120 mJ, 150 mJ, 200 mJ) and two spark plug configurations (1.1 mm nickel alloy and 0.7 mm pin-to-pin iridium) on combustion characteristics, fuel economy, the misfire-limited EGR rate (hereinafter the EGR misfire limit), and engine-out emissions. Results show that above 23% EGR, intake condensate weakens ignition and destabilizes combustion. Raising ignition energy to 200 mJ extends the EGR misfire limit from 23% to 28%, shortens ignition delay (CA0-10) and combustion duration (CA10-90) by 4.5°CA and 2.8°CA and reduces BSFC by 3.2 g/kWh. The 0.7-mm iridium plug outperforms the 1.1-mm nickel alloy plug above 27% EGR: CA0-10 and CA10-90 shorten by 2.9°CA and 2.5°CA, the EGR misfire limit extends by 0.5 percentage points, and BSFC improves by 0.9 g/kWh. The combined optimization extends the EGR misfire limit to 28.5% with a cumulative BSFC reduction of 4.5 g/kWh. HC emissions decrease with reduced spark plug gap, while NOx and CO remain insensitive to the ignition strategy. The coupled optimization of high-energy ignit

title: Experimental and Machine Learning Analysis of a CI Engine Fueled with American Saffron Biodiesel–Diesel Blends
abstract: Alternative fuels come from non-traditional sources and can partly replace fossil fuels to cut environmental impact and support sustainable energy use. A single-cylinder diesel engine with rated power 5.2 Kw at 1500 rpm was tested with American Saffron Biodiesel blends. B0 (diesel), B10 (B10D90), B20 (B20D80), and B30 (B30D70), under different loads, and the results were compared with diesel. B20 showed the best improvement, with 13.41% higher brake thermal efficiency and 30.3% lower fuel usage than conventional fuel, at 100% load. B30 reduced HC by 5.88%, while B10 gave the lowest CO, reduced by 8.51%. The main contribution is the use of decision tree machine-learning regression to predict and optimize performance and emissions. The model achieved R = 0.91 and R² = 0.83, supporting the prediction of multivariable engine responses across operating conditions.

title: A Comprehensive Study of the Long-Period Cataclysmic Variable V630 Cassiopeiae
abstract: We present a comprehensive review of V630 Cassiopeiae, which is a very long-period cataclysmic variable. Based on new observations combining spectroscopy and high-resolution photometry provided by TESS and precise distance data from GAIA, we confirm and extend previously described characteristics. The light curves show differential behaviors between different epochs, attributed to changes in the disk's brightness distribution, likely due to non-axial structures such as precessing eccentric disks. The spectroscopy reveals complex Ha line profiles, with dual components and an emission distribution that suggests a large, asymmetric, and possibly precessing disk, rather than a classic shock structure in the matter-flow impact region. Doppler tomography indicates that the emission originates at the periphery of the disk, distributed in an asymmetric pattern rather than a compact point, complicating the interpretation of radial velocities and limiting their use for accurately determining masses. Through photometric and spectroscopic analysis, we established a donor mass estimate with an approximate value of 0.38 Ms at the adopted distance of 2409 pc, with significant uncertainty related to distance and other systematic factors. Finally, using the parameters of V630 Cas, binary evolution simulations were conducted with MESA incorporating CARB magnetic braking prescription to identify an evolutionary sequence that explains its properties.

title: Synergistic Regulation of Common Rail Pressure and Injection Angle on Heavy‐Duty Diesel Engine Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates a commercial heavy‐duty diesel engine equipped with a DOC + DPF + SCR + ASC aftertreatment system, which already meets China VI emission standards. Through coordinated optimization experiments of injection timing and common‐rail pressure under typical operating conditions, the comprehensive effects of injection parameters on the power performance, fuel economy, emission characteristics, and vibration levels of the engine are systematically studied. The results indicate that increasing common rail pressure enhances the power performance of heavy‐duty diesel engines: when the injection timing is maintained constant at 5°CA before top dead center (BTDC) and the rail pressure is gradually increased from 100 MPa to 130 MPa in 10 MPa increments, the engine's torque and power increase continuously with rising rail pressure, specifically increasing from 1330.5 N·m and 166.8 kW (at 100 MPa) to 1368.1 N·m and 177.0 kW (at 130 MPa), respectively. However, the influence of injection advance angle on power performance does not exhibit a monotonic positive correlation; instead, an optimal injection advance angle exists. Regarding fuel economy, increasing common rail pressure effectively reduces the engine's brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), while the injection advance angle exhibits an optimal calibration value for its impact on BSFC, and the effect of increasing common rail pressure on BSFC varies under different injection advance angles. For emissio

title: Development and experimental evaluation of common rail direct injection methanol (MD97) fuelled compression ignition engine
abstract: Methanol has emerged as a promising alternative to fossil fuels for powering internal combustion (IC) engines due to its higher fuel-to-oxygen ratio and lower tendency to form soot. Given the widespread use of compression-ignition (CI) engines in heavy-duty applications, there has been significant interest in adapting methanol for their operation. However, methanol’s inferior autoignition characteristics and longer ignition delay (ID) compared to diesel make its direct use in CI engines challenging. To overcome these limitations, engine modifications are essential to optimise the engine performance and ensure stable combustion. In this experimental study, a single-cylinder, four-stroke CI engine was modified by increasing its compression ratio (CR) and by incorporating an intake air preheating system to improve methanol ignition. The engine’s mechanical fuel injection system was replaced with a custom-built common-rail direct-injection (CRDI) system, and an in-house developed controller was utilised to inject methanol supplemented with an ignition improver (MD97: 97 % w/w methanol and 3 % w/w catalyst). The performance, combustion, and emission characteristics of MD97 were analysed and compared with baseline diesel (FIP 600 bar, SoI 14° bTDC). MD97 achieved stable ignition with a minimum ID of 7° CA, compared to the baseline diesel’s 7.5° CA. Injection timing was further optimised to achieve a balanced trade-off between the engine performance, combustion, and emission charact

title: Exploring the Benefits of Multiple Injections in a Premixed Charge Compression-Ignition Engine Operated with Modified Injector Orientation and Diesel–Gasoline Blends
abstract: The current study examines the combined effects of injection strategy, injector configuration, and fuel blending on the combustion performance and emission behavior of a light-duty compression-ignition (CI) engine operated in premixed charge compression-ignition (PCCI) combustion mode. Experiments were conducted in PCCI combustion mode using a diesel–gasoline blend (D80G20, 80% diesel and 20% gasoline by volume). A modified injector configuration, with a split-injection scheme comprising pilot and main injection events, was implemented to enhance mixture preparation and control combustion characteristics. The baseline configuration utilized PCCI mode with diesel (D100) and an inclined injector orientation. The results indicate that blending gasoline into diesel prolongs ignition delay and facilitates charge premixing, hence improving the stability of the PCCI combustion regime. Using a vertically oriented injector with a symmetric spray pattern significantly improves air–fuel mixing, and split-pulse injection enables more accurate control of combustion phasing. Among the tested strategies, the D80G20 blend, combined with a vertical injector and optimized split injection, achieved the highest brake thermal efficiency at 60% load, improving by 10.1% over the baseline case. In addition, unburned hydrocarbon (HC) and carbon monoxide (CO) emissions were significantly reduced by 54.1% and 49.4%, respectively. Additionally, the load extension was increased to 77%, which is limited t

title: Circular polarimetry of suspect wind-accreting pre-polars II
abstract: The origin of white dwarf magnetic fields is an open question. Furthermore, such fields play a vital role in the evolution of interacting binary stars. Here we present a study of white dwarf fields in so called pre-polars (or low accretion rate polars, LARPs) , i.e. magnetic cataclysmic variables (CVs), where the mass-losing secondary star is not in Roche lobe contact, but the systems experience accretion via stellar wind. Such systems play a crucial role in understanding the magnetic braking and the angular momentum evolution of close binaries. We aim to identify a set of wind-accreting pre-polars amongst our sample of nine candidate systems. We also attempt to measure the white dwarf magnetic fields and study the accretion geometry associated with wind-accreting pre-polars. We obtained optical circular imaging photopolarimetry and circular spectropolarimetry of the targets. These are used to model the cyclotron emission and to estimate the white dwarf magnetic field strengths. We find that in at least four out of our nine candidate systems, we can confirm the magnetic nature of the white dwarf. Of these, one system, ZTF J1737+4013, appears to be an eclipsing polar. Furthermore, ZTF J2220+0721 and ZTF J2353+4153 appear to be very strong candidates for wind-accreting pre-polars (or LARPs), with the fourth, ZTF J0056+4926, showing strong variable H_α emission, atypical of pre-polars. However, the emission could be related to the strong activity of the donor star dominating the

title: Experimental Investigation of Diesel Engine Characteristics Fueled with Cerium Oxide Nanoparticle-Doped Toluene-Diesel Blends
journal: International Journal of Automotive Science And Technology
abstract: Multi-component alternative fuel blends have the potential to improve diesel engine performance and combustion while reducing harmful exhaust emissions. In this study, the effects of toluene and cerium oxide (CeO2) nanoparticles added to diesel fuel on engine performance, combustion, and emissions were experimentally investigated. The experiments were conducted on a single-cylinder diesel research engine at a constant engine speed of 1800 rpm and at four different engine loads: 10.98, 16.48, 21.97, and 27.46 Nm. Commercial diesel fuel was employed as the reference fuel, whereas the alternative fuels comprised a T10D90 blend containing 10 vol. % toluene and T10D90C40, T10D90C80, and T10D90C120 blends, containing 40, 80, and 120 ppm CeO2 nanoparticles, respectively. The effects of the fuels were evaluated in terms of in-cylinder pressure, heat release rate (HRR), indicated thermal efficiency (ITE), brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), exhaust gas temperature (EGT), indicated mean effective pressure (IMEP), coefficient of variation of IMEP (COVIMEP), maximum pressure rise rate (MPRR), combustion phase (CA50), carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbon (HC), and nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions. The findings revealed that adding 10% toluene by volume to diesel fuel prolonged the ignition delay due to the low cetane number, delayed the CA50, and reduced the ITE while increasing BSFC and CO, HC, and NOx emissions. In contrast, CeO2 nanoparticles improved combustion particularly at medium a

title: Persistent carcinogenic risk from PM2.5-bound metals despite substantial concentration reductions: Evidence from a Chinese megacity during the COVID-19 lockdown
abstract: Health benefits from emission controls are often inferred from reductions in fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) mass, yet this metric can underrepresent toxicity from PM 2.5 -bound metals. Using the COVID-19 lockdown as an intervention-like natural experiment, this study quantified how PM 2.5 -bound metals, emission sources, and inhalation health risks changed in Guangzhou, China. Hourly measurements of 16 metals were coupled with positive matrix factorization and source-specific risk apportionment for pre-lockdown, lockdown, and post-lockdown periods. The lockdown controls reduced PM 2.5 mass by 28.8% and total metal concentrations by 36.3%, while total non-carcinogenic and carcinogenic risks decreased by 50.4% and 41.7%, respectively. However, carcinogenic risks during the lockdown remained approximately 9.6 times the safety criteria adopted in this study (1 × 10 -6 ) for children and 38 times for adults, driven mainly by Cr(VI) and As. Vehicle emissions remained the dominant carcinogenic-risk source, contributing more than 70% even under strict mobility restrictions, indicating a persistent role of non-exhaust brake and tire wear. Ship-related non-carcinogenic risks rebounded after the lockdown, consistent with port congestion and prolonged berthing during logistics recovery. Under the proportional-reduction assumption used in the scenario analysis, reaching the safety criteria would require further uniform reductions of 89.5–97.4% in source-attributed carcinogenic metal co

title: Experimental investigation and RSM-based optimization of combustion characteristics in an ABE-fueled HCCI engine
abstract: Homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) combustion is an advanced low-temperature combustion (LTC) strategy that combines the high thermal efficiency of compression ignition (CI) engines with the low nitrogen oxide (NOx) and soot emission advantages of spark ignition (SI) engines. However, difficulties in controlling self-ignition timing and a narrow operating range are among the main issues that limit the practical application of HCCI engines. In this study, the effects of n-heptane and acetone-butanol-ethanol (ABE) blends on the combustion, performance, and emission characteristics of an HCCI engine were investigated both experimentally and statistically. In the experiments, ABE mixtures at 20%, 40%, and 60% ratios were added to n-heptane fuel, and engine tests were conducted at engine speeds ranging from 800 to 1200 rpm and lambda values ranging from 2.5 to 3.5. In the experimental design and analysis processes, response surface methodology (RSM) based on the central composite design (CCD) was employed, and a total of 15 experimental combinations were conducted. The variable response parameters evaluated were engine torque, brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), exhaust temperature, maximum pressure rise rate (MPRR), start of combustion (CA10), combustion phase (CA50), combustion duration (CD), indicated thermal efficiency (ITE), as well as carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrocarbon (HC) emissions. As a result of RSM optimization, the optimal operating conditions were de

title: Enabling High-Efficiency Spark-Ignited Natural Gas Engines via Variable Valve Actuation and In-Cylinder Sensing
abstract: Stringent greenhouse gas and criteria pollutant regulations for medium- and heavy-duty vehicles have accelerated the adoption of cleaner engine technologies. While zero-emission solutions are growing, the widespread deployment of internal combustion engines powered by alternative fuels remains essential in the near term. Among these, natural gas spark-ignition (SI) engines have gained prominence due to their lower CO₂ and NOₓ emissions compared to diesel, as well as the economic and supply chain advantages of widely available natural gas infrastructure.Despite these advantages, natural gas engines face several technical challenges that hinder further efficiency gains and emissions reduction. While stoichiometric operation is preferred over lean-burn strategies due to its compatibility with cost-effective three-way catalysts, it introduces significant throttling losses during part-load operation, reducing overall efficiency. Moreover, during rapid transients, maintaining precise lambda control becomes difficult due to the limited observability of key in-cylinder states such as trapped mass and residual gas fraction, increasing the risk of high emissions. These challenges underscore the need to explore technologies that can mitigate efficiency losses and enable more effective control across a wide range of operating conditions.In this study, variable valve actuation (VVA) is investigated as a technology to improve efficiency and emissions performance in stoichiometric natural g

title: Fluid-Thermal Analysis of the Impact of 2026 vs 2025 Formula 1 Technical Regulations on Sustainability
journal: Edunity Kajian Ilmu Sosial dan Pendidikan
abstract: This study aims to analyze the comparative impact of the 2025 and 2026 Formula 1 technical regulations on aerodynamic performance, drag force, power unit efficiency, and their correlation to reducing fuel consumption and CO2 emissions. The research method employed is library research conducted through six systematic stages, utilizing descriptive quantitative analysis with data sourced from official FIA regulations, scientific journals, and technical F1 articles.The findings indicate that the complete transition to e-fuels and the restriction of fuel energy flow directly result in a reduction of the internal combustion engine's (ICE) raw power. To compensate for this power loss, the 2026 F1 chassis is designed to be sleeker to slash the drag coefficient (Cd), supported by active aerodynamics systems (Mode X and Mode Z) to dynamically minimize drag force on straightaways. However, in the electrical sector, the surge in MGU-K power to 350 kW following the removal of the MGU-H triggers extremely high thermal loads on the energy store (ES) and electric motors. To maintain high brake thermal efficiency (BTE), these new regulations necessitate the integration of more complex liquid cooling systems and ERS thermal management.Overall, the success of the 2026 F1 regulations in achieving net-zero carbon targets relies not only on the adoption of environmentally friendly fuels but also on the absolute synergy between active fluid drag reduction and thermal mitigation to consistently prev

title: Study of performance and combustion in ammonia-fueled CI engines via diesel simultaneous injection
abstract: Abstract Ammonia is a promising carbon-free hydrogen carrier with wide industrial availability; however, its low flame speed, high latent heat, and narrow flammability characteristics create significant challenges for compression ignition engines. This study investigates ammonia/diesel dual-fuel operation at 50% and 80% load conditions, with diesel injection pressure varied from 200 to 340 bar and ammonia energy share (AES) ranging from 0 to 40%, to evaluate the sustainability of ammonia utilization in light-duty engines. Experimental results showed that increasing injection pressure enhanced cylinder pressure by nearly 10% at lower AES conditions and advanced peak pressure occurrence, partially compensating for ammonia’s slower combustion behaviour. Heat release rate (HRR), delayed by nearly 5–9°CA with increasing AES, improved considerably at higher injection pressures, with combustion shifting toward the controlled combustion phase. Ignition delay increased with AES, reaching nearly 4.5°CA at 40% AES and 200 bar, but reduced to 2.78°CA at 320 bar due to improved atomization and ignition support. Cycle-to-cycle variations quantified using CoV imep increased with ammonia substitution because of prolonged combustion duration, whereas optimized injection pressure reduced cyclic fluctuations by nearly 27%; however, beyond 300 bar at 40% AES, combustion stability improvement became marginal. Brake-specific fuel consumption increased by nearly 48% at high AES because of ammonia’s

title: Which Roads Should Cities Control First? A Health-Risk Framework for Mobile-Source Air Pollution
abstract: U rban air-quality management has become increasingly effective in determining whether pollutant concentrations comply with regulatory standards and quantifying transport emissions.However, it remains less suited to answering a practical management question: which road should be controlled first to achieve the greatest health benefit?This mismatch matters because many mobile-source interventions, including freight restrictions, truck routing optimization, traffic-signal improvements, school-hour traffic controls, and local exposure mitigation, are implemented at road links, intersections, freight corridors, and neighborhood streets rather than at citywide averages.As mobile-source pollution remains a central challenge in urban environmental management, the missing operational unit is therefore not another pollutant metric, but the road segment itself.Roads should be considered not only as line sources in emission and dispersion models but also as health-risk units for management decisions.This approach does not replace ambient air-quality standards, emission inventories, or regional transport models.Instead, it adds a decision layer that connects where pollution is generated, where people are exposed, and where interventions can realistically be implemented.Such a framework is increasingly needed because long-term exposure to traffic-related air pollution is consistently associated with adverse health outcomes and mortality, while pollutant concentrations and population expos

title: Reduced graphene oxide nanoparticles and integrated DOC + SCR aftertreatment in a diesel engine fueled with sunflower biodiesel-n-butanol ternary blends: Combustion, performance, and aftertreatment response
abstract: Reducing gaseous emissions from compression ignition engines while maintaining engine efficiency remains a key challenge for biodiesel-alcohol fuel strategies, particularly when fuel modification and exhaust aftertreatment are considered together. This study experimentally investigated the effects of reduced graphene oxide (rGO) nanoparticles (30, 60, and 90 ppm by mass) added to a ternary B30D60BUT10 fuel, consisting of 30 vol% sunflower oil methyl ester, 60 vol% diesel, and 10 vol% n-butanol, in a single-cylinder direct-injection diesel engine equipped with an integrated diesel oxidation catalyst and selective catalytic reduction (DOC+SCR) system. Experiments were conducted at 1800 rpm under four steady-state loads (8.24–24.72 Nm), using D100 and B30D70 as reference fuels. Combustion was evaluated from 50 consecutive pressure cycles, while gaseous emissions were measured upstream (P 1 ) and downstream (P 3 ) of the aftertreatment system. The results demonstrate a strongly load- and concentration-dependent rGO response. At 19.22 Nm, the 90-ppm formulation achieved the highest brake thermal efficiency of the complete test matrix (34.81%), exceeding D100 by 3.22 percentage points, while at 24.72 Nm, the unmodified B30D60BUT10 blend provided the highest BTE (32.66%). At 24.72 Nm, 90 ppm rGO also produced the highest mean IMEP (6.378 bar) and the lowest COV-IMEP (2.10%), with an IMEP standard deviation of 0.130 bar, 22.2% lower than D100. title: Predicting Car Acceleration From Vehicle Specifications Using Machine Learning
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Acceleration from 0 to 100 km/h is one of the most widely quoted indicators for vehicle performance, yet it is the outcome of a large number of interacting design decisions, planning from power train, the drivetrain, the body and chassis. Most machine learning work on vehicle behavior has concentrated fuel consumption, emissions, or electric range, and has typically been trained on small instrument fleets under controlled or gnarly defined operating conditions. The study takes a different approach. Using a catalogue data set of course specifications covering models from years 1945 to 2020, they develop variables or partitioned into functional groups, being engine, configuration, engine, performance, dimensions, weight, draft drive, train transmission, chassis, suspension and brakes, fuel consumption, body capacity, production, news, and vehicle identification and each group trained separately with acceleration as a target. The algorithm using parameters isolates information content of each group. A random forest regressor trained on performance features alone achieves the best single group result with a mean absolute error of 0.67 seconds. Engine configuration coming second reached a mean absolute error of 0.989 seconds while groups describing only the structural envelope of the vehicle fell between 1.37 and 1.552 seconds. title: Prompt and Afterglow Constraints on the Central Engine of GRB 240825A
abstract: Abstract GRB 240825A shows unprecedented temporal and spectral features that constrain the properties of its inner engine: (1) a prompt emission three-component spectrum consisting of a Band function continuum, a quasi-thermal bump, and a hard MeV tail; and (2) an X-ray afterglow fitted by a power-law decay with index 1.29 ± 0.02; and (3) a 6.37 ± 0.05 Hz quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) identified in the 100–300 keV band during the 2.07–3.25 s time interval, coinciding with the photospheric radiation phase. We compare two central-engine candidates: (a) a newborn millisecond magnetar undergoing multipolar spin-down, free precession, and global magnetoelastic oscillations of its interior; and (b) a Kerr black hole powering a Blandford–Znajek jet subject to Lense–Thirring disk precession. In principle, both channels can reproduce the observed QPO frequency but impose different constraints on the energetics, temporal evolution, and the origin of the oscillation. We first demonstrate that the X-ray afterglow is quantitatively reproduced by a hexapolar magnetar spin-down model with an initial spin period of P 0 ≃ 1.38 ms and a surface field of B hexa ≃ 2.04 × 10 16 G. The decay index measures a braking index rather than the field multipolarity, does not exclude a fallback-regulated flow, and leaves P 0 and B hexa uncertain by a factor of a few. title: Adaptive Neural Network Fuel Mass Correction for Structural Model Error Compensation in Diesel Engines with Variable Biodiesel Properties
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: Compression-ignition engines operating with biodiesel blends often exhibit variability in fuel properties, such as density, viscosity, and cetane number, which can lead to systematic deviations in injected fuel mass when using conventional physics-based models. These deviations can reduce combustion efficiency and increase brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC). This study proposes a lightweight neural network–based approach to compensate for structural errors in baseline injection models, using a single-layer perceptron trained on the relative error (delta) between actual and modeled injected mass. By normalizing engine and fuel parameters and introducing a small amount of measurement noise, the network learns to predict a corrective factor that adapts the injected mass to match the desired target under varying fuel conditions. Simulation results demonstrate that the neural correction significantly reduces systematic bias: in test cases with intentionally introduced structural error, the average injection deviation of −1.7% in the baseline model is reduced to approximately 0.002% after correction. Root-mean-square (RMS) error over training and validation datasets remains below 0.16%, indicating robust generalization. The proposed method offers a computationally efficient solution suitable for embedded engine control units, requiring minimal additional complexity while ensuring precise fuel delivery.
